item.title: Kuwait sentences 3 to death over plot to kill first deputy PM
item.description: A Kuwaiti court has sentenced three men to death over a plot to assassinate the country’s first deputy prime minister, in a case involving spying for Iran.
item.content:encoded:
A court in Kuwait has sentenced three men to death over an alleged plot to assassinate the country’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad al-Yusuf al-Sabbah, in a case involving charges of spying for Iran, joining Hezbollah and planning hostile acts against the state.

The Criminal Court’s State Security and Terrorism Division issued the sentences on Monday, while eight other defendants received prison terms.

Kuwaiti media reported that the eight were sentenced to five years in prison each. The verdicts are not final and can be appealed, according to Kuwait Times newspaper.

The three men sentenced to death were identified as Shia cleric Hussein Abdullah al-Maatouq, secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Hassan Abdulhadi Hajieh and Iranian national Abdulreza Haidar Dehqani, according to local media reports.

The defendants were convicted of charges including alleged harming of Kuwait’s national interests, collaborating with Iran, plotting to assassinate senior officials and joining the Lebanese Shia militant group Hezbollah, which Kuwait classifies as a terrorist organisation.

According to two judicial sources cited by AFP, one of the men sentenced to death had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received an amnesty from the emir before being arrested again in April.

The prosecution said the case involved 11 defendants, including nine Kuwaitis, an Iranian national and another non-Kuwaiti. Three of the defendants were outside the country. It also said that three defendants had previously received final criminal sentences in state security cases in 2015 and 2017.

According to Kuwait’s Al-Qabas newspaper, prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination plot. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.

In its reasoning, the court said the defendants had sought to undermine Kuwait’s security, spread social unrest and erode public confidence in the authorities’ ability to protect lives and property.

Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai reported that the indictment accused the defendants of seeking assistance from and communicating with Iran and groups acting in its interests, including Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on 28 February, at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The indictment also accused the defendants of joining and participating in a banned organisation, knowingly supporting its objectives and spreading ideas intended to undermine the country’s fundamental political and social systems through unlawful means.

Prosecutors further alleged that the defendants had engaged in activities harmful to Kuwait’s national interests, including attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination and cause public panic. One defendant was accused of attempting to procure explosives to enable the others to commit the alleged crimes.

The court’s ruling is subject to appeal.

In March, Kuwait announced the arrest of dozens of people it said were linked to Hezbollah and plotting attacks in the Gulf state, which was repeatedly targeted by Iranian missiles and drones after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a regional war.

Hezbollah, engaged in conflict with Israel for more than three years, has denied it has a presence in Kuwait.

item.title: Syria closes Jordan border after strikes kill seven civilians
item.description: Jordanian strikes in retaliation for a deadly church attack kill seven Syrian civilians, triggering a diplomatic crisis and border closure.
item.content:encoded:
A major diplomatic dispute has erupted between Syria and Jordan after Jordanian airstrikes, launched in retaliation for a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church, killed seven Syrian civilians, including three children, and prompted Damascus to close its main border crossing with the kingdom.

The Syrian government condemned Monday's bombardment of southern Syria as a violation of its sovereignty, accusing Jordan of carrying out the operation without prior coordination and demanding an explanation for the strikes.

Jordan launched the attacks in response to Friday's killing of nine people at a church funeral in the village of Hamoud, in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak, claiming that the perpetrators were linked to militant organisations operating across the border in Syria.

However, Syrian authorities said the airstrikes hit civilian areas in Daraa and Suweida provinces, killing five members of one family and two elderly men.

Syrian Civil Defence said rescue teams responded to four locations targeted by Jordanian warplanes, recovering the bodies of seven people, including three children, three men and a woman.

Five members of one family were killed and three others injured when a strike hit a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of rural Daraa.

An 80-year-old man was also killed when Jordanian aircraft struck a farm near the Nasib border crossing, while a 60-year-old man died after a house was bombed in the countryside of Suweida.

Jordan acknowledged the civilian deaths on Tuesday and expressed regret, but insisted its operation had targeted Islamic State militants connected to the church attack.

Jordanian government spokesman Mohammed al-Momani said Amman respected Syria's sovereignty and remained committed to cooperation with Damascus against terrorism and cross-border arms and drug smuggling.

Jordan claimed that its aircraft had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants and destroyed a large weapons depot during the operation, which its military named "Jordanian Deterrence – Hamoud".

The Syrian Foreign Ministry said it had formally conveyed its objections to Amman, stressing that military operations inside Syrian territory without prior coordination were unacceptable.

It added that communication between the two countries was continuing to establish the circumstances of the operation and address its consequences.

The dispute deepened on Tuesday when Syria's General Authority for Ports and Customs announced the closure of the Nasib border crossing, suspending passenger movements and commercial trade in both directions.

The crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, is a vital commercial artery linking the two countries and facilitating trade between Syria, Jordan and the wider Gulf region.

Syrian authorities said the closure was necessary to protect travellers and border personnel amid the security situation in Daraa, without specifying when operations would resume.

The Jordanian strikes followed Friday's attack on mourners attending a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, which left nine people dead and 34 wounded.

Jordanian security forces subsequently arrested three suspects, identified as two brothers and their brother-in-law, following an extensive manhunt.

Public Security Director Obeidallah al-Maaytah described the men as extremists who had adopted takfiri ideology, but said they had decided to carry out the attack spontaneously, without advance planning.

Jordanian authorities also indicated that the suspects did not belong to an organised militant group.

However, the Jordanian military subsequently asserted that the attackers were connected to the organisations targeted in southern Syria, without publicly identifying those groups or presenting evidence establishing their involvement.

The apparently conflicting accounts have raised questions about the justification for the cross-border military operation, particularly given the civilian casualties reported by Syrian authorities.

The bombardment and subsequent border closure mark a significant setback in relations between Damascus and Amman, which had sought closer security and economic cooperation following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

Despite their disagreement over the operation, both governments have indicated that diplomatic and security contacts will continue in an effort to prevent further deterioration in relations.

item.title: Turkey pushes to reunify Libya as rival factions hold talks
item.description: Turkey is pushing to reunify Libya's rival administrations, but talks in Ankara have stalled over military leadership and political authority.
item.content:encoded:
Turkey has intensified diplomatic efforts to reunify Libya's rival eastern and western administrations, hosting negotiations aimed at establishing a unified military command and government capable of managing the country's vast natural resources.

The latest talks, held in Ankara on Friday and Saturday, ended without a final agreement, as disagreements persisted over the structure of the military leadership and its relationship with civilian political authorities, Libyan sources familiar with the discussions told The New Arab.

Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based military leadership, and Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, undersecretary at the defence ministry of the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, arrived in Ankara on Friday evening for Turkish-sponsored negotiations.

The discussions centred on a draft agreement to unify Libya's institutions, although the two sides remained divided over whether the deal should focus exclusively on military and technical arrangements or extend to senior political positions, including the Presidential Council.

Sources said the negotiations produced broad understandings on the structure of a unified military institution, but no decisive breakthrough.

Both delegations agreed to consult their respective leaderships in Tripoli and Benghazi before resuming negotiations, although no date has been set for further talks.

The initiative comes as Ankara seeks to consolidate its influence across Libya, strengthen its position in the eastern Mediterranean and secure the future of a controversial maritime boundary agreement signed with Tripoli in 2019.

The agreement has faced opposition from Greece, Egypt and other regional actors over competing maritime claims.

The Benghazi-based House of Representatives' approval of the maritime agreement has been viewed as an important step in Turkey's efforts to build closer relations with eastern Libya, after years of maintaining stronger ties with the Tripoli authorities.

Erdogan calls for Libyan unity

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reiterated Ankara's opposition to Libya's continued division on Monday, saying his government wanted to see unity and solidarity across the country.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting, Erdogan said Turkey was working to reduce regional disputes and expand cooperation.

He also defended the 2019 maritime agreement, rejecting suggestions that Ankara was seeking to undermine other countries' interests in the eastern Mediterranean.

"Our policy towards the eastern Mediterranean is completely clear. We are not seeking to score goals against any party in the eastern Mediterranean," Erdogan said.

He maintained that Turkey was seeking to protect its maritime jurisdiction, rights and interests while advocating dialogue to resolve disputes.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also acknowledged Egyptian reservations about the maritime agreement last Friday, calling for dialogue to address Cairo's concerns.

Turkey's renewed engagement with both Libyan camps comes as the country's oil resources attract growing international attention, particularly as the war involving Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices.

A unified Libyan government could help stabilise oil production and exports to European markets, although significant political and security obstacles remain.

Ankara also hopes to expand commercial and investment opportunities, particularly in construction and infrastructure, sectors in which Turkish companies have historically maintained a substantial presence in Libya.

Military leadership remains major obstacle

Turkish researcher and writer Cahit Tuz told The New Arab that Ankara viewed Libya as a single state and opposed its permanent division.

He said Turkey's priorities included preserving Libya's territorial integrity, establishing a single administration and ensuring that the country's natural resources benefited its population.

Tuz argued that Turkey's diplomatic efforts had already produced tangible results, pointing to the eastern parliament's approval of the maritime agreement as evidence of improving relations.

He also claimed that some regional and international actors, including Israel, were uncomfortable with Turkey's expanding influence in Libya.

Journalist and political commentator Hamza Tekin told The New Arab that Ankara's approach had evolved from working primarily with one Libyan faction to establishing direct relationships with influential political and military figures on both sides.

He said this shift had helped Turkey reopen channels of dialogue between Tripoli and Benghazi.

"Turkey's efforts in Libya stem from a fundamental conviction that the continuation of political and institutional division does not serve Libyans," Tekin said.

He argued that Ankara was seeking to create the conditions for a unified Libyan state rather than merely bringing rival factions together for negotiations.

However, he warned that the central challenge was translating broad agreement on reunification into workable arrangements.

"The real test begins when determining who will assume military command, how responsibilities will be distributed, which political authority the institutions will answer to, and how to ensure that no single party monopolises power," he said.

Tekin stressed that any lasting agreement would depend on the willingness of Libyan factions to compromise and avoid turning institutional reunification into another arrangement for dividing political influence.

He said Turkey's expanding contacts with both camps offered an opportunity for progress, but cautioned that a sustainable settlement must reflect the will of Libyans rather than an externally imposed agreement.

Libya has remained politically divided for years, with rival authorities and competing military structures obstructing efforts to establish a unified government.

item.title: Israel destroys West Bank memorials in war on Palestinian memory
item.description: Israeli forces have destroyed dozens of Palestinian memorials across the West Bank, prompting warnings of a campaign to erase Palestinian national memory.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli forces demolished around nine memorials commemorating Palestinians killed by Israel across six towns and villages near Nablus in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, as part of a widening campaign targeting Palestinian national symbols and public spaces.

The demolitions took place in Madama, Burin, Iraq Burin, Beit Furik, Rujeib and Azmut, where Israeli forces destroyed stone monuments, memorial plaques and structures bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces.

The latest raids follow days of similar operations across the occupied territory, during which dozens of memorials have been destroyed in Palestinian cities, villages and refugee camps.

Palestinian academics and analysts told The New Arab that the campaign represented an attempt to reshape public spaces in the West Bank by removing symbols of Palestinian identity, resistance and collective memory.

The operations come as Israeli forces and settlers continue attacks on Palestinian communities, including the destruction of agricultural land, attacks on olive harvesters, livestock theft and restrictions on movement through military checkpoints and gates.

Beyond these attacks, Palestinians say Israel is increasingly targeting the physical symbols through which communities commemorate those killed during decades of occupation.

Across the West Bank, memorials bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces have long been a feature of streets, public squares, refugee camps and university campuses.

Many have stood for decades, serving as reminders of individuals whose deaths remain part of local and national history.

Their destruction has coincided with the growing visibility of Israeli flags and Hebrew-language signs along roads connecting Palestinian towns and cities, particularly near Israeli settlements.

Settlers have also written threatening messages on concrete barriers at military checkpoints, including the Arabic phrase "No future in Palestine".

Israeli forces target memorials in Palestinian cities

On 5 October, Israeli forces raided Birzeit University near Ramallah and destroyed a memorial commemorating Palestinians killed by Israel, leaving no trace of the structure.

Similar operations have taken place in central Nablus, its historic neighbourhoods and Jenin, where Israeli troops deployed military vehicles and bulldozers to demolish stone monuments bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians.

Memorials have also been targeted in Ramallah and Tulkarm, including areas classified as Area A under the Oslo Accords, where the Palestinian Authority was granted responsibility for internal security and civil administration.

Israeli forces have distributed leaflets warning Palestinians against erecting or maintaining monuments commemorating people Israel accuses of carrying out attacks.

Israeli authorities have justified the removal of memorials on the grounds that they allegedly glorify "terrorism".

However, Palestinian academics argue that the campaign goes beyond individual monuments and forms part of a broader effort to suppress expressions of Palestinian national identity.

'A war on memory'

Abduljawad Omar, a writer and assistant professor at Birzeit University, told The New Arab that the demolitions served two purposes.

The first, he said, was to reinforce the visible presence of Israeli military forces in Palestinian communities and deter political and social mobilisation.

The second was a direct attack on Palestinian collective memory.

Omar drew parallels with Israel's destruction of Palestinian homes and neighbourhoods in Gaza, arguing that the loss of buildings and personal possessions also erased physical records of Palestinian lives and history.

He said the campaign in the West Bank had taken two forms: the proliferation of Israeli flags and symbols asserting control over the territory, and the removal of Palestinian flags, monuments and other expressions of remembrance.

According to Omar, Israel was using legal and political language centred on incitement to justify targeting memorials and other social practices associated with Palestinian identity.

He argued that the occupation itself, rather than the commemoration of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces, remained the principal source of resistance.

'A war on Palestinian consciousness'

Adel Shadid, an analyst specialising in Israeli affairs, told The New Arab that Israel viewed the commemoration of Palestinians killed during the occupation as a means through which resistance remained embedded in collective memory.

He argued that memorials gave those commemorated a lasting social, religious and moral significance, allowing their stories to influence subsequent generations.

Shadid said Israeli authorities were attempting to undermine the cultural and political significance of Palestinian resistance by removing the symbols associated with it.

The campaign, he argued, reflected a wider effort to reshape Palestinian political consciousness through military pressure, educational changes and restrictions on public commemoration.

He also questioned the continued relevance of the territorial divisions established under the Oslo Accords, pointing to Israeli military operations in areas nominally under Palestinian Authority control.

According to Shadid, Israeli forces now operate across virtually the entire West Bank, with Palestinian Authority security headquarters among the few places generally treated differently.

He argued that the demolitions demonstrated the extent to which Israel was prepared to deploy military resources against even small monuments made of stone or marble.

"Israel is forced to bring out its tanks, not to confront another tank, but to confront a memorial made of a piece of marble or stone bearing their name and photograph," Shadid told The New Arab.

item.title: UK charges two men on suspected Iran links in RAF Fairford plot
item.description: Two British men have been charged under national security laws following an incident at an airbase used by US bombers to strike Iran.
item.content:encoded:
British prosecutors charged two men on Tuesday under the National Security Act over an incident involving RAF Fairford, a military airbase in southwest England previously used by US bombers to launch strikes against Iran.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from London, had been charged with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from London, was separately charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom on 22 August.

Both men were due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators believed the foreign country Abdulkarim was suspected of assisting was Iran.

The charges follow a major security operation at RAF Fairford on 27 September, when police arrested five British men outside the base in the early hours.

The facility had been used by US strategic bombers to conduct strikes against Iran during the war, although the aircraft were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after the arrests.

British authorities also evacuated residents living near the airbase as police and military bomb disposal specialists examined three lorries suspected of containing explosives.

The vehicles were subsequently found to contain no explosives.

The investigation has continued for several weeks, with authorities examining suspected threats to the military facility and possible links to foreign intelligence activity.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham had previously said there were strong indications of Iranian involvement in the Fairford incident.

Six others remain under investigation

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said the decision to bring charges followed an investigation by counterterrorism police into a significant incident involving the RAF base.

He said prosecutors would continue working closely with investigators on what he described as a complex and ongoing inquiry.

Six other men arrested in connection with the investigation have been released on bail and remain under investigation.

Counterterrorism police confirmed on Tuesday that a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national was among those released on bail without charge.

The CPS stressed that the decision to prosecute did not establish or imply guilt and that the charges would be determined through the criminal justice process.

Prosecutors said their role was to assess independently and objectively whether there was sufficient evidence to bring the case before a court.

RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, has served as an important operating location for US military aircraft, including strategic bombers deployed during the US-Israel war on Iran.

The United States had previously announced the withdrawal of its strategic bombers from the facility, with security concerns surrounding the base drawing increased attention following the September incident.

The investigation has also added to tensions between London and Tehran, with Iran previously summoning the British ambassador over allegations relating to the Fairford case.

The two defendants face separate charges under the UK's National Security Act 2023, legislation introduced to address threats including foreign intelligence activity and conduct considered harmful to national security.

item.title: Qatar emir meets Iran president in Moscow amid mediation efforts
item.description: Qatar's emir and Iran's president discussed regional tensions, negotiations and the Strait of Hormuz amid diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed conflict.
item.content:encoded:
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday to discuss regional tensions, ongoing negotiations and the Strait of Hormuz, as Doha reaffirmed its commitment to preventing renewed conflict in the region.

The meeting took place at the emir's residence in the Russian capital ahead of the eighth summit of heads of state and government of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), according to Qatar's Amiri Diwan.

The two leaders discussed regional developments, the latest progress in negotiations, maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and energy supplies, alongside issues on the summit's agenda.

The talks came as Qatar's foreign ministry said mediation efforts aimed at halting regional tensions and securing a lasting agreement were continuing in coordination with Pakistan and other regional and international partners.

Ibrahim al-Hashimi, director of the ministry's Media and Communication Department, told a weekly press briefing in Doha on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts were moving in a positive direction.

He said the mediation was being conducted in coordination with Pakistan and other partners, with the aim of reaching a sustainable agreement that would bring the regional crisis to a definitive end.

Al-Hashimi also confirmed that a recent Qatari delegation's visit to Tehran formed part of ongoing consultations and mediation efforts.

The visit involved exchanges of messages, proposals and views aimed at resolving the crisis, he said, stressing that contacts through mediators and with the parties to the conflict had continued without interruption.

Qatar calls for reopening of Strait of Hormuz

Al-Hashimi said efforts by the countries involved in the Mecca Pact complemented the mediation led by Qatar and Pakistan, with diplomatic contacts focused on encouraging dialogue and preventing a resumption of hostilities.

He reiterated Doha's position that the region needed a collective security framework based on respect for state sovereignty and non-aggression.

Qatar and other Gulf Cooperation Council states were prepared to begin work towards establishing such a framework, he added.

The spokesman said Doha had heard positive statements from Iran regarding regional security but stressed that these needed to be translated into practical measures demonstrating goodwill and a commitment to stability.

He called on Tehran to stop threatening countries in the region and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic, describing the restoration of navigation as an important part of efforts to resolve the crisis.

His remarks followed a meeting in Tehran on Monday between senior Iranian officials and representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey under the framework of the Mecca Pact.

A joint statement issued after the meeting said the four countries had agreed to continue dialogue and consultations to strengthen cooperation, particularly in regional peace and security.

The meeting was hosted by Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.

The participants agreed to maintain consultations aimed at promoting stability and cooperation across the region.

Energy cooperation on Moscow agenda

Meanwhile, Iranian news agencies Tasnim and IRNA reported that Pezeshkian and Sheikh Tamim had discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and expand political and economic cooperation.

The leaders reviewed developments in relations between Tehran and Doha and emphasised the importance of making greater use of both countries' economic capabilities to deepen their partnership.

Energy cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, alongside trade and investment and coordination between gas-exporting countries.

The Iranian agencies did not provide further details about any agreements reached during the meeting.

Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani attended the talks, alongside Amiri Diwan chief Abdullah bin Mohammed Al Khulaifi and other members of the Qatari delegation.

Iran was represented by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei and other senior officials.

Sheikh Tamim arrived in Moscow on Monday for the gas exporters' summit, where he was received at Vnukovo International Airport by Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov and Qatar's ambassador to Russia, Sheikh Ahmed bin Nasser bin Jassim Al Thani.

The summit brings together leaders of major gas-exporting countries at a time when regional tensions and disruptions to maritime trade have placed energy supplies and transport routes at the centre of diplomatic discussions.

Separately, al-Hashimi reiterated Qatar's support for dialogue between rival parties in Libya, calling for a political settlement based on relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and other UN decisions.

item.title: What Lula’s victory means for Palestine solidarity in Brazil
item.description: Lula’s return to power offers Brazil's Palestine solidarity movement new opportunities to challenge the country's ties with Israel, writes Rula Shadeed.
item.content:encoded:
Over the weekend, Brazilians elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva president once more by a very narrow margin, defying polls that had him trailing. No candidate had won a Brazilian runoff from second place since 1989. That precedent is broken, and it was broken from below: by student-led rallies in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Porto Alegre.

The rallies were called without Lula, by pop-star fan communities and influencers who injected energy into a campaign that had flagged all year, and by widespread mass communications like Deputy André Janones's WhatsApp channel, which passed 10 million followers. Many of those young figures have been vocal on Palestine. Their job now is to make sure their government hears them.

That mobilisation will matter all the more given the political landscape Lula faces. The Congress that convenes on 1 February will comprise 594 members, 513 deputies and 81 senators, with the right and its allies holding a comfortable majority in both houses. With 90 members close to the Palestinian struggle, the challenge will be to turn that support, alongside pressure from civil society, into concrete political action.

Palestine

Lula's words have been strong in recent years. He recognised the State of Palestine in 2010, the first in South America to do so, condemned the genocide in Gaza as early as October 2023, and did not back down when the Israeli colonial regime declared him persona non grata over his Holocaust comparison.

Brazil joined South Africa's case at the International Court of Justice and has had no ambassador in Tel Aviv since May 2024. His actions, however, were fewer. Diplomatic and trade relations with Israel were never fully cut. The Army’s planned purchase of 36 armoured howitzers from Elbit Systems was stalled in 2024 amid political opposition over military ties with Israel. The deal resurfaced in October 2026 after Brazilian defence company Avibras, reached an agreement with Elbit’s Brazilian subsidiary, AEL Sistemas, paving the way for local assembly.

The proposed purchase, worth almost $200 million, remained controversial after renewed public backlash, and the army subsequently cancelled the planned signing of the initial contract for two units. However, the wider procurement was not cancelled.

Lula has always been a conciliator. But a fourth and last term with popular backing opens room for much bolder steps, including ending trade relations with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, withdrawing from the Mercosur–Israel Free Trade Agreement, imposing a total embargo on weapons and technology transfers with the Zionist regime, and investigating and halting any indirect exports of Brazilian oil through third-country intermediaries.

The recognition of Palestine itself came at the end of his second term, and was then seen as his last.

For Palestinian solidarity movements, Lula’s victory above all means keeping the conditions they work under today, which are far more favourable than those a Flávio government would offer. The government remains open to dialogue with civil society, its own rhetoric lends legitimacy to the cause, and the state does not throw its weight behind the campaign against it.

Holding the line

Lula's government is not immune to Zionist lobbies, however. They continue to influence leaders close to the president and elected officials within his Workers' Party (PT) and Congress, where it needs centrist allies.

Even under Lula, part of the work will be to contest the government itself.

The institutional climate will remain turbulent. The reaction from Bolsonaro's supporters, especially if backed by Trump, is a challenge the PT anticipates. But the balance has shifted. Flávio will lose the privileged forum his Senate seat gives him, and with investigations advancing, he could face arrest.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, second in the family's line of command, is a fugitive in the United States after a Supreme Court justice issued an arrest warrant and cancelled his passports. He was sentenced to four years and two months for coercing the judicial process through lobbying Washington for sanctions against Brazilian magistrates.

From Florida, he has advised his brother to flee if defeated and joked about US Marines intervening. The family cannot hold political capital while their assets disperse.

Lula's path is to strengthen republican institutions – the Supreme Court included –, but he would be boxed in by a Senate taken over by the Bolsonarista party, which confirms justices and can impeach them.

Sustained public mobilisation in the streets and online could also help expose the networks of corruption and patronage that sustain the far-right’s power in Congress. Investigations into Banco Master and parliamentary budget amendments could weaken some of these networks and make it harder for politicians to convert economic power into political influence.

For the Palestinian movement, this matters. Challenging the interests that protect Zionist politicians is part of building a Congress more accountable to the public and less willing to enable complicity in the occupation.

Brazil’s importance in the region and to the cause is based on many factors; Brazil holds a third of Latin America's population and GDP, its main instrument abroad has never been economic or military might but diplomacy, and the country has built its influence on multilateralism, mediation and coalitions such as the BRICS. Gains made in Brazil tend to spread, as the wave of recognition of Palestine that followed 2010 showed.

In the region, Brazil is now an exception. Seven South American governments are aligned with Donald Trump, and Brazil is the largest country still holding out. Israel and the United States – as governments but also through Big Tech companies like META - invested here for years to change that. They have failed, for now.

Ultimately, a generation of young political figures carried this campaign, vocal on Palestine and with a strong presence online. In a contest increasingly fought on social media, a terrain the right had long dominated, the left has begun to close the gap. The platforms themselves are part of that dispute, and Meta's seeming interference in the campaign has become a matter of national and international debate.

The dispute over Brazil's public digital payment system (PIX) has also exposed US interest in challenging a model that threatens the dominance of American payment companies.

Furthermore, Brazil has a vibrant independent press that is often more receptive to the Palestinian cause. The country’s media landscape also includes major broadcasters such as TV Globo (formerly Rede Globo), Brazil’s largest television network and one of the country’s most influential media organisations. Its televised political debates attract large audiences and shape public discussion, with their coverage and political implications often resonating beyond Brazil’s borders.

Internationally, Lula's surprising victory and popular mobilisation must inspire and trickle to other countries where people are protesting in their masses against growing authoritarianism, fascism and neoliberal economic policies - all aligned with the Zionist regime - in France, India, Spain, and Serbia.

The pendulum is likely to swing in Brazil by 2030, and the next four years must be used to build irreversible actions toward liberation.

Rula Shadeed is the Co-Director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy.

Follow Rula on Instagram: @pipdbrasil and X: @rabetbypipd

item.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
item.description: "The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Saree posted.
item.content:encoded:
Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile on Tuesday, as blasts shook the capital of the world's top crude exporter.

Saudi Arabia, the Middle East's largest economy, has suffered weeks of strikes from the Iran-backed Houthis against oil and civilian sites including Riyadh's international airport.

"The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused "massive fires".

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis earlier said it had shot down three missiles fired by the group towards the Eastern Province.

A resident in the city of Al Khobar, south of the Ras Tanura complex, told AFP he heard explosions around dawn and received a text message alert.

"We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang," the resident said.

Maritime security agency Vanguard said a fire was reported in the Ras Tanura area in the early hours of Tuesday after an attack.

"The fire has reportedly been contained, while the extent of damage and any impact on oil-loading operations remain unclear at current," Vanguard said.

The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and a cornerstone of the kingdom's energy sector.

The complex has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by strikes blamed on Iran, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.

Meanwhile a series of explosions echoed across the capital, Riyadh, shaking office windows in the city centre. A text message alert warned residents to seek shelter.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted two ballistic missiles that were fired at Riyadh.

Egypt 'declared war'

Earlier, a Houthi official said the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorise defensive military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to a declaration of war.

Egypt's parliament authorised the measure on Monday, following a request from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.

"It is truly remarkable that while these people go to discuss what they call 'peace in the region', Egypt and its parliament declare support for the so-called defence of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, declare war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, in a Telegram post.

It was not clear exactly what support was on offer from Egypt, which has the Arab world's largest military.

Al-Houthi's statement also pointed to Monday's visit to Tehran by the Saudi defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief, in a bid to de-escalate tensions in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad recently signed a NATO-style defence pact in Mecca, pledging to consider an attack on one country as an attack on all three.

Turkey and Pakistan have not announced any strikes on the Houthis during the group's weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia.

'Not afraid of any alliance'

The Houthis said the group was "not afraid of any alliance that may be formed".

Yemen's largely dormant conflict reignited in July, further destabilising the region months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.

The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing swathes of Red Sea coastline in a major offensive in September.

The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.

This month the Houthis ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing the cancellation of flagship events and shutting down Riyadh's airport for two weeks.

The Houthis' war with the Saudi-led coalition began in 2015, months after they ousted the internationally recognised government from the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

item.title: Israel detains Egyptian man who crossed the border fence
item.description: Israeli troops detained an Egyptian man who crossed the border fence into Israel overnight on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli forces have arrested an Egyptian man who crossed the border fence into Israel overnight on Tuesday, in an event the army described as "serious".

The Israeli military said it identified a man crossing the border from North Sinai into Israeli territory near the Nitzana settlement.

Soldiers detained the man and transferred him to security forces for interrogation, it said in a statement on social media.

It said it "views the incident with severity and continues to maintain a high level of defensive readiness in the area".

Egyptian authorities are yet to comment on the incident.

There have been a number of security incidents on the Egypt-Israel border since the Israeli military began its genocidal offensive in Gaza.

In June 2023, an Egyptian policeman shot and killed three Israeli soldiers after crossing the border near Nitzana.

There have been several exchanges of fire between Egyptian and Israeli troops since Israel began its genocidal offensive in Gaza.

In October 2023, an Israeli tank struck an Egyptian military position at the Kerem Shalom border crossing into Gaza. The following May, Egyptian and Israeli troops fired on each other after Israeli forces invaded Rafah.

There have been dozens of incidents involving drones, which are used to smuggle drugs and weapons over the border.

Tensions have risen between the two countries over Israel's assault on Gaza, which sparked concerns in Cairo that Israeli forces could attempt to forcibly displace hundreds of thousands of Palestinians into Egypt.

Egypt has responded by increasing military deployments in the Sinai, triggering accusations from Israel that it is in breach of the 1979 peace treaty.

item.title: Iraq PM sacks spy chief as provincial leader faces legal action
item.description: The Iraqi premier has removed the head of the country's intelligence service among dozens of other advisers and staff in his office to cut down on spending.
item.content:encoded:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has removed the head of the country’s National Intelligence Service, while a Baghdad court has issued an arrest warrant for the chairman of a southern provincial council over threats to start civil disobedience in protest against the closure of a border crossing with Iran.

The state news agency INA reported on Monday that al-Zaidi had ordered the termination of Hamid al-Shatri’s appointment as head of the National Intelligence Service. Al-Shatri had held the post since December 2024.

The agency did not provide a reason for the decision or name a successor.

Separately, the Third Karkh Investigative Court issued an arrest warrant for Maysan Provincial Council chairman Mustafa al-Muhammadawi, following a complaint submitted by the prime minister’s office over his threat to declare civil disobedience and block roads unless the government reopened Al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran.

Al-Muhammadawi was later released by the court on Tuesday after complying with the relevant legal procedures, his office said, according to the privately-owned National Iraqi News Agency (NINA).

The legal action followed remarks al-Muhammadawi made during a news conference at the crossing on Sunday, when he gave the federal government until 29 October to reopen it. He threatened to declare civil disobedience and block major roads if the government failed to meet his demand and used language that al-Zaidi’s media office described as inappropriate.

Al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the remarks on Monday. His office said the move was intended to ensure compliance with the law and constitutional and administrative procedures when dealing with public service and administrative matters. It added that the relevant authorities would determine any legal responsibility arising from the statements.

Dozens of protesters also blocked the nearby Bazargan road, a key route used by oil companies in Maysan, in protest against the continued closure of the crossing. Security forces were deployed around the demonstrations.

Members of Maysan Provincial Council have warned that the closure could have serious consequences for the province’s economy and residents’ livelihoods and called on the government to reopen the crossing.

The Iraqi government ordered the closure of Al-Sheeb crossing on 20 October, with the suspension taking effect the following morning and remaining in place until further notice. Baghdad said the move was intended to improve the crossing’s technical and logistical readiness. An Iraqi border official separately told Reuters that security measures at the crossing were weak and inadequate.

The decision prompted criticism from Iran’s Interior Ministry, which said Tehran had not received prior notification from Baghdad.

Iraq also ordered the temporary closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran in September as a precaution following drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Iraqi security sources. Riyadh said the drones had been launched from Iraqi territory.

On 28 July, joint US-Saudi airstrikes targeted Iran-backed militias in Iraq, which they said were reportedly responsible for attacks on US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.

Wider government shake-up

Separately, al-Zaidi has ended the contracts of 69 advisers, experts and other staff working in his office, as part of a wider government shake-up that has also included a change at the top of the prime minister’s office.

INA reported on Monday that the decision was set out in an administrative order dated 22 October, which cited the “public interest” but did not provide specific reasons for ending the appointments.

Records reviewed by 964media news site showed that the affected positions covered areas including security, foreign affairs, economic policy, health, education and public administration. Paid posts carried salaries of between one million and five million Iraqi dinars, while several contracts were unpaid.

Some of those dismissed had worked in the office for several years, while others had contracts due to run until 2027.

The list also included political figures, former ministers and judges, The New Arab had learned. The appointments had generated additional costs, including allowances for protection, accommodation and transport.

The prime minister’s office director, Ihsan al-Awadi, was also replaced by Rashad Khalaf Hashim, who took over at a handover ceremony on Monday.

Bloated public sector

The changes come amid expectations of further dismissals and retirements across Iraqi ministries and state institutions.

An unnamed official at the prime minister’s office told The New Arab that the government would begin a campaign to address excessive employment in the public sector, using performance assessments to determine whether officials should remain in their positions or leave public service.

The official said there was broad political agreement on the measures, which would extend beyond Baghdad to include ministries, security institutions and provincial administrations. A recent government review had identified dozens of surplus positions draining the state’s operating budget, some of which had been created under previous governments as political or personal favours rather than to meet administrative needs.

Iraqi political affairs expert Ahmed Ali al-Hamdani told The New Arab that at least 30 other advisers had been retained because they performed actual duties within the government office.

He said some of those whose contracts were terminated had remained in government for as long as 19 years without producing research, policy proposals or ideas, adding that many of the appointments had been made for political reasons.

Al-Hamdani also said the list included the daughter of a former president, the son of a minister, former lawmakers and ministers, and politicians who had lost elections but were subsequently appointed as advisers.

item.title: Egyptian court convicts Lina Attalah, orders Mada Masr closed
item.description: The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
item.content:encoded:
A court ordered a leading independent Egyptian news site closed on Tuesday after its editor-in-chief was convicted of running the site without a licence and taken into custody pending bail, her lawyers and the outlet said.

Lina Attalah of the news site Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters.

The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.

After prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday, a group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an "unprecedented attack on press freedom".

US Senator Chris Van Hollen said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that "journalism is not a crime".

Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.

Founded in 2013, Mada Masr is the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a landscape mostly dominated by media owned by or closely affiliated with the state, and it regularly publishes on politically sensitive topics.

It has been blocked inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.

The case against Attalah—named one of the world's 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020—follows the arrest last month of the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash.

The CPJ said the arrests risked "deepening a climate of fear that threatens independent journalism".

Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and only learned of a rejection when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.

The outlet contested that decision in court, and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.

The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets which meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year.

item.title: 'What are they hiding?': UK MP slams Israel's West Bank ban
item.description: A UK MP accuses Israel of intimidation and blocking scrutiny of its West Bank occupation after a European delegation was detained and denied entry.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli authorities barred a delegation of European politicians and campaigners from entering the occupied West Bank on Monday, detaining its members for eight hours before sending them back to Jordan, SNP MP Lara Bird told The New Arab.

Bird said Israel was deliberately preventing international observers from witnessing its actions against Palestinians, questioning what the authorities were trying to conceal as settler violence and military raids intensify across the occupied Palestinian territory.

"What is abundantly clear is that there is still a very systematic and intentional effort to stop people from coming into the West Bank to witness what is going on in the illegally occupied West Bank," Bird told The New Arab.

"And that’s the thing that needs to be discussed – not our experiences of being denied entry, but what it is that they are so terrified of people seeing."

The Progressive International delegation had travelled to the region to meet Palestinian farmers, students, academics and civil society organisations, and to participate in the annual olive harvest, which has been targeted by escalating Israeli settler attacks.

The delegation included Labour MP Clive Lewis, Scottish Green MSP Kate Nevens, Spanish senator Josu Estarrona Elizondo of the Basque EH Bildu party, and former Labour MP Sam Tarry.

Bird said the group attempted to enter the West Bank through the Allenby Bridge crossing from Jordan but were detained, interrogated and refused entry "with no justification".

"Everyone is safe, which is important, but it wasn’t a particularly pleasant experience," she told The New Arab after returning to Jordan.

Israeli authorities took delegates to a separate section of the crossing and confiscated their passports.

"Within three minutes, they knew a lot of information about me," she said. "Some people were harassed, shouted at, there was a lot of manipulation – a lot of psychological aggression," Bird added, describing the ordeal as traumatic for several members of the delegation.

Lewis also condemned Israel's decision to prevent the delegation from entering the occupied territory, saying its members had travelled to show solidarity with Palestinians following Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.

"What’s happening here in Palestine is unjust. We’ve just witnessed what Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and many others have called a genocide unfold in Gaza," he said.

"We came here to show the world, and to show solidarity with the Palestinian people. The Israeli government didn’t allow that."

A post shared by Lara Bird SNP (@larabirdsnp)

Palestinian olive harvest under attack

The delegation's exclusion comes as Israeli military restrictions and escalating settler attacks deprive thousands of Palestinian farmers of access to their land during the annual olive harvest, a vital source of income and a longstanding symbol of Palestinian attachment to their land.

Palestinian communities have reported attacks involving live ammunition, arson, the destruction of centuries-old olive trees and the theft of harvested olives and agricultural equipment.

Israeli settlers have carried out attacks under the protection of, and in some cases alongside, Israeli forces, as Palestinians face mounting pressure on their land and livelihoods.

The United Nations has described attacks on the olive harvest as "yet another tool of displacement and dispossession".

"We know that violence and demolitions and crackdowns are happening more and more in the West Bank, and that experiences of Palestinians in the West Bank are getting more and more horrific," Bird said.

She also warned that the detention and exclusion of international observers and NGO workers was becoming increasingly normalised, further restricting outside scrutiny of Israel's occupation.

Erik Edman, political director of the left-wing European political alliance DiEM25, said the delegation had intended to meet Palestinian farmers facing attacks on their own land, alongside students, academics and civil society organisations living under Israeli occupation.

"This is an attempt to isolate Palestinians and intimidate those who stand with them. It will fail," he said. "European governments must stop supplying the weapons and diplomatic protection that allow this violence to continue."

Israeli elections offer little hope of change, MP warns

The incident took place on the eve of Israel's parliamentary elections, with Bird warning that a change of government would not necessarily bring an end to the occupation, settlement expansion or violence against Palestinians.

She rejected the portrayal of Netanyahu's political opponents as a meaningful alternative for Palestinians, arguing that support for Israel's settlement project extends beyond the prime minister's governing coalition.

"With the Israeli elections going on today, there is a false picture being painted that the opposition to Netanyahu’s party is more left-leaning, is more centrist, could be a better alternative or solution to the occupation and apartheid," Bird told The New Arab.

"But that is completely untrue because both parties have made it clear that they agree that settlers should be allowed to rage terror and violence in the occupied West Bank and they believe in the expansion of settlements."

Bird called for sustained international pressure on Israel regardless of the outcome of Tuesday's vote, warning against allowing a change in leadership to divert attention from the treatment of Palestinians.

"It is so important at the moment that we do not continue to lose the pressure that we are placing on the Israeli government, whichever Israeli government comes next," she said.

Otherwise, she warned, "we risk completely eliminating the Palestinian people, their culture, their history, their right to be on their land".

item.title: Syria defends textbook changes erasing women and democracy
item.description: Syria's education ministry has defended controversial textbook revisions that cover up female figures, remove historical art and delete democracy lessons.
item.content:encoded:
Syria's education ministry has defended controversial revisions to school textbooks that include covering up female figures, removing historical artworks and deleting lessons on democracy and political participation.

The changes, independently verified by Syrian fact-checkers, have provoked criticism from educators and women's rights advocates, who fear the country's new authorities are imposing an increasingly conservative ideological vision on its education system.

In a statement on Monday, the Ministry of Education insisted that revisions made since the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 were limited to a single round of changes announced in January 2025, intended primarily to remove symbols and ideological material associated with the former regime.

The ministry said its reforms were designed to protect Syria's social and religious diversity, promote citizenship and encourage respect for others, dismissing some of the information circulating online as inaccurate.

However, the independent Syrian fact-checking organisation Ta'akkad said the statement did not address the specific alterations it had verified, including the removal of lessons concerning democratic participation and changes to depictions of women.

Ta'akkad also found that one of the illustrations published by the ministry to demonstrate diversity was itself a revised image previously identified by investigators.

Women covered up, historical artworks removed

The controversy erupted after Syrian journalist Mohammed al-Salloum published comparisons between older editions of school textbooks and versions distributed to pupils for the 2026–2027 academic year.

Ta'akkad examined digital and printed copies of the books and confirmed that female characters had been removed from some illustrations, while others had been altered to include hijabs or more conservative clothing.

In one first-grade textbook, an illustration of a female doctor was modified to include a hijab, although the same character appeared without one elsewhere in the book.

Other changes included replacing illustrations of women and girls, modifying depictions of historical figures and removing artwork.

An image of an ancient Egyptian statue was altered to cover its exposed torso with a striped shirt, while illustrations of ancient sculptures associated with the civilisations of Mari and Ugarit were removed.

A depiction of Elissa, the legendary Phoenician founder of Carthage, was also altered to cover her neck and chin.

The changes extended beyond illustrations. 

A sixth-grade social studies textbook originally published during the Assad era was reissued without several lessons addressing local government, political life, citizenship, the media and democratic participation. Content glorifying the former regime was also removed.

Ministry insists changes reflect Syrian values

 

Ismat Ramadan, director of Syria's National Centre for Curriculum Development, told The New Arab that the previous textbooks had been shaped by Baathist ideology and that the new authorities were seeking to rebuild the country's educational identity.

He acknowledged that images had been altered, but argued that the changes were intended to reflect Syria's cultural and religious diversity.

Ramadan said the curriculum should also respect the values of the majority of Syrian society, including parents' wishes that younger children not be exposed to material they considered inappropriate, such as nude statues.

He argued that removing a particular illustration did not necessarily mean removing knowledge of the historical period it represented.

However, critics say the changes risk replacing the ideological restrictions of the Assad era with new forms of exclusion.

Aswan Nahar, director of the Syrian educational organisation Roya for Change, told TNA that the problem was not the inclusion of women wearing hijabs, but the exclusion of other representations of women.

She argued that textbooks should reflect the full diversity of Syrian society and allow girls to see women occupying different roles.

Nahar also warned that deleting lessons on citizenship, local administration and democratic participation could deprive children of important opportunities to understand their rights and responsibilities.

Educationalist Abdullah al-Shahrour similarly criticised the alterations to historical artwork, warning that concealing sculptures and depictions of the human body risked presenting art and history as something shameful.

The Syrian Feminist Lobby has called for the revisions to be reviewed with the participation of educators, specialists and civil society representatives, to ensure that school curricula respect equality, social diversity, human rights and democratic values.

Syria's Education Ministry announced in August that a unified curriculum would be adopted across the country's provinces for the 2026–2027 academic year, with further work underway on new national educational standards.

The controversy has revived questions about the direction of education under Syria's post-Assad leadership, particularly whether reforms intended to remove decades of authoritarian propaganda will also preserve the country's cultural and political diversity.

item.title: New homes but for whom? Syria's housing faces affordability test
item.description: In-Depth: As new housing developments promise a fresh start, many Syrians remain unable to afford a home, repair what they lost, or reclaim their property
item.content:encoded:
Driving through Damascus, billboards for new residential developments offer a vision of the future: modern apartments, landscaped surroundings, and the promise of a fresh start.

But for Syrians navigating damaged homes, rising rents, and the cost of returning after years of displacement, the question is how much of that future they can actually afford.

In Qudsaya, west of the capital, Abyat Hills illustrates both the ambitions and the limits of Syria’s investment-led housing drive.

The development brings together Saudi company Abyat Investment and Real Estate Development and Syria’s General Housing Establishment, which operates under the Ministry of Public Works and Housing. Under the partnership, the state provides the land while Abyat develops the buildings and facilities.

Its published subscription contract sets first-phase prices at $950–$1,150 per square metre. On a simple 100-square-metre illustration, that amounts to somewhere between $95,000–$115,000.

These prices are not unprecedented within Damascus’s property market. Listings published by local agency Elmas include a 150-square-metre apartment in Mashrou Dummar, just south of Qudsaya, advertised at $300,000 and a 180-square-metre property in the southwestern neighbourhood of Kafr Souseh at $450,000.

But the relevant comparison for many Syrians is not with another expensive neighbourhood. It is with what they earn.

The European Union Agency for Asylum’s July country report cited February figures putting average monthly wages at roughly $102 for entry-level public-sector employees and $120 in the private sector, indicating the scale of the gulf between locally earned income and the capital required to enter such developments.

"A housing development may attract substantial investment while its residential units remain beyond the financial reach of families who lost their homes, jobs, and savings during the conflict," Fadel Abdulghany, founder and director of the Syrian Network for Human Rights, told The New Arab.

"If public reconstruction policies fail to take these families’ needs into account, urban development may expand without contributing sufficiently to the conditions necessary for displaced people to return sustainably."

Investment promises, everyday pressures

The affordability question has become more politically visible as households confront rising living costs.

In September, a government decision to raise diesel prices by 40 percent and petrol prices by approximately 26–28 percent triggered protests and roadblocks across Syria. Demonstrators burned tyres, blocked major routes, and demanded the increases be reversed.

The government subsequently announced cheaper diesel categories for heating, agriculture, and some productive sectors, while leaving the standard diesel price and the higher petrol and gas prices in place.

The fuel protests essentially exposed the economic pressures against which promises of recovery and foreign investment are being judged: whether households can afford transport, heating, and daily necessities, rather than simply whether new projects attract buyers.

For many displaced Syrians, the immediate challenge is even more dire - not about purchasing a new apartment but making their existing home habitable.

Liban Abdullahi Jimale, housing, land and property advisor for the Norwegian Refugee Council in Syria, said families frequently tell the organisation that they want to return but cannot afford repairs.

"The choice is often stark," he told The New Arab.

Some live in damaged properties, pitch tents nearby or repair a single room. Others go back to displacement camps or sites because they offer better shelter than what remains at home.

Renting can also be precarious. According to a sector assessment cited by NRC, rents rose in 84 percent of assessed communities in rural Damascus, with the increases attributed mainly to returns.

NRC’s legal-needs assessment found that only 48 percent of surveyed returnee households reported owning or renting a dwelling, compared with 70 percent across the surveyed population. Around one in five renting returnee households faced eviction risk, mostly because of unpaid rent.

These figures therefore illustrate why increasing the number of apartments does not automatically give displaced families somewhere secure to live.

Whose land, whose recovery?

At Abyat Hills, questions about access to housing have been accompanied by another dispute: the rights of people claiming an interest in the land beneath it.

On 26 September, residents from Qudsaya and other rural Damascus communities protested over expropriation, compensation, and ownership claims concerning land allocated to developments. Some told state news agency SANA that they had received no compensation; others said historical payments were inadequate.

The governorate subsequently opened an office to receive claims concerning land within Abyat Hills and Sham View. The ministry said most contested expropriation decisions dated back decades and that each property’s status had to be established through land records and compensation documents.

It also argued that public housing projects could include commercial components and private partners. Abyat maintained that its work was lawful and that government bodies and courts should settle ownership disputes.

Similar tensions surfaced in Homs, where residents protested over expropriated land they associated with the Boulevard project. The city council said the properties had entered public ownership through legal procedures and were designated as a park under an older approved plan; residents sought a review of the records and compensation arrangements.

For Abdulghany, the danger is that redevelopment can make unresolved claims harder to remedy.

"The greatest risk is that reconstruction projects may consolidate the consequences of past property seizures, making them increasingly difficult to remedy or reverse," he told The New Arab.

Once disputed land is transferred, built on, used as collateral or sold to new purchasers, additional interests and financial obligations can emerge. Recovering an original property may become more complicated even where an earlier claim has a sound legal basis.

More than a new apartment

Abyat Hills’ contract includes measures presented as supporting residential use rather than speculation: one subscription per family, restrictions on transferring subscriptions and controls on resale. It states that the homes are intended for Syrian families. But these provisions do not themselves bridge the gap between a household’s income and the money required to buy.

Nor does building an apartment resolve the documentation problems that can prevent a family from reclaiming a different home.

Abdulghany said lost records, incomplete registration, inheritance disputes, and properties registered in the names of detained or disappeared people continue to obstruct recovery.

"The fundamental distinction is between the legal recognition of rights and enabling rights holders to recover and exercise them in practice," he said.

Families of missing people face a particularly difficult bind when a property remains registered in their relative’s name. Abdulghany said Syrian law allows them to seek a judicial representative without first obtaining a declaration of death, but the representative’s limited powers mean significant property transactions or some legal proceedings may require further court approval.

Women face additional barriers. Abdulghany said SNHR’s July report documented how property confiscations intersected with discriminatory registration practices, inheritance obstacles and economic dependency. For these families, rebuilding a house does not necessarily mean being able to reclaim, manage or securely inhabit it.

Jimale described civil documentation as a foundational need. Missing identity and family-status records can obstruct inheritance claims, access to services and legal proceedings, leaving families navigating expensive and complicated procedures after they return.

The contrast with a fully serviced new development is therefore about more than finishes or sale prices. It is about the conditions that allow people to live somewhere securely.

What should count as recovery?

Private investment can expand housing supply and help finance reconstruction. Abdulghany’s argument is not that commercial development should stop, but that it cannot replace a public response to housing need.

He called for priority to be given to repairing existing neighbourhoods, restoring essential services, strengthening tenure security and developing affordable housing and rental programmes.

Jimale also stressed the need for international financial and technical support, alongside continuing assistance for people who cannot yet return.

"When people return to their areas but lack housing, basic services, livelihood opportunities, or legal documentation, pressure to leave temporary shelters may simply transfer displacement from camps into informal settlements and urban areas rather than resolve it," he said.

Abyat Hills may demonstrate that there are buyers for new housing around Damascus. What it cannot establish on its own is whether families living in damaged homes, struggling with rent or contesting old expropriations are gaining a viable route to recovery.

Agnese is a journalist at The New Arab, with previous experience in breaking news and OSINT investigations across the Middle East

Follow her on X: @AgneseBoffano
