item.title: Iraq revives shipping line after 50 years as Hormuz crisis bites
item.description: Iraq revives its national shipping line after more than 50 years, seeking to reduce reliance on foreign carriers as the Hormuz crisis drives up shipping costs.
item.content:encoded:
Iraq has resumed operations on its national commercial shipping line after more than five decades, as rising freight and insurance costs linked to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz place growing pressure on the country's import-dependent economy.

The relaunch marks an attempt by Baghdad to restore its presence in regional maritime trade, reduce reliance on foreign shipping companies and expand transport options for Iraqi businesses.

The General Company for Maritime Transport, which operates under Iraq's Ministry of Transport, announced on Monday that the vessel Basra had arrived at Umm Qasr port carrying containers from Jebel Ali port in the United Arab Emirates.

The voyage marked the first step towards reviving the Iraqi Line, the country's national commercial shipping service, which had been inactive for more than 50 years.

Ahmed Jassim, director-general of the company, said the resumption would provide traders and importers with additional shipping options while strengthening commercial links between Iraqi and Emirati ports.

He added that the initiative formed part of wider efforts to develop Iraq's national maritime carrier and expand its role in regional and international trade.

The transport ministry announced on 5 October that the shipping line was preparing to resume commercial operations, noting that its last voyages dated back to the mid-1960s.

The ministry also said Iraq's ports had a combined annual handling capacity exceeding 79 million tonnes and a container capacity of more than 3.6 million containers, with measures underway to ease congestion and improve roads and storage facilities.

However, Iraq's national fleet currently consists of just six vessels, raising questions about whether the revived service can compete with established international shipping operators.

Hormuz disruptions drive up shipping costs

The relaunch comes as instability in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime route connecting the Gulf to international markets, has increased freight and insurance costs and disrupted delivery schedules.

Jassim al-Moussawi, a member of Iraq's parliamentary Oil and Gas Committee, said developing the national fleet had become increasingly important as regional tensions drove up transport costs.

Speaking to The New Arab, Moussawi said Iraq needed a larger fleet of nationally owned vessels to reduce its dependence on foreign companies.

He estimated that transport costs had risen sharply because of regional disruptions, reaching almost half the value of exported oil, according to his calculations.

Expanding Iraq's maritime transport capacity could save the state treasury millions of dollars, he argued, by reducing freight and insurance expenses and improving the country's ability to respond to disruptions in international shipping.

Iraqi trader Halim Hamid also welcomed the reopening of the route between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr, describing it as an opportunity to provide importers with more shipping options.

"The resumption of the line between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr represents a positive step towards expanding shipping options for importers, particularly following the rise in freight and insurance costs and delays in the arrival of goods caused by the Hormuz disruptions," he told TNA.

Hamid said fluctuations in shipping costs and unreliable delivery schedules were affecting the price of imported goods in Iraqi markets.

He added that an effective national carrier could increase competition with foreign companies, provided it offered competitive rates, reliable sailing schedules and efficient customs clearance.

"The success of the line depends on providing integrated services covering booking, transport, unloading and delivery according to clear schedules," he said.

Traders, he stressed, make shipping decisions based on overall costs and reliability rather than the nationality of the carrier.

While expanding the service could gradually reduce import costs, Hamid cautioned that it would not necessarily lead to an immediate fall in consumer prices without sufficient shipping capacity and competitive logistics services.

Can Iraq's shipping revival deliver economic gains?

Economists say the return of the national shipping line could help Iraq develop an additional source of non-oil revenue by capturing a greater share of the country's substantial import and freight market.

Economic expert Karim al-Hilu said Iraq's heavy reliance on foreign shipping operators presented an opportunity for domestic companies to expand their role in maritime transport and logistics.

Citing Ministry of Planning figures, Hilu said Iraq imported approximately 23.46 million tonnes of goods through its ports in 2025, an increase of 10.5% from the previous year.

Despite the growth in cargo volumes, revenues at the General Company for Maritime Transport fell by 10.9% to 213 billion Iraqi dinars ($163 million), highlighting a gap between expanding trade activity and the earnings of the national carrier.

Iraq's merchandise imports totalled approximately $72.3 billion in 2025, including $49.3 billion transported through seaports, according to Hilu.

He said the figures demonstrated the potential for greater investment in shipping, warehousing, maintenance and other port-related services, which could create jobs and generate more economic value domestically.

However, Hilu warned that reviving the national line would require a carefully planned commercial strategy, particularly given the small size of Iraq's fleet and competition from international operators.

"Unplanned expansion could turn the project into a financial burden rather than a sustainable source of revenue," he said, calling for a clear operational and investment plan to ensure economic viability and strengthen the national carrier's regional competitiveness.

item.title: Shortage of Arabic ballot papers reported in Israel elections
item.description: Arab voters report shortages of Arabic-language ballot papers in Israel's elections, as parties allege voting obstruction and arrests of campaign activists.
item.content:encoded:
Palestinian citizens of Israel have reported shortages of Arabic-language ballot papers at several polling stations during Tuesday's parliamentary elections, prompting a rights group to demand urgent intervention over concerns that Arab voters are being denied equal access to the vote.

The Haifa-based Adalah Legal Centre for Arab Minority Rights said it had received complaints from voters and election observers since polling stations opened on Tuesday morning, reporting the absence of Arabic-language ballot papers in several Arab towns and mixed cities.

The complaints came from Baqa al-Gharbiyye, Haifa, Nazareth, I'billin, Eilabun, Shefa-Amr and Nof HaGalil, according to a statement issued by the organisation.

Adalah subsequently sent an urgent letter to the head of Israel's Central Elections Committee, demanding that Arabic-language ballot papers be supplied immediately to all affected polling stations and that clear instructions be issued to election officials.

The organisation warned that the shortages undermined the right of Palestinian citizens of Israel to participate in elections on an equal footing.

It stressed that Arabic is the mother tongue of hundreds of thousands of eligible voters and that providing ballot papers in the language is essential to ensuring fair and accessible elections.

Rami Haidar, media coordinator for the Joint List, told The New Arab that most reported shortages had occurred in mixed cities, where Palestinian and Jewish residents live alongside one another.

"We are in contact with the relevant authorities to resolve this problem," he said.

Arab party alleges systematic attempts to obstruct voting

Separately, the United Arab List (Ra'am) filed a formal complaint with the Central Elections Committee, alleging a systematic campaign to obstruct voting for the party.

The party said the alleged interference included the arrest of several campaign activists, the disappearance of its ballot papers and the deliberate destruction of voting slips in several Arab communities.

According to Ra'am, Israeli police arrested several prominent party activists in the Negev early on Tuesday, including Sayyaf Abu Riyash from Rahat, Hussein Masoudin from Shaqib al-Salam and Ibrahim al-Quraibi from the village of al-Sirr, along with others.

The party said the arrests had taken place without any clear justification.

Ra'am also reported widespread shortages of its Arabic-language ballot papers, marked with the letters "ع م", in several towns, including Nazareth and Shefa-Amr.

It said torn ballot papers had also been discovered, raising suspicions that they had been deliberately damaged.

The party urged supporters to check that their ballot papers were available and undamaged, and to demand replacements immediately if they found any missing or defective slips.

Ra'am accused Israel's right wing of seeking to weaken its electoral strength and prevent it from securing eight seats in the Knesset, which it said could obstruct the formation of an alternative government led by the opposition's "change camp".

"Your vote is your power, so do not give it up," the party told supporters.

Meanwhile, the Joint List issued video messages explaining that voters might encounter two versions of its ballot papers at some polling stations.

One version carries text in both Arabic and Hebrew, while the other is printed in Hebrew only.

The party stressed that both versions were valid and could be used to vote.

It urged supporters to ensure that their ballot papers were free of markings or damage and matched the officially approved versions.

The Joint List also called on Palestinian citizens to turn out in large numbers, presenting the election as an opportunity to defeat the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

item.title: Israel elections 2026: 10 factors that could shape the vote
item.description: From Arab voter turnout and ultra-Orthodox divisions to youth participation and coalition negotiations, several factors could shape Israel's election results.
item.content:encoded:
Israelis headed to the polls on Tuesday in what Israeli media report to be one of the country's most dramatic elections in recent years, with the political future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hanging in the balance.

The vote comes against the backdrop of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, growing political divisions and uncertainty over whether Netanyahu's right-wing coalition or the opposition, also rightwing politically, can secure enough seats to form the next government.

But the outcome will depend on more than which party wins the most votes. Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, the mobilisation of ultra-Orthodox voters and the performance of smaller parties could all influence the balance of power in the 120-seat Knesset.

The counting process could also take longer than usual, with an unprecedented number of special ballots expected to delay a clear picture of the results until Wednesday afternoon.

The following are 10 factors that could shape the election results:

1. How high will voter turnout be?

Voter turnout is one of the most closely watched indicators in Israeli elections, particularly because it can affect the prospects of smaller parties seeking parliamentary representation.

Turnout in the previous election stood at around 70%, while estimates suggest it could rise to 75% this time.

A higher turnout increases the number of votes a party needs to cross the electoral threshold, making it more difficult for smaller parties to secure seats.

This could have significant implications for both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition, particularly if parties aligned with either camp fail to enter parliament.

2. Which cities will turn out in the largest numbers?

Beyond the national turnout figure, the geographical distribution of voters could provide important clues about the election outcome.

Traditionally, peripheral towns and settlements such as Ofakim, Yeruham, Kiryat Shmona and Sderot have been strongholds of Netanyahu's Likud party.

By contrast, more liberal cities, including Herzliya, Ramat Hasharon, Tel Aviv and Kfar Saba, have been more closely associated with the opposition's so-called "change camp".

That camp includes prominent political figures with military and security backgrounds, such as Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan, alongside Yair Lapid and Avigdor Lieberman.

Turnout figures in these areas could reveal where political enthusiasm is strongest and where voter apathy may affect the results.

3. Why could special ballots delay the results?

Around 650,000 special ballots, known as "double envelopes", have been registered for this election, an unprecedented figure.

These ballots are used by eligible voters who cannot cast their votes at polling stations near their registered addresses.

They include soldiers, diplomats, Foreign Ministry employees, people with disabilities and settlers evacuated from their homes.

The special counting procedures mean that a clearer picture of the election results may not emerge until Wednesday afternoon.

The unusually large number of these ballots could also affect the final distribution of seats, potentially pushing some smaller parties above the electoral threshold.

4. Could Palestinian voters determine the balance of power?

Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel is expected to be one of the most consequential factors in the election.

The Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List (Ra'am), led by Mansour Abbas, are running separately but have both launched extensive campaigns to encourage Palestinian citizens to vote.

Their performance could affect the prospects of both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition.

If Arab parties secure more than 14 of the Knesset's 120 seats, analysts believe it would represent a significant achievement, while potentially making it harder for either political bloc to form a government.

However, concerns have emerged over the conduct of voting in Palestinian towns and cities. Several polling stations in Arab communities were delayed in opening on Tuesday morning.

According to sources speaking to The New Arab, some polling committee members claimed to have lost their way in Arab towns, while residents in certain areas alleged that the delays were deliberate.

Arab voters also complained about the absence of Arabic-language ballot papers at some polling stations, raising concerns about accessibility for citizens who are not proficient in Hebrew.

Another controversy concerns the presence of armed election observers.

On Monday, Israel's Supreme Court rejected a petition filed by the Haifa-based legal rights organisation Adalah and the Joint List seeking to prohibit observers from carrying weapons inside polling stations.

The petition followed announcements by Likud and Religious Zionism that they intended to deploy approximately 2,000 observers in Arab towns and mixed cities.

Petitioners warned that the presence of armed representatives from right-wing parties could intimidate Arab voters and provoke confrontations.

The Israeli authorities argued that there was no operational or security justification for banning weapons, saying armed observers would receive specific instructions limiting their use to self-defence.

The court declined to intervene in the decisions of the police and Central Elections Committee, saying the concerns raised had been considered in election security preparations.

Adalah criticised the ruling, arguing that it failed to address the potential intimidation of Arab voters by organised groups of armed right-wing activists.

5. Will young Israelis turn out in greater numbers?

Young voters could play a more prominent role in this election following a campaign heavily conducted on social media.

According to Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, political parties believe their online campaigns have encouraged greater engagement among younger Israelis, including those who previously showed little interest in electoral politics.

Celebrities and social media influencers have also joined the campaign, with several publicly revealing which parties they intend to support.

Their endorsements have generated debate among followers and helped bring political discussions to audiences that might otherwise have remained disengaged.

Party estimates suggest that younger voters could turn out in greater numbers than usual, potentially increasing their influence on the results.

6. How will ultra-Orthodox voters respond?

Israel's ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, community has traditionally voted in large numbers, often following the guidance of religious leaders.

However, analysts and prominent figures within the community say voting patterns are particularly difficult to predict this year.

One major source of dissatisfaction is the government's failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military conscription during the current parliamentary term.

The emergence of new Haredi parties challenging established political organisations has also created uncertainty.

Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which represents sections of the ultra-Orthodox community, has undergone a leadership change, with Knesset member Yaakov Asher replacing veteran politician Moshe Gafni.

According to Yedioth Ahronoth, it remains unclear whether ultra-Orthodox voters will maintain their traditional party loyalties or use the election to register a protest vote.

Their decisions could have significant consequences for Netanyahu, whose governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties.

7. Does winning the most seats guarantee power?

Not necessarily.

Although considerable attention is focused on which party will emerge as the largest in the Knesset, winning the most seats does not automatically give its leader the right to form a government.

Under Israel's political system, the president assigns the task of forming a government to the candidate considered most capable of assembling a governing coalition.

The president has considerable discretion in making that decision.

As a result, a party could finish first in the election but still find itself in opposition if another political leader can secure broader parliamentary support.

The ability to negotiate alliances and build a viable coalition may therefore prove more important than the number of seats won by any single party.

8. Why does the first mandate to form a government matter?

The candidate tasked with forming a government initially has 28 days to assemble a coalition.

That period can be extended by a further 14 days.

However, securing the first mandate is important for reasons beyond coalition negotiations.

According to the report, the candidate who receives the initial mandate also gains influence over the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which plays a central role in parliamentary procedures before permanent committees are established.

Control over parliamentary arrangements can allow political factions to advance legislation and potentially replace the Knesset speaker.

This means the first candidate given the opportunity to form a government could influence parliamentary developments even if their coalition negotiations ultimately fail.

9. What role could the Elector app play?

Political parties are also relying on technology to mobilise supporters and monitor turnout throughout election day.

One tool attracting particular attention is Elector, a sophisticated voter-management application reportedly worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.

According to Israeli news website Ynet, the application contains information gathered about individuals who have declared support for particular parties or have been identified as potential supporters.

It allows campaign teams to monitor whether those voters have cast their ballots, providing parties with a clearer picture of their mobilisation efforts.

The system can help parties identify supporters who have not yet voted and focus their efforts on encouraging them to reach polling stations.

However, its use has raised questions about consent and the collection of personal information.

Central Elections Committee chairman Judge Noam Sohlberg expressed reservations about the application but ultimately permitted its use.

The effectiveness of parties' voter mobilisation operations could prove important in closely contested races.

10. Could the weather affect the result?

Even the weather could play a role in determining turnout.

Political parties are closely monitoring forecasts for rain in several Israeli cities on election day.

Rainfall could discourage undecided voters or those with little enthusiasm for participating from travelling to polling stations. This could be particularly significant for parties that depend on mobilising less committed supporters.

item.title: Israeli elections offer scant hope of change for Gaza: analysts
item.description: Gaza's Palestinians await Israel's election results with anxiety, as analysts warn a change of government would likely not end the genocide.
item.content:encoded:
In the Gaza Strip, where three years of Israel's genocidal war have devastated Palestinians, expectations surrounding Tuesday's Israeli Knesset elections vary widely.

Some Palestinians hope the vote will bring about the end of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while others believe that any incoming Israeli government will not differ much from its predecessor.

The anticipation reflects the narrow range of alternatives available to Gaza's Palestinian residents, amid stalled political processes, continuing suffering and the absence of a clear prospect for ending the war and its impact.

While Israelis await the ballot results to determine their next government, Palestinians find themselves closely connected with the outcome, hoping that something might change in their dire reality.

The contradiction is particularly stark given the postponement of Palestinian elections, while Palestinians follow the Israeli vote and await its results as a potential factor in changing conditions in Gaza.

While Palestinian elections are supposed to serve as a means of renewing political legitimacy and determining national priorities, Palestinians find themselves compelled to look towards another electoral contest in search of a possible way to stop the war or alleviate its consequences.

Yet this anticipation does not mean the results will deliver what Palestinians hope for.

A change in the Israeli government may alter some calculations, but it does not guarantee an end to the war, the lifting of restrictions or the launch of a comprehensive reconstruction process in Gaza, unless it is accompanied by actual shifts in policy and international pressure capable of influencing Israeli decisions.

Differing hopes in Gaza

For Palestinian Mohammad Zakaria, who lives in a tent in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza after being displaced from Beit Lahia in the north, the upcoming Israeli elections represent an opportunity he hopes will lead to the downfall of Benjamin Netanyahu's government, which he holds responsible for what Palestinians have endured during the years of genocide.

Zakaria told The New Arab that the departure of the current government could open the door to a different approach towards the Gaza Strip and give residents a chance to escape the reality of killing, destruction and siege, and recover the minimum conditions necessary for life.

However, this hope is not shared by all Palestinians.

Ibrahim Hammad believes the problem extends beyond Netanyahu and his government to the nature of Israeli society and its current political tendencies. He argues that the rise of the right and the growing prevalence of extremist rhetoric make relying solely on a change of government insufficient.

Hammad told TNA that Palestinians have no guarantees that the arrival of a new Israeli government will lead to a genuine change in the policies pursued towards them.

He noted that positions concerning Gaza, the occupied West Bank and displacement cannot be reduced all on Netanyahu as an individual. He also argues that a change in political figures may not alter the substance of these policies, as long as large sections of Israeli society continue to support hardline positions towards Palestinians.

Saeed al-Aila, meanwhile, views the Israeli elections from a different perspective, one linked to the exhaustion and despair experienced by Gaza's residents after years of war.

Al-Aila told TNA that Palestinians being compelled to follow Israeli elections and link their fate to their results reflects the extent of their inability to influence their own circumstances, as well as the absence of a Palestinian political horizon capable of offering solutions or pathways out of the crisis.

"Gaza's residents can't endure further waiting and suffering, at a time when the necessities of life are deteriorating and basic needs are increasing," he said.

"Perhaps the painful irony lies in the postponement of Palestinian elections, while Palestinians await the Israeli elections to find out whether changes will occur in their lives, as if determining their future has become more dependent on the decisions of the Israeli voter than on their own political will."

A consensus that extends beyond Netanyahu

Political writer and analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that Palestinian hopes pinned on the Israeli election results reflect a state of despair stemming from the absence of a clear political horizon for solutions, amid the continuation of the war and a lack of sufficient indications that it can be ended through existing political channels.

Ibrahim said the elections could produce an Israeli government that is less hardline on certain issues or create greater room for the opposition and sections of Israeli society calling for an end to the war.

However, he stressed that this does not necessarily mean a fundamental change in Israeli policies towards Palestinians.

He emphasised that any genuine shift will require real international pressure to push the Israeli government to stop the war and commit to clear standards for ending it.

He also highlighted the importance of European and international positions, alongside US pressure, in pushing the political process towards tangible results.

According to Ibrahim, the Israeli elections do not appear to be an independent factor capable of changing the Palestinian reality. Rather, they represent one of several variables that could interact with external pressure and broader political positions.

The change Palestinians are waiting for depends not only on the identity of the next prime minister, but also on the willingness of influential parties to impose a different course from the policies that have led to the continuation of the war and the worsening humanitarian crisis.

For his part, Israeli affairs analyst Adel Shadid argues that a change in the Israeli government will not necessarily lead to a fundamental shift in policies towards Palestinians or a tangible improvement in their circumstances, even if different political forces come to power.

Shadid told TNA that Palestinian, Arab and international reliance on the Israeli elections as a gateway to change revealed the absence of alternatives and the tendency to await transformation from within Israeli society, rather than building effective political and international pressure to force Israel to change its policies.

He noted that Netanyahu's re-election could amount to the legitimisation of the continuation of the existing political approach, and potentially even its intensification.

However, the arrival of another premier would not guarantee fundamental change in Israel's treatment of Palestinians and their rights.

Regarding Gaza, Shadid pointed to broad Israeli consensus on several key issues concerning the territory, making expectations of a major shift simply through a change of government uncertain.

He argued that the next government could adopt even harsher policies towards Gaza, even if Netanyahu does not remain prime minister.

item.title: Dutch broadcaster pulls out of Eurovision over Israel
item.description: The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation, in protest of the country's genocide of Gaza.
item.content:encoded:
The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster NPO said Tuesday, citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation.

"We have known for some time that Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division... therefore, after consultation with the Board of Broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027," Jurre Bosman, NPO's media director, said in a statement.

Jet de Ranitz, NPO's executive chairman, acknowledged this would disappoint many Dutch Eurovision fans and stressed that the contest would still be aired on the public channels.

However, he said: "We must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027."

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being," added De Ranitz.

The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation, in protest at the country's genocide of Gaza, ongoing since October 2023.

Earlier this month, the Czech public broadcaster also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Ireland has already announced it will not be taking part, while the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.

item.title: Gazan filmmaker Iyad Hajjaj's short movie on war wins 19th award
item.description: Hajjaj, who grew up in the border city of Rafah, has spent decades in Hollywood. His screen credits include "Ms. Marvel", "Will and Grace", and "Black Monday".
item.content:encoded:
Iyad Hajjaj, a Hollywood actor and filmmaker originally from Gaza, has won 19 awards for his short movie based on Israel's genocidal war.

The film, "My Foot is in Heaven", inspired on real events, tells the story a father (played by Hajjaj) whose daughter's lower leg is severely wounded in an Israeli airstrike. The family, who have already lost their other children in the war, quickly learn that their daughter's foot can only be amputated without anesthesia.

The aim of the film, which has won 19 awards to date, is to educate audiences though the medium of film about the three-year-long war and genocide in Gaza through a human and realistic story.

"The film has fulfilled its message," Hajjaj told The New Arab during his film festival tour, which is taking him to cities around the world, including London and New York City. One of his next stops will be at the Egyptian American Film Festival in Staten Island.

"The message is for the general public to hear about what is happening in Gaza," he said. "This film is a slice of life of life in Gaza. I wanted the audience to live with this family to see what they go through. It represents the rest of the families in Gaza."

In addition to major cities, the film is also being shown in conservative rural areas in the US, including Kentucky and South Carolina.

"The film was accepted in states I would never dream about. It shows people are changing towards Gaza. For us to have a chance to show these audiences a story from Gaza is a success by itself," Hajjaj said.

In his post-screening discussions with audiences, many people comment on how realistic it looks—and are surprised to learn that it was filmed in southern California. Hajjaj spent months creating an authentic set and wardrobe to depict Gaza, where he has family he speaks with nearly daily. Many have died in Israeli airstrikes. 

“In the discussions, as a filmmaker, they ask how I did it, where I filmed it. I always say I do have family in Gaza. The feelings I portrayed in those scenes are real feelings. I lived in that environment. I lived through that war. I experienced it through my family,” he said. 

Hajjaj, who grew up in the border city of Rafah, has spent decades in Hollywood. His screen credits include "Ms. Marvel", "Will and Grace", and "Black Monday". Through his work, he hopes to be an ambassador of Palestinians for American audiences through the accessible medium of film.

"I'm their ambassador. I've accepted this message and mission. I am trying to fulfil this mission I have," he said.

"It's a lot of work. I am in Hollywood and I'm going against the current. We might have seen a lot of celebrities change their perspective, but that control in Hollywood has not changed. We're still facing the same issues." He said.

"Surprisingly, I haven’t had anybody get up and speak against the film and what I say. The story of a girl in Gaza could happen to anyone," he said. "People are hungry for these kinds of stories."

item.title: Israel elections: High Arab turnout seeks to punish Netanyahu
item.description: Palestinian voters in Israel are turning out in large numbers, hoping to punish Netanyahu's far-right government and influence the election outcome.
item.content:encoded:
Palestinian towns and villages across Israel saw significant voter turnout on Tuesday morning as polls opened for the 26th Knesset elections. Voters began arriving at polling stations as early as 7am, with a heavy presence of Jewish observers, including representatives from far-right parties.

Despite reported delays in opening several polling stations due to administrative procedures, activists from both the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am) mobilised to urge Arab citizens to cast their ballots early in the day to avoid anticipated congestion during the afternoon and evening.

The elections come three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, with widespread expectations of strong mobilisation by Palestinian citizens of Israel seeking to punish the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court, and his far-right coalition partners.

According to the Central Elections Committee, the total number of eligible voters stands at 7,331,981, an increase of 543,177 compared to the previous election. Arab citizens account for roughly 18% of the eligible electorate, numbering approximately 1.172 million voters.

Most opinion polls project an increase in Arab voter participation.

Data from the Midgam Research Institute indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in the previous elections.

Meanwhile, Yousef Makladeh, director of the Stat-Net research institute, which specialises in polling within the Arab community, projected that turnout could reach around 68% if current campaign momentum is sustained.

 
 
 
 
View this post on Instagram
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

A post shared by The New Arab (@thenewarab)

Polling analysts further suggest that if turnout exceeds 70% on election day, Arab parliamentary representation could climb to 16 seats.

Writer and researcher Marzouq Halabi told The New Arab that the anticipated mobilisation reflected a defensive response to the policies of Netanyahu's government, including the genocide in Gaza, forced displacement, home demolitions and growing anti-Palestinian incitement.

"This is purely defensive voting, more than anything else," he said, arguing that Palestinian citizens of Israel increasingly view the election as an opportunity to resist the far right rather than simply choose between competing political programmes," he said.

"They are not asking about party platforms; rather, they are asking how the fascist right can be repelled and its agendas obstructed," Halabi said.

He added that the vote was also about asserting Palestinian presence and identity in the face of attempts to marginalise and silence the community.

Maha Karkabi, a candidate representing the Joint List, similarly argued that higher Arab turnout could prevent some far-right parties from crossing the electoral threshold and potentially deny Netanyahu the parliamentary support needed to form another government.

"Most opinion polls indicate that a high Arab turnout will prevent extremist and racist right-wing parties from crossing the electoral threshold, and could, to a certain extent, prevent Netanyahu from forming a government with the far right," she told The New Arab.

Karkabi said the Joint List would nevertheless remain in opposition, ruling out participation in Israeli governments because of their policies towards Palestinians, including occupation, ethnic cleansing and home demolitions.

However, analysts cautioned that Netanyahu's defeat would not necessarily bring an immediate end to Israel's policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Muhanad Mustafa, a researcher at the Haifa-based Mada al-Carmel Center, told The New Arab that much would depend on the election results, but that even a victory for the opposition would be unlikely to produce an immediate change.

Instead, he suggested that an alternative government could gradually shift towards political arrangements centred on Israeli security interests, rather than the religious ideology that has shaped the current coalition's approach.

"An alternative government would not bear the burden of the 7 October failure, and its approach would be primarily security-driven rather than rooted in messianic religious ideology," Mustafa said.

He added that a more ideologically diverse coalition could be more inclined towards internal compromises when addressing Gaza and the West Bank, although this would not necessarily translate into a fundamental change in Israeli policy.

Discussing the broader political and psychological shifts within Israeli society since 7 October, Mustafa said that the war had intensified anti-Palestinian sentiment and normalised increasingly extreme attitudes towards Palestinians.

"The fundamental shift is the desire for revenge against the Palestinians and treating them as a dehumanised population that can be annihilated, with a sense of relief following such actions," he said.

Mustafa also argued that religious narratives portraying the war as part of a broader struggle for salvation had gained influence, while much of Israeli society continued to view the events of 7 October in isolation from decades of occupation, siege and settlement expansion.

He said this had reinforced a widespread denial of Palestinian humanity and obscured the broader political context of the conflict.

Beyond domestic political shifts, the vote has drawn intense international scrutiny amid concerns over a potential resumption of war on Iran and its geopolitical and economic consequences.

Meanwhile, many Israelis, including expatriates who travelled back specifically to vote, hope the election outcome could help restore Israel's international standing, which has suffered significant damage in global public opinion following the war on Gaza.

Honida Ghanim, director of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies (MADAR), told The New Arab that Israel's international reputation had deteriorated sharply, particularly among Western publics, even as governments continued to provide political support.

"Israel's international standing has declined sharply, to the point that it is closer to a rogue state, at least at the level of public opinion, and the United States is the clearest illustration of this," she said.

Ghanim argued that the Trump administration had given Israel's far-right leadership considerable freedom to pursue its policies despite mounting international criticism and concerns over violations of international law.

She warned that one of the most dangerous election outcomes for Palestinians would be a political deadlock that left Netanyahu in power as caretaker prime minister for an extended period.

"The most dangerous possible outcome of the elections is therefore a stalemate, with Netanyahu's government remaining in office as a caretaker government for what could be two years under Trump," she said.

Ghanim warned that such a scenario could allow the Israeli right to intensify its policies of forced displacement and territorial control while enjoying continued backing from Washington.

Even a victory for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, she argued, would be unlikely to reverse Israel's international isolation or produce a fundamental shift in its policies towards Palestinians.

She suggested that Western governments might seek to rehabilitate Israel's image by presenting a new leadership as a departure from Netanyahu's far-right coalition, but questioned whether such a distinction would be credible.

Ghanim pointed to changing attitudes towards Israel in the United States, the difficulty of forming a stable alternative coalition and the continued support among mainstream Israeli politicians for policies that violate international law.

She also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's occupation, arguing that settlement expansion had become so deeply embedded in the Israeli political system that a change of government alone could not resolve the underlying issues.

"Israel has moved beyond the stage of repair: the settlement, which the world has regarded as a violation of international law, most notably in UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, is today Israel itself," Ghanim concluded.

item.title: Libya says international aviation restrictions lifted
item.description: ICAO has lifted Libya’s airspace restrictions, paving the way for a surge in international transit flights and increased revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Libya's Ministry of Transport said on Monday that the UN's International Civil Aviation Organisation removed airspace restrictions it issued in 2015 during the country's civil war.

The ministry said ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar announced the decision, formally issued on 23 October, at the opening of a meeting of civil aviation officials from the Middle East in Doha.

"This measure comes as a result of the notable progress made and the confidence placed in the capabilities of the Libyan civil aviation sector in recent times," the Tripoli-based Ministry of Transport said in a statement on its verified Facebook page.

In a separate statement, the ministry said the North African country has received requests for permits to transit Libyan airspace, which it characterised as "unprecedented demand from international airlines".

"The total number of permits registered for 2026-2027 winter season has surged to 61,968 flights per month, effective from this November," the ministry said, calling it a significant jump from an average of 2,000 transit flights per month during the 2025-2026 season.

"Such an increase will generate substantial financial revenues using Libyan airspace," it added.

Libya slid into chaos after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011. Three years later, a civil war broke out between armed factions vying for power, dividing the country between eastern and western administrations.

The war caused damage to up to 20 aircraft, including Airbus models, at Tripoli International Airport in 2014.

Few airlines currently operate flights in and out of Libya, and they have long been limited to destinations such as Tunisia, Jordan, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Sudan.

The ministry added that ICAO's decision would be circulated to all 193 member states for implementation.

item.title: US rapper Macklemore launches 'Free Palestine Tour'
item.description: Macklemore launches his Free Palestine Tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran drops him, drawing sold-out crowds and pro-Palestinian support.
item.content:encoded:
US rapper Macklemore launched his new "Free Palestine Tour" in Dublin on Monday after British pop star Ed Sheeran dropped him as a supporting act over pro-Palestinian comments.

At the first show in the Irish capital, promoters said the venue had sold out, and excited fans lined up outside to praise the 43-year-old's stance.

"Macklemore's support for Palestine is huge. He's stood up and he's put himself on the line instead of taking the easy way out," said Michael Keating, a 31-year-old who works in insurance, told AFP.

"He's risking his popularity, his future, his family's future, everything just for peace. And it is very important."

The "Thrift Shop" star was removed from Sheeran's US tour after shouting "Free Palestine!" on stage and telling Palestinians they were "not forgotten".

Sheeran has said tour promoters, not he, made the decision to drop Macklemore, provoking outrage among musicians and pro-Palestinian activists.

"The USA is supposed to be the country of free speech, and instead people are being shut down. (Sheeran) should have stood up for what Macklemore was doing," said Grainne Healy, a 60-year-old retiree who had come to the Dublin concert with a former schoolfriend.

Four other supporting artists, including American singer Finneas, also pulled out of Sheeran's tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and Sheeran later broke his silence on the situation in Gaza at a concert in Philadelphia, calling it "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

Last month Macklemore announced his Free Palestine Tour, with shows in London and Paris in late October and US dates also planned, saying all proceeds would benefit pro-Palestinian organisations.

Outside Dublin's 3Arena, traders sold fans half-Irish, half-Palestinian flags, Free Palestine bucket hats, and Palestinian-style keffiyeh scarves.

"Ever since (Macklemore) started talking about Palestine, it makes us like him even more," said one fan, Freya Dorrity, an 18-year-old student.

Maria Liddy, 40, wearing a red-and-white Palestinian-style keffiyeh scarf, said she was there "to show solidarity" with the people of Palestine, adding that "artists should never be censored in any capacity".

item.title: Jordan strikes groups in Syria after church attack
item.description: Jordan launches airstrikes in southern Syria after a deadly church attack killed nine people in Jordan, as authorities arrest three suspects.
item.content:encoded:
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.

It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.

Syria's state news agency SANA, citing a local health official, said the strikes across Daraa province in the country's south had killed eight civilians, including women and children.

Syria's government said that Jordan did not coordinate with it before launching deadly strikes on the country's south.

A Syrian government statement carried by state news agency SANA said "no prior coordination with the Syrian side was carried out concerning the military operation" by Jordan.

It said that authorities were investigating the strikes and discussing them with Amman while stressing the need for joint security coordination in border areas.

SANA quoted Syria's foreign ministry as saying that it had informed Jordan of "our complete reservation regarding the conduct of operations inside Syrian territory without prior coordination".

"Communication and coordination" was underway with Jordan "to address the repercussions of this incident in a manner that preserves security and the sovereignty of Syrian territory", it said.

Syria also closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions due to developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.

On Friday, gunmen killed nine people during a funeral service at the Greek Orthodox St George's Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate, southern Jordan.

Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.

Major General Abdullah al-Maaytah, Jordan's director of public security, on Monday named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.

The trio, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage, were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces.

"All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to hospital and are still receiving treatment," Maaytah told a press conference.

'We will show them'

One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan's state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. It added that there were no casualties among the security forces.

"This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it," Maaytah said.

Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging.

A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said.

Jordan's King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces "chased them to the very end".

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he wrote.

Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in a hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip.

"We will show them," he vowed.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".

"There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties," he said.

Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said, "we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan's security".

Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016, an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead.

On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.

Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed.

The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday.

item.title: Can Serbia's student movement now govern the country?
item.description: Serbia’s student protest movement ousts Aleksandar Vucic but faces challenges in tackling corruption, forming a government, and shaping relations with the EU.
item.content:encoded:
By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's election, Serbia's student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now comes the gritty business of governing, something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience with.

Tens of thousands took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.

But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?

The answers will determine Serbia's political stability, its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.

The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement's limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.

Winners, but can they stick together?

The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024, and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.

Without a figurehead, the students won widespread support before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.

The movement and some of the top candidates on its list give an idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.

It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia's former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia's accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.

Prominent figures include the head of the students' candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic; former central bank governor Dejan Soskic; and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students after their victory.

But it is uncertain whether any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.

"(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts," said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.

"We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system."

Reforming public institutions

Under Serbia's constitution, candidates for the government have 90 days to form a government once parliament convenes after the state election commission announces the final results.

Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid rising public and private debt, while any attempt to end corruption will require overhauling the police and intelligence services and reforming the judiciary.

State institutions require "detoxification" after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.

Prelevic warned that Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.

Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.

International relations

In Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.

"We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector," Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia's RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia's foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.

Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia's four-year-long invasion.

European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country fight corruption.

"I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms," said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.

item.title: 'Smells of freedom': Serbians hopeful after landmark election
item.description: Serbia’s student-led movement defeats Aleksandar Vucic’s party in a snap election, sparking celebrations and renewed hope for political change in Belgrade.
item.content:encoded:
Emotions ran high in Belgrade on Monday after a student-led movement upset the right-wing populist Aleksandar Vucic's party in Serbia's snap election.

A celebratory mood gripped the capital, with drivers honking their horns and passers-by holding up three fingers, the winning list's ballot number, and a Serbian greeting.

Many wore badges and other symbols of the student movement, while a large group of residents spent the day cleaning up a park between parliament and the presidency after Vucic loyalists, who had camped there for more than a year, fled.

The convincing upset victory in Sunday's vote follows nearly two years of anti-government protests and ends 14 years in power for Vucic's party.

On the city's streets, people told AFP that they felt hope, relief and exhilaration a day after the upset vote.

Unforgettable moment

"The moment we learned that he had conceded defeat is one that, I am certain, no one from my generation will ever forget," 23-year-old medical student Milutin Kandic told AFP, referring to Vucic's concession.

"People are now walking around freely, smiling, and some are crying," she said.

'Smells of freedom'

"Today, I think, we have finally found freedom," design student Katarina Malesevic said.

"You can feel it everywhere in Belgrade, at last, there is peace, and we can walk around," the 23-year-old said.

"We have just been walking around, looking at the people and the atmosphere, and you can feel that the air is completely different. Everything smells of freedom."

'Awakening'

Ljubisa Vujosevic, 75, said that he was "extremely pleased that the gap between the student list and Vucic's list was so wide and decisive that the latter have no longer any grounds for dissatisfaction or complaints.

"This change of government also means a political awakening among the people, the gaining of freedom and a change in how Serbia is portrayed in the international media."

'A celebration'

"At last, Serbia has won. The right thing has been done, and at the right time," Dragan Miladinovic, 73, said.

"What happened last night genuinely thrilled me," he said.

"I was at a celebration, and there were smiling faces everywhere. It was incredible."

item.title: Oil spill off UAE widens, prompting more beach closures
item.description: An oil spill off the UAE coast has expanded after a tanker strike, prompting beach closures and raising concerns about marine life and coastal pollution.
item.content:encoded:
Satellite images show that an oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.

Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated 24 October show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is nearing the shores of northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along the coastline.

Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.

October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.

The UAE said on Friday that it was working to contain oil leaking from an offshore tanker, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.

Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill came from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

Images from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.

Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.

The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that it temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.

"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Centre, told Reuters.

In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that they would close all beaches in the emirate until further notice.

The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.

item.title: What Israel's election could mean for the West Bank's future
item.description: Analysis: Across the political spectrum, Israel has abandoned any pretence of ending the occupation, halting settlements, or allowing Palestinian statehood
item.content:encoded:
Ramallah - Driving in the occupied West Bank, motorists are confronted with a barrage of campaign billboards for the Israeli elections.

The messages are geared towards Israeli settlers in the territory, not the Palestinians barred from voting.

Many of the posters express support for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party, as he draws his core voter base from settlers.

But there are also numerous posters for Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud party, including an ominous ad along the road to Jerusalem featuring Zohran Mamdani and Ayatollah Khomeini, warning against the power of Palestinian allies.

Against this radicalised backdrop, Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday in an election that many hope will spell the end of Netanyahu’s 19-year non-consecutive rule as prime minister.

The election comes in the wake of growing domestic resentment against Netanyahu over reports of his advanced knowledge of the 7 October attacks. 

Netanyahu’s Likud is seemingly facing an uphill battle against a bloc of four Jewish opposition parties that have joined forces to defeat him: the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beitenu party, and the Together alliance.

After the bloc’s establishment, the parties announced their goal was to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”. 

The elections are projected to be a near deadlock with no bloc winning an absolute majority. That outcome would trigger a period of negotiations and coalition building, where different parties must agree to come together to form a government.

But as settler violence reaches record levels in the West Bank, many Palestinians are left wondering: will any electoral outcome change the facts on the ground?

West Bank violence surges ahead of election

Approximately 750,000 Israelis live in settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem today, illegal under international law.

The settlers comprise a disproportionately powerful bloc in Israeli politics, despite accounting for around 7-8% of the total Israeli population.

Under Netanyahu’s current administration, which has brought settlers from the far-right fringes into a governing coalition, the settlers’ political influence has coincided with a rapid acceleration of settlement expansion.

But it’s unlikely that another government would slow the pace of settlement building.

“In order to ameliorate pressure from the settler lobby, the left often are tempted to expand settlements even more than the right,” Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, a political commentator and former Israeli diplomat, tells The New Arab.

“It [the opposition winning] might even lead to an increase in settlement construction in order to pay them off for concessions.”

As settlements expand, so does the pressure on Palestinians living nearby. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded an average of six settler attacks per day this year thus far.

Those numbers were released before the autumnal olive harvest commenced, when violence dramatically escalates as settlers launch coordinated attacks against Palestinian farmers in their olive groves.

And after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli checkpoint on 23 October, Ben-Gvir suggested that Palestinians should be barred from driving on the roads in the West Bank - or the land of Judea and Samaria, as he refers to it.

The Israeli army subsequently launched a collective punishment operation and began home demolitions across the neighbourhood where the shooters hailed from, displacing 400 families thus far.

Netanyahu has promised the biggest military occupation in the West Bank since 1967, though many experts say he may be bluffing to bolster support for Likud ahead of the elections. 

The election will now take place against a backdrop of expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement, fuelling fears that tensions across the West Bank are near boiling point.

“There are a lot of people in the Israeli security forces who want Palestinians to have a better quality of life, just so that the West Bank doesn't explode into another Intifada,” says Ben-Ephraim.

Projected electoral outcomes

Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar!, is seen as the leading centrist alternative for Prime Minister.

Eisenkot has promised to rein in settler violence while firmly opposing a two-state solution. Once the Israeli army Chief of Staff, Eisenkot was the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2006, which advocates "disproportionate force” against Israel’s perceived enemies. 

“None of the Israeli governments that would come is going to give a Palestinian state to the Palestinians, but change may come, depending on how you define change,” Muhanned Qafesha, a Palestinian journalist from Hebron, tells The New Arab.

An Eisenkot government could mean greater restrictions on settler violence and a slight change in settlement policy, without fundamentally interfering with the settler project.

Alternatively, if Netanyahu secures another term or temporarily heads a caretaker government if a stalemate arises, the settlers in his administration may feel their time is limited and accelerate their existing plans for the annexation of the West Bank.

As it stands, neither major political bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.

While the opposition bloc has sworn not to form a coalition with either of the Palestinian parties on the ballot - the left-leaning Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) - that pledge may not hold, as they could be a potential lifeline to forming a government.

“The two Arab parties can maybe win like 15 seats or something, and this will make a huge difference because if they can make a coalition with the opposition, they can kick out Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir,” Qafesha tells The New Arab.

“I do believe that the opposition in Israel is saying they won’t form a coalition with the Arabs because they want to get as many votes from the Jewish community as possible. But if they need the Arab parties to form a coalition to kick out Netanyahu, they might do it,” he adds. 

But any coalition will also depend on parties that oppose Palestinian statehood, and thus a fundamental shift in Israel’s approach to the occupation is virtually impossible.

Even if Eisenkot eventually forms a government, his fragile coalition across the ideological spectrum would struggle to agree on significant changes towards settlement policy in the West Bank. 

Will the opposition improve life in the West Bank?

The 3.4 million Palestinians living in the West Bank under military occupation cannot vote in Israeli elections, but Palestinian citizens of Israel can.

Arab voters have long boycotted Israeli elections, but there has been a recent push for their participation - with a record turnout for the group anticipated.

The vast majority of Palestinians in the West Bank want Palestinian citizens of Israel to vote in the elections to improve their daily lives, explains Qafesha, who himself cannot vote.

He believes an administration without settlers at the helm may alleviate some of the daily struggles in the West Bank.

“We live in hell. We just want to breathe,” Qafesha says. 

But if Netanyahu finally goes down, some Palestinians believe Western governments may attempt to rehabilitate Israel’s image under a new administration - and lift the recent round of European sanctions against settlements that were years in the making.

“The upcoming election is between fascists and ultra-fascists. If Netanyahu loses the chance to lead the next government, his loss can be used to alleviate the pressure that is just starting to build from the international community,” Mazin Qumsiyeh, Director of Palestine’s Natural History Museum in Bethlehem, tells The New Arab.

Yet Qafesha remains adamant that the reality on the ground is more important than the views of the international community, which could promote a new government as an example of Israel’s return to democracy.

“Over the past three years, Israel has killed more than 100,000 Palestinians in Gaza. What has the world done for us? Has anything changed in our life? I don't want the view of the world to change at the expense of the blood of Palestinian children, whether it's in Gaza, West Bank, or Jerusalem,” says Qafesha.

An opposition government less reliant on far-right parties could potentially curb some of the policies driving unchecked violence and forced displacement, ameliorating a few of the numerous obstacles to a dignified life under occupation. But any improvement would likely be limited in scope.

“If the opposition wins, the intensity of the ethnic cleansing will probably somewhat lessen, but it's only temporary,” concludes Ben-Ephraim.

“I think that the Israeli public opinion has turned so far in favour of genocide and ethnic cleansing that it will just be a respite at best.”

Kate McMahon is a freelance journalist and foreign correspondent focused on the Middle East and South Asia. She reports on environmental change, human rights, and geopolitical conflicts

Follow her on Instagram: @katemontanaa

Edited by Charlie Hoyle

item.title: Algeria's Kaylia Nemour wins double gold at gymnastics worlds
item.description: Kaylia Nemour turned around a difficult start at the WOrld Artistic Gymnastics Championships, winning two gold for her country.
item.content:encoded:
Algerian gymnast Kaylia Nemour won gold on the balance beam on Sunday at the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships, a day after claiming another gold medal on the uneven bars.

The two gold medals came after a difficult start for the 19-year-old, whose poor vault performance on Friday dashed her hopes of an all-around medal in Rotterdam.

"I'm extremely happy, but I'm completely in shock. In shock at this gold medal on beam," Nemour was quoted by International Gymnast as saying. "My goal was to do a nice routine, and that's what I did, so I was already proud of myself. And with the score, I was hoping it would be enough for a medal. And now, having the gold medal is unimaginable. I think I'll need a lot of time to digest it. Maybe a month, knowing me."

Nemour was first to compete in the uneven bars final, scoring 14.566 before seven other gymnasts took their turns. China's Zhang Qingyang finished second with the same score, with Nemour taking gold on the execution-score tiebreak.

"I knew there was the Chinese gymnast, last year's world champion, who is extremely strong, with a big start value and exceptional cleanliness," she said. "And then we had the same score, so I think it was the execution score that made the difference, and it's exceptional."

Nemour's success at the championships was celebrated by Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on social media on Sunday.

"Warmest congratulations, Kaylia... Like all Algerians, I am happy and proud of you for this double gold at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in the Netherlands," Tebboune wrote.

"You always deserve our full appreciation for making the nation’s flag proud. Long live Algeria."

item.title: Israel's Hebron raid displaces nearly 4,000 Palestinians
item.description: Israeli forces have displaced nearly 4,000 families in Hebron, including hundreds of children, as Netanyahu rejected military advice to end the operation
item.content:encoded:
Israeli forces have forced nearly 4,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron since Friday, leaving hundreds of families displaced as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly rejected military advice to end the operation in the southern occupied West Bank.

The number of displaced Palestinians reached around 3,971 on Monday, according to figures reported by Palestinian news agency WAFA. This includes approximately 200 children under the age of two, at least 258 elderly people and 137 pregnant women.

Riyad Khamis, spokesperson for Hebron’s Follow-up, Support and Relief Committee, said 619 families had been affected, including 266 unable to find safe accommodation.

More than 80 Palestinians have been arrested, while hundreds of others have been detained and interrogated, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club. Israeli troops have also raided and ransacked hundreds of homes, leaving residents unsure when they will be allowed to return.

Hebron's Governor Khaled Dudin reported that Israeli authorities established 128 gates and 120 checkpoints across the southern governorate, saying that it fragments the area and severly restricts movement as well as access to healthcare and basic services.

The Israeli operation followed a shooting attack on Friday in which two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron. Israeli forces killed both gunmen.

Netanyahu subsequently ordered the evacuation of residents from the neighbourhood where the attackers lived ahead of house-to-house searches. The ensuing assault has extended to Palestinian homes, businesses and industrial facilities.

In a statement issued on Monday, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) warned that these actions "raise grave concerns about ethnic cleansing and collective punishment".

"Palestinians in Hebron are being driven from their homes and cut off from healthcare and basic supplies," Aseel Baidoun, MAP's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications, said. "This is collective punishment. People are being punished simply for being Palestinians."

A home turned into a military outpost

For Ramadan Faisal al-Hashlamoun, a 47-year-old Palestinian displaced with his family, the uncertainty centres on a house he says Israeli soldiers have turned into a military outpost.

Speaking to The New Arab, Hashlamoun said troops entered his home and took it over because it overlooks the main road. He has been unable to return since.

His household numbers 10, including children, the youngest of whom is aged 12. The family has been split apart since residents were ordered to leave the entire area, he said.

"You can only feel at ease in your own home," he told The New Arab.

Hashlamoun said neighbours had heard the sound of objects being smashed inside his house, leaving him deeply worried about the condition of his belongings, including money, gold and other personal possessions. Unable to enter, he has no way of checking what has happened to them.

He also said Israeli forces had marked four X signs on the exterior walls of the house – a mark that has since been circulating in images across social media on multiple houses whose inhabitants had been forcibly displaced.

Israeli occupation forces mark several Palestinian homes with "X" signs in the Ein Deir Bahha neighborhood of Hebron, south of the occupied West Bank, after forcibly displacing their owners. https://t.co/3lNmvZ4yO7

— Quds News Network (@QudsNen) October 24, 2026

At the time of the interview, his family had received no aid or essential supplies, although Hebron Municipality had contacted them. He told The New Arab that his immediate concerns were the separation of his family and the uncertain fate of their home.

Local relief officials said on Monday that a first batch of aid and basic supplies was being distributed to displaced and affected families. Hundreds of other residents remained trapped inside homes in neighbouring areas, according to WAFA.

Israeli forces have sealed off the neighbourhoods of Deir Baha and al-Jilda, where much of the displacement has taken place, while imposing closures at entrances to Hebron and surrounding towns and refugee camps. The restrictions have disrupted movement and access to homes, businesses and services.

A staff member at a MAP local partner in Hebron described the sudden incursion, saying it was "unexpected to see this kind of mass forced displacement" where residents including persons with disabilities, pregnant women, and children "left their homes carrying whatever they could. A lot of those who were displaced are elderly people with chronic illnesses, meaning there is a need for medicines as well."

Netanyahu reportedly rejected an end to the operation

The sudden displacement of thousands of residents comes as Israeli media reported that Netanyahu had rejected Israeli Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir's recommendation to end the operation, despite being told its objectives had been 'achieved' and there was no justification for continuing to prevent residents from returning home.

Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported on Monday that Zamir had recommended ending the operation, telling Netanyahu during a situational assessment on Sunday that its objectives had been met.

According to Kan’s reporting, Zamir said there was no operational justification for continuing the raid and no legal justification for keeping displaced Palestinians from their homes.

Netanyahu nevertheless insisted that the operation continue despite the military having wanted to announce as early as Saturday night that the operation was winding down.

The reported disagreement emerged a day before Israel’s general election, as displaced Palestinian families remained unable to return.

“Across the West Bank, we are living in high uncertainty, especially with Israeli elections this week; there is no safe place due to the situation deteriorating day by day," MAP's staff member said.

"We are wondering if this will last days, weeks, or months. People are worried about forced displacement and it's becoming a real fear, especially when looking at what happened in Jenin and Tulkarem in the past couple of years. We are losing trust in the international community."

item.title: Israel's mediacide in Gaza seeks to bury genocide evidence: UN
