item.description: A UN report exposes Israel's 'mediacide' in Gaza, detailing how journalists are killed and media destroyed to erase evidence of genocide.
item.content:encoded:
Israel is attempting to "systematically eliminate" journalists in occupied Palestine in a bid to cover up evidence of genocide and war crimes, according to a UN report.

The paper, authored by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, says that "destruction of truth" has been integral to the assault on Gaza, and describes Israel's attempts to control information as "mediacide".

Israeli forces have killed hundreds of journalists in the occupied territories since October 2023 while most of Gaza's infrastructure lies in ruins.

“Genocide is never sustained by killing alone. It requires destroying the conditions in which killing can be seen, documented, remembered and judged,” Albanese said while presenting the report to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday.

The report identifies three ways in which Israel and its supporters attempt to destroy or hide evidence of crimes committed in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

These include the systematic targeting of journalists and communications infrastructure, and the Israeli government's attempts to censor and manipulate information.

It also highlights the complicity of Western news organisations and technology platforms, which it accuses of promoting Israeli narratives and suppressing Palestinian voices.

"These practices have not merely accompanied genocide but have facilitated its commission and obstructed accountability," the report reads.

The UN documented the killing of almost 300 Palestinian journalists between October 2023 and February this year. Hundreds of others have been wounded or unlawfully detained by Israeli authorities.

Some were killed in indiscriminate attacks while at least 70 are known to have been deliberately targeted.

Israel has replicated its assault on Palestinian journalists in its other conflicts in Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, where dozens of other media workers have been killed in airstrikes.

The report says that the Israeli military has wiped out more than 80% of Gaza's communications infrastructure and damaged another 12%. By October 2025, Israeli forces had destroyed 125 media offices and institutions, including news agency headquarters, broadcast towers and radio stations, it says.

Blackouts caused by the damage have prevented local journalists from broadcasting events and people outside the strip from verifying information.

The destruction has gone hand-in-hand with the Israeli government's media restrictions, which have prevented foreign journalists reporting from Gaza and censored thousands of articles related to the war.

"In the ongoing genocide, the systematic elimination of media witnesses and the destruction of the means of documentation are probative of genocidal intent," the report says.

"They reveal an effort not only to destroy a protected group, but also to destroy the conditions in which that destruction can be seen, documented, remembered and ultimately adjudicated," it continues.

item.title: Fears for Palestinians as Israel election observers allowed guns
item.description: Israel's high court rejected a petition to prevent 2,000 'observers' carrying guns in Palestinian-majority elections, raising fears of intimidation
item.content:encoded:
Israel’s High Court of Justice on Sunday rejected a petition to ban polling station officials and party representatives from carrying weapons at voting sites during Tuesday’s general election, amid concerns from rights groups that an armed presence could intimidate Palestinian voters and undermine the electoral process.

Filed on Thursday by Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel and the Joint List, the petition argued that "an armed presence could deter voters, undermine the electoral process, and could even lead to violent confrontations that endanger human life".

Adalah attorney Ariel Remez, who led the petition, told The New Arab: "by declining to intervene, the Court has left Palestinian voters exposed to intimidation and placed responsibility for any violence on Election Day on the police and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a minister previously convicted of incitement to racism who has driven the mass arming of Israeli civilians."

The petition followed an announcement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism parties that they would deploy approximately 2,000 'observers' to polling stations in what they called "Arab population centres". Police also issued a directive allowing licensed gun owners to carry firearms at polling stations.

More than one million Palestinian citizens of Israel are eligible to vote, with their turnout potentially decisive in determining whether Netanyahu can form another government.

"Our concern is that these so-called 'observers' will take advantage of their authorization to enter multiple polling stations during the day, thus recreating the 1981 'National Ballot Security Task Force' in the [gubernatorial] elections in New Jersey," Remez said, referring to the Republican National Committee (RNC)-led initiative that deployed armed, off-duty police officers and used targeted mailing lists in minority neighbourhoods.

"We have no doubt that the Likud and its partners from the extreme right intend to copy the RNC’s playbook of voter suppression of minorities," he added.

Adalah argues that fears of intimidation of Palestinian citizens are heightened by the sharp rise in licensed firearms under Ben-Gvir, whose tenure has seen the number double from around 150,000 to 300,000.

"The danger lies in the branding of the entire Palestinian public in Israel as prone to voter fraud, amid widespread incitement against Palestinian citizens," Remez said.

"At the same time, the violent settler movement in the West Bank is increasingly active inside Israel, including, for example, an outpost established near Majd al-Krum. Against this backdrop, the threats to Arab votes are real and immediate."

Majd al-Krum is a Palestinian village in the Galillee region where settlers recently set up a West Bank-style outpost.

Adalah also pointed to a survey published by the Israel Democracy Institute in November 2025, in which 81 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel surveyed said civilians carrying weapons in public spaces made them feel less safe.

The 2,000 individuals set to be deployed have no legal authority to oversee the voting process. Police are required to enforce strict rules governing who may enter polling stations and what they are permitted to do there.

Israel’s Election Law prohibits campaigning inside polling stations and wearing clothing or symbols identifying a political party. It also bars individuals from interfering with another person’s vote.

Adalah will operate an election-day hotline, Remez told The New Arab, with legal teams working alongside Arab parties to monitor and respond to voting irregularities.

"Where necessary, we will turn to the Central Elections Committee, the police and, if needed, the courts. We will advise activists who contact us to carefully document any disruption at polling stations, so that we can assess whether the integrity of the results has been affected," he said.

item.title: Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran
item.description: Hezbollah has received fresh funding from Iran and is rebuilding its military capabilities as tensions with Israel raise fears of renewed conflict in Lebanon.
item.content:encoded:
Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.

The group, founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.

Invading Israeli forces now occupy its heartland of villages in southern Lebanon, and political pressure has built up in Beirut for its disarmament.

It nevertheless remains committed to fighting Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.

One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the group received from Tehran to aid displaced families in its Shia heartlands, which Reuters reported earlier this month.

The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.

In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office said Israel's occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right. It rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.

Israel's military declined to comment. Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters questions.

A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.

Hezbollah on alert

Hezbollah's effort comes amid continued tensions in the wider Middle Eastern conflict ignited by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.

Hezbollah opened fire in support of Iran on 2 March, triggering an Israeli offensive that killed more than 4,000 people and uprooted a quarter of Lebanon's population, mostly members of Hezbollah's Shia Muslim constituency.

Hostilities largely abated over the summer as an interim Iran-US deal included a Lebanon ceasefire and Washington-mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel. Full-scale hostilities have not resumed in Lebanon despite the collapse of the US-Iranian deal, though Israel continues deadly strikes in the south.

Hezbollah is on alert for a possible US-Iran escalation, potentially reigniting the Lebanon front.

Sources told Reuters the group has not yet fully prepared its stockpiles or fighting force.

Hezbollah is still restocking, acknowledging this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to it and were intended for use against Israel. A ⁠Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters they were specifically ​for its explosive drones.

Israel's remote warfare proved a challenge, sources say

The group will also need to repair its command-and-control capabilities after losses on key fronts, including the flashpoint town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, according to one Lebanese source and three security officials.

They said Hezbollah's tactic of operating in small units and rationing the use of anti-tank rockets left some units isolated on those fronts, struggling to confront Israel's remotely operated systems, including weaponised drones and armed remote-controlled vehicles.

The Israeli military told Reuters it uses remotely-operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce troops' threat exposure.

Hezbollah has not explicitly said whether it would take part in the eruption of fresh hostilities, but its media office said it was wary of giving Israeli leaders any justification to escalate in Lebanon, particularly as the group was concerned about its constituents being displaced once more.

item.title: Lebanon watches Israel vote amid fears of renewed war
item.description: Lebanese officials are seeking to keep the country out of a potential US-Israeli war with Iran, amid fears of renewed Israeli attacks after Tuesday's election
item.content:encoded:
Lebanon is closely watching Tuesday's Israeli parliamentary election and the US midterms on 3 November amid fears of renewed war in the region, as Lebanese officials intensify contacts with Hezbollah to prevent the country from being drawn into another conflict.

The concerns centre on the possibility of new US-Israeli attacks on Iran following the elections, with Lebanon particularly vulnerable as diplomatic negotiations remain stalled and Israeli military operations continue in the south.

The New Arab has learned that intensive domestic and international contacts are under way to keep Lebanon out of any wider confrontation.

Consultations are taking place between advisers to Lebanon's three top leaders - the president, prime minister, and Speaker of Parliament, while Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri has been urging Hezbollah not to get involved if war erupts between Iran and the United States and Israel.

Hezbollah has expressed concern for Lebanon's stability, but its position remains dependent on developments on the ground and Israeli actions inside Lebanon, according to information obtained by The New Arab.

The group has also discussed the possibility of military support with Iranian officials, although there is considerable hesitation about taking such a step given the potentially devastating consequences of another war, particularly for Hezbollah's support base.

The consultations follow media reports that Hezbollah had assured Berri it would not intervene militarily in support of Iran, despite having previously joined the war on 2 March.

A Hezbollah parliamentary source told The New Arab that the group prioritised Lebanon's stability and accused Washington and Israel of threatening the country.

"Instead of focusing on us, the Lebanese state should act to stop Israeli attacks and stop submitting to American dictates that will bring no good to our country," the source said.

Asked whether Hezbollah had promised Berri not to intervene, the source declined to confirm the reports.

"We are confident in Iran's capabilities, and as we always say, the final word belongs to the battlefield," the source said.

Hezbollah denies taking orders from Iran

Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah separately rejected claims on Monday that the group's military decisions were dictated by Tehran.

"The resistance's decision is a Lebanese decision taken by its leadership, and no one abroad or at home dictates it," he said in a statement distributed by Hezbollah's media office.

Fadlallah insisted that Iran had never asked Hezbollah to intervene militarily on its behalf against US-Israeli attacks.

"On the contrary, when we meet Iranian officials, they ask what we want and what is in our interest and Lebanon's interest so they can support us," he said.

He also rejected calls for Hezbollah's disarmament while Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory, arguing that the issue should be addressed through national dialogue after Israeli withdrawal, the return of displaced residents and the release of prisoners.

Lebanese officials are concerned that Israel could intensify military operations after Tuesday's Knesset election, potentially provoking a Hezbollah response and reigniting the war.

Israel has continued its attacks despite the framework agreement signed on 26 June, while insisting on maintaining its designated security zone in southern Lebanon.

The continued military operations and Israel's refusal to compromise have obstructed negotiations, including military-level talks held in Tampa, Florida, last week.

On Saturday, Israel's public broadcaster reported that the military had raised its alert level ahead of the election, deploying tens of thousands of soldiers across several fronts, including Lebanon, Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Military officials said there was no specific intelligence warning of an imminent attack, but confirmed preparations for an exercise simulating a surprise assault.

Israeli artillery targeted Khiam, Zawtar al-Sharqiya, Mansouri, Wadi al-Hujeir and Wadi al-Slouqi in southern Lebanon on Monday, highlighting fears that renewed fighting could erupt regardless of the election outcome.

item.title: Italian father, son recall abuse by Israeli forces in West Bank
item.description: Israel detained and deported two Italian activists from the West Bank, raising concerns over efforts to deter internationals from documenting Israel's abuses.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli violations in the occupied West Bank are increasingly targeting foreign activists as well as Palestinians, with Italian NGO researcher and campaigner Manuel Tartarotti telling The New Arab how he and his father, Alberto, were arrested by Israeli police near Masafer Yatta in the southern occupied West Bank on 20 October.

The two men were blindfolded, transported in a military jeep to a base in Hebron, beaten and detained for 24 hours on suspicion of "terrorism" before being deported to Italy, according to Tartarotti.

Manuel Tartarotti, 35, is a doctoral researcher in NGO management at the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano in Italy, while his father, Alberto, is 67.

The Tartarotti family's West Bank experience

"They didn't tell us where they were taking us, and they beat me in the back of the vehicle. I didn't know what was going to happen. I was scared," Tartarotti said.

The father and son arrived in the West Bank on 18 October to deliver funds raised in Italy to Youth of Sumud, a Palestinian grassroots organisation that received the Alexander Langer International Award in 2024 in recognition of its peaceful resistance in the southern Hebron Hills.

Tartarotti said he had travelled with Palestinian members of the group and three Al Jazeera journalists to monitor and document demolitions in Palestinian villages after his friend Sami Huraini, a Palestinian activist and one of the group's founders, informed him that further demolitions were taking place.

Around half an hour later, Israeli police arrived and checked their IDs before taking the two Italians away.

They were interrogated, fingerprinted and had DNA samples taken, Tartarotti said. They remained handcuffed until the evening.

Israeli authorities subsequently informed them that they would be deported over suspected links to terrorism because they had entered an area declared off-limits and were associated with Youth of Sumud, which Israel designates as a terrorist organisation.

According to Tartarotti, they were told that their presence with the group, which does not advocate violence, meant they were linked to a terrorist organisation.

Israeli police, however, said the two men were suspected of illegally entering a military zone and having links to Al-Haq, a Palestinian human rights organisation that Israel also designates as a terrorist group.

Police also said the pair had participated in olive harvesting without a permit near the village of At-Tuwani and had fled with Palestinian farmers into a military training zone when officers arrived.

Tartarotti said their phones and social media posts were searched, after which they were both given a 10-year ban from entering Israel.

He expressed regret that he would no longer be able to return to the area and feared that the consequences of being accused of terrorism could last a lifetime.

He believes the deportations are intended to deter international solidarity activists from travelling to the West Bank to support Palestinians during the olive harvest season.

Tartarotti said Israeli authorities had provided no concrete evidence of any crime. During questioning, officers showed them social media posts published by the two men, which he said expressed support for Palestine and opposition to the Israeli occupation rather than advocating terrorism.

The authorities then handed them documents revoking their visas and imposing the 10-year entry ban. He and his father were not considering appealing the decision, he added.

However, Tartarotti remains in contact with Luisa Morgantini, president of Assopace Palestina, an organisation promoting solidarity with the Palestinian people, peace and human rights.

Morgantini, who has previously been expelled from the region, hopes to organise a collective return trip for people who have received deportation orders, he added.

Palestinian activists face greater risks

Tartarotti said Palestinian activists faced the greatest dangers, risking their lives daily to document violations by Israeli soldiers and settlers.

"All my friends have been arrested and tortured simply for documenting violations by settlers and the army," he said.

He remains in touch with members of Youth of Sumud, who, he said, continue to face repeated attacks by settlers and the military.

Tartarotti also referred to the detention of Italian women activists in the al-Buweib area of Hebron on 22 October while they were accompanying Palestinian farmers.

He said he had met the women at a guesthouse run by Youth of Sumud but did not know them personally. He added that they, too, were due to be deported.

"What happened to the women was the same as what happened to us: people are on the ground accompanying Palestinians and witnessing what is happening, only to be detained and expelled," he said.

No contact with Italian authorities

Tartarotti said neither he nor his father had contacted an Italian diplomatic mission in Israel following their arrest, and they had received no assistance from Italy's foreign ministry or government.

Upon their return, Italian authorities briefly listened to their account before returning their passports, he said.

He believes such incidents are specifically intended to discourage international volunteers and observers from travelling to the West Bank and documenting abuses by settlers and the Israeli military.

European governments, beginning with Italy, should acknowledge what he described as Israeli violations of international law, he said, arguing that Israel systematically treats the West Bank as a colony under military rule.

Tartarotti, who has visited the West Bank for several years, said conditions had steadily deteriorated, particularly since 7 October 2023.

"Palestinians live in terrible conditions. They are constantly afraid of demolitions, arbitrary arrests without trial, and the confiscation of land, livestock and equipment," he said.

"Settlers have become more violent. People are killed daily by settlers and the army, yet very little is said about it."

He added that the presence of international volunteers had previously provided a degree of protection for Palestinian activists, as Israeli soldiers were more cautious about committing abuses in front of foreign observers.

That protection has significantly weakened, he said, with international activists now also facing detention, arrest and deportation.

Their expulsion, he warned, further restricts the ability to document events in the West Bank and communicate them to the outside world.

item.title: Trump praises Libya after 'sh*thole countries' backlash
item.description: Trump appeared to climb down from remarks made during a campaign rally, after officials from across the Libyan political divide expressed their anger.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has issued a statement praising the Libyan people after his earlier remarks describing the country as "terror-infested" sparked protests from Libyan officials and prompted the summoning of the US chargé d'affaires.

Writing on his Truth Social platform on Sunday evening, Trump praised Libya and its people while urging the country to tackle "illegal migration".

"The Libyan people are proud, resilient, hospitable, and deserving of peace and prosperity. The United States and Libya share a strong and enduring partnership in combating terrorism, building on our historic success in defeating ISIS in Libya together," he said.

"We respect the Libyan people and the sacrifices that brave Libyans made fighting ISIS, the common enemy of both our peoples, but Libya cannot remain a corridor for illegal migration, and this must end now."

Trump's post came after he made derogatory remarks about Libya during an election rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday.

During the rally, Trump attacked Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, accusing him of sponsoring a bill that allowed large numbers of immigrants to enter the US from countries he described as "infested with terrorism".

The president also referred to Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia as "sh*thole countries".

The remarks sparked anger in Libya, where the internationally recognised government's Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned Inga Hiemink, the US chargé d'affaires, on Sunday.

The ministry delivered an official diplomatic protest note demanding clarification of Washington's position and a correction of Trump's remarks.

It also emphasised that Libya is a sovereign state and would not accept its name or people being dragged into foreign electoral disputes.

The Tripoli-based High Council of State also issued a statement, declaring: "Libya will not be humiliated, and history does not bend for the arrogant."

Trump's remarks also drew criticism from Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), based in the country's east.

Haftar said electoral debates could not be used as "a justification for insulting nations or undermining the dignity of their people".

"Libya is an independent, sovereign state, and its national dignity is above all considerations," he added.

The LNA-aligned House of Representatives in Tobruk also condemned Trump's remarks, saying they contained "descriptions that undermine the standing of the Libyan state and run counter to the principles of mutual respect and political and diplomatic responsibility in international relations".

item.title: Israel election 2026 explained as Netanyahu faces key vote
item.description: Palestinian voters could potentially play a pivotal role in Tuesday's election, which could have far-reaching consequences for Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli voters head to the polls on Tuesday in a closely fought election that will determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and the direction of Israel's policies towards Palestinians.

The vote pits a coalition of opposition parties led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot against the far-right bloc led by Netanyahu, whose opponents accuse him of undermining Israel's democratic institutions.

It is the first Israeli election since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 and Israel's subsequent genocidal war on Gaza, which has been followed by wider regional conflicts involving Lebanon, Iran and Yemen.

While much of the campaign has focused on Netanyahu's leadership, the war and domestic divisions, the outcome will also affect millions of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank who have no vote in the election.

Palestinian citizens of Israel, meanwhile, could play a decisive role in determining the balance of power in the Knesset, even as the main Jewish-led political blocs remain reluctant to cooperate with them.

How will the vote work?

Polling stations will open at 7am on Tuesday and close at 10pm.

Major Israeli news organisations will publish exit polls shortly after voting ends, with counting beginning the same evening.

More than three dozen parties are contesting the election, with around 7.4 million people eligible to vote at polling stations across Israel.

Israel uses proportional representation, meaning voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate. The 120 seats in the Knesset are allocated according to each party's share of the national vote.

Candidates enter parliament according to their positions on their party's electoral list.

Parties must win at least 3.25% of the vote to enter the Knesset, equivalent to four seats.

No single party has ever secured an outright majority, meaning Israeli governments have always depended on coalitions.

When will the results be announced?

The official results must be declared by 4 November, although the likely distribution of seats should become clear as early as Wednesday morning.

Attention will then turn to coalition negotiations, with parties seeking to assemble a parliamentary majority of at least 61 seats.

After the official results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions before selecting a Knesset member to attempt to form a government.

These negotiations could take weeks, particularly if neither of the main blocs wins enough seats to govern.

What are the polls saying?

The final opinion polls suggest that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition coalition led by Eisenkot is on course to secure a majority.

Surveys published over the weekend put the opposition on 54 to 56 seats, compared with around 50 for Netanyahu's Likud-led alliance.

Eisenkot's Yashar party was projected to become the largest party with 22 to 23 seats, ahead of Likud on 19 to 21.

The polls also pointed to gains for the far right, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party projected to win eight seats.

But the remaining seats could prove crucial.

Parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel were projected to win between 14 and 16 seats, potentially leaving them with considerable influence over whether a government can be formed.

Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian-led parties, leaving questions over how the opposition could secure the parliamentary support it needs.

Could Palestinian voters decide the election?

Palestinian citizens of Israel account for a substantial share of the electorate, but their political representation has long been constrained by divisions between parties, low turnout and the reluctance of major Jewish-led parties to include them in governing coalitions.

This election could nevertheless give their parties considerable influence over whether Netanyahu remains in power.

The two main Arab-majority electoral lists are Ra'am, also known as the United Arab List, and the Joint List, bringing together Hadash, Balad and Ta'al.

Their performance will depend partly on turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes could influence both the number of seats won by Arab-led parties and the overall balance of the Knesset.

In an interview with The New Arab, Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh highlighted the importance of Palestinian voters in an election where neither main bloc appears assured of a majority.

The campaign has also been marked by attempts to exclude Palestinian-led parties and candidates.

Israel's Central Elections Committee voted in September to bar the Joint List and Ra'am from contesting the election, but the Supreme Court overturned the decision.

The court nevertheless upheld the disqualification of Abu Shehadeh over an article in which he described the 7 October attacks as an important historical event.

The episode has renewed questions about the political rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the limits placed on their participation in Israeli politics.

Netanyahu has also repeatedly portrayed the possibility of opposition cooperation with Arab-led parties as a campaign warning, seeking to pressure his rivals into ruling out such an arrangement.

What about Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank?

Millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip cannot vote in the election that will help determine the policies governing their lives.

The next Israeli government will have a major influence over military operations, movement restrictions, settlement expansion and the future of Gaza.

In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians face an expanding network of military checkpoints, road closures and settler attacks.

Israel has also announced the closure of land crossings into the West Bank for election day, adding to restrictions that have intensified since October 2023.

In Gaza, the central questions include whether Israel will ease its blockade, withdraw troops from occupied areas, allow displaced Palestinians to return home and permit reconstruction after three years of devastating war.

However, Netanyahu's principal challengers have offered little indication that a change in government would bring a fundamental shift in Israeli policy towards Palestinian statehood or the occupation.

Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state, while other prominent opposition figures have supported Israel's military campaigns and taken hardline positions towards Gaza.

Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, whose party is part of the opposition coalition, has criticised Netanyahu for being too soft on Gaza and called for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled.

Meanwhile, far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have advocated annexing Palestinian territory and ethnically cleansing the Palestinians.

The election could therefore change Israel's leadership without necessarily bringing major changes to the policies Palestinians face.

 

 

What are the main election issues?

Netanyahu's opponents have sought to make the vote a referendum on his leadership, focusing on the security failures surrounding the 7 October attack, his long-running corruption trial and Israel's growing international isolation.

According to the Israel Democracy Institute, the October 2023 attack is expected to play an important role in the voting decisions of more than two-thirds of the electorate.

Other major issues include military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and Netanyahu's attempts to overhaul the judiciary in 2023, which sparked widespread protests.

The election also comes after years of Israeli military operations in Gaza and regional conflicts involving Hezbollah, Iran and the Houthis.

Yet there is considerable overlap between the main Jewish-led parties on questions relating to Palestinian rights, the occupation and Israel's military operations.

While opposition politicians have criticised Netanyahu's handling of the wars and the diplomatic damage caused by his government, few have advocated a fundamental reversal of settlement expansion or a renewed peace process leading to Palestinian statehood.

The most explicit calls for annexation and Palestinian displacement have come from the far right, particularly Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.

What happens if coalition talks fail?

If neither bloc can assemble 61 seats, Israel could face prolonged negotiations over a possible minority government or another election.

A minority government would need support or abstentions from parties outside the governing coalition to survive key parliamentary votes.

That could make Palestinian-led parties particularly important, even if they are excluded from formal coalition agreements.

If negotiations fail altogether, another election could be called in 2027, with Netanyahu potentially remaining as caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office.

The result could therefore leave Israel facing continued political deadlock, with Palestinian parties holding potentially important seats but little guarantee of a role in government.

For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, the immediate consequences will depend less on which party wins the most seats than on the policies the next government adopts towards the occupation, military operations, settlements and displacement.

item.title: Mecca pact countries in Iran in bid to stop war restarting
item.description: Saudi Arabia, Iran and regional allies seek to prevent renewed war as Egypt backs Saudi defence and UN experts raise Gaza genocide allegations.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome,

Here are the updates:

- Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from resuming.

- Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia to defend itself - a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.

- The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.

- A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday.

item.title: How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
item.description: Analysis: Turkey has entrenched its forces in Syria and Iraq, but shifting political realities could now test its resolve to stay
item.content:encoded:
Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has clarified that Turkey will retain its military presence in Iraq and Syria until certain conditions are met.

The original justifications for Turkey’s cross-border deployments have dwindled in recent years. Now, analysts believe Ankara is offering new justifications for its open-ended military presence in these neighbouring states.

“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said in a recent interview.

“When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered.”

Open-ended conditions

Turkey sent troops into Syria in 2016. Its cross-border operations primarily focused on targeting the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

The SDF were a coalition formed by the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK)’s main Syria affiliate, which became an invaluable ad hoc US ally against Islamic State (IS).

Early this year, following a Turkish-backed offensive by the new Syrian government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the SDF agreed to integrate its fighters into the new Syrian military.

Complete SDF integration could remove Turkey’s decade-long justification for retaining troops in much of northern Syria.

“Ankara conditions its decision to withdraw from Syria not only on border security and the elimination of the terrorist threat in Syria, but also on the al-Sharaa government’s ability to establish state authority throughout the country,” Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, told The New Arab.

“This condition could signal Ankara’s desire to maintain a Turkish military presence and use it as leverage against, for example, Israel if tensions in southern Syria escalate into military confrontation between Syria and Israel.”

Consequently, Turkey’s military presence in Syria may continue even if there is a successful Kurdish peace process in Turkey.

“There may be mainly two minimal conditions: the total and actual disarmament of the PKK-linked groups in both Iraq and Syria, and the absence of Israeli military pressure on Syria,” Ozeren said.

In Iraq, Turkey has made repeated forays into northern Iraq’s Nineveh province and Iraqi Kurdistan as part of the conflict with the PKK. Turkey has had bases in these areas since the 1990s.

In the second half of the 2010s, it advanced deeper into the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, establishing and maintaining a vast network of outposts and forward-operating bases in strategic areas to relentlessly pressure the Kurdish fighters.

Now, with a major peace effort underway aimed at having the PKK lay down its arms for amnesties and a conclusive end to the conflict possibly on the horizon, Turkey’s justifications for these bases could become defunct.

Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), specified that Guler’s remarks aren’t a withdrawal signal.

Rather, he was merely articulating the “latest version of an open-ended condition” which Ankara adjusts as events change.

“In 2024, Turkey tied any exit from Syria to a new constitution, elections and full border security. Earlier this year it said the Damascus-SDF deal was still not enough,” Abdullah told The New Arab.

“Withdrawal is possible, because the presence is costly for Turkey economically and politically, but it will be slow and conditional.”

He also outlined how the minimum conditions for withdrawal differ by country.

“In Iraq, the PKK must be disarmed and out of Sinjar and Qandil,” Abdullah said.

“Since the (Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia) Mecca alliance, Ankara’s concerns now also include the weapons of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and the threat they pose to Turkey’s ally Saudi Arabia, including PMF drone attacks on the Kingdom,” he added.

“In Syria, the minimum is a completed SDF integration, PKK cadres out of the northeast, and a Syrian army able to hold the border on its own.”

Reality on the ground

ACLED data has documented a rapid decrease in Turkish strikes in Iraqi Kurdistan in the past two years since the latest PKK peace talks began. In 2024, Turkey executed 4,861 strikes in the region. That fell rapidly to 634 in 2025, then to zero so far in 2026.

“The security case for staying is weakening, but the political conditions are not yet met,” Abdullah said.

In September, Turkey agreed to gradually withdraw from the Bashiqa base in Nineveh in tandem with Iraq’s removal of PKK-affiliated fighters from Nineveh’s Sinjar, the homeland of the Yazidi minority subjected to the 2014 IS genocide.

Abdullah described Turkey’s willingness to hand over Bashiqa as a “low-cost concession” rather than the start of any strategic withdrawal. Turkey only established its presence there a decade ago to train local forces battling IS. It is also the furthest base from Turkey’s border.

Nevertheless, it’s important since it is linked to a network of forward bases along the border that support Turkey’s broader counter-PKK mission.

“The handover is also a trade, not a gesture,” Abdullah said. “In return, Baghdad committed to establishing full state authority in Sinjar and removing PKK-linked groups."

The agreement also specifies a “gradual handover” tied to security steps taken on the Iraqi side. As a result, the withdrawal timeline is wide open to delay.

“The real test is on the ground,” Abdullah said. “An Iraqi commander expects Bashiqa to be vacated by the end of this year. If it is, that is a genuine signal. A phased withdrawal begins only when the forward bases start closing, not Bashiqa.”

Therefore, statements and agreements don’t reflect reality on the ground. What would be considered a clear signal that the Turkish withdrawal has begun, the ACLED expert added, is an “actual withdrawal on the ground rather than another statement of agreement between the two sides.”

Syria's status quo

Turkey’s support for Syrian government forces in their January offensive against the SDF proved vital. Ankara is still supporting Syrian government forces in their efforts to establish complete authority in hitherto SDF-controlled areas.

The situation remains unsettled, with ACLED’s Abdullah pointing to reports of armed groups, including the PKK-affiliated Revolutionary Youth Movement, opposed to the Damascus-SDF agreement still operating in those areas. Still, Turkey-Syria collaboration isn’t limited to the SDF. 

“Basically, while the Turkish concerns are mainly related to the SDF/PKK activities in Syria, it is also related to the IS activities in Syria,” Abdullah said.

“So yes, the nature of the Syrian-Turkish relationship has changed mostly from cross-border operations and military support on the ground to more of intelligence and training collaboration.”

In his interview last week, Guler noted that Turkey has established “close coordination in the field of security” with Syria’s post-Assad authorities and seeks to “strengthen the capacity” of the new armed forces “to ensure the security of our borders.”

“While the al-Sharaa government has been pushing to take full control of the northern border and end Turkish military control there, Ankara has been pushing for at least a measured understanding with Damascus that would allow Turkish military presence to continue,” Ozeren said.

The Orion Policy Institute’s senior fellow contends that if the present Kurdish resolution process ultimately results in the PKK’s total disarmament and the return under amnesty of ex-PKK fighters to Turkey, then Ankara’s pretext for its military presence in Iraq will become unviable.

“However, two developments could alter the security landscape across the region: an expansion of the Saudi-led conflict with Iran-backed Houthis into a regional conflict, and an escalation of the US and Israel war against Iran into ground operations,” Ozeren told The New Arab.

“Such developments would force non-state actors, including PMFs in Iraq and PKK-linked groups in Iran and even Iraq, to reconsider current arrangements.”

That possibility could especially become a reality if Turkey decides to “pursue military involvement” through its commitments under the Mecca Defence Pact.

"If, and this is a big if, Damascus establishes full governance across the country, Turkey’s security- and defence-oriented influence may diminish, as the al-Sharaa government has tried to diversify its defence and military engagements with other actors,” he said.

In September, President al-Sharaa said that his country is “now entering the stage of giving legal status to the Turkish bases in northwestern Syria,” subject to the approval of the Syrian People’s Assembly.

He clarified that Syria does not have a long-term need for such foreign bases but also wants to “maintain diplomatic relations and mutual respect with neighbouring and friendly countries.”

ACLED’s Abdullah assesses that Sharaa’s statement implies that Syria doesn’t want any long-term Turkish presence on its soil to avoid turning the country into an arena of regional conflict.

That is especially urgent considering the growing tension between Turkey and Israel, which could transform Syria into a flashpoint between these two regional heavyweights.

Israel’s repeated targeting of Syrian airbases that Turkey evaluated for potential use demonstrated how quickly Turkey’s presence could potentially draw Syria into a regional confrontation.

“At the same time, Damascus cannot yet do without Turkish support,” Abdullah said. “As-Suweida remains unresolved, and IS and other groups may expand their activity.”

“Legal status for the bases is Damascus’s way of regulating Turkey’s presence now, so it can reduce that presence later."

In early August, Syria reached a memorandum of understanding on the future conditions of Russia’s access to the coastal naval and air bases of Tartus and Hmeimim under which the bases will become joint training centres after a three-month transitional process.

While Abdullah anticipates that’s the direction Damascus is pushing regarding the Turkish presence, he stressed that any comparison with Russia has significant limits.

“Russia’s presence is two bases far from Syria’s borders, and their value to Moscow is regional reach," he said. “Turkey’s presence sits on a 900-km land border and is tied to a security concern Ankara considers existential. That makes it much harder to reduce to a residual training mission.”

“Expect a smaller footprint over several years, but not a Turkey that fully leaves northern Syria.”

Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.

Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon
