item.title: Macron promises 'concrete measures' to French students' demands
item.description: “I have asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement,” Macron said.
item.content:encoded:
French President Emmanuel Macron said the government would announce "concrete measures" on Monday to address school students’ demands for more resources and better learning conditions, after weeks of class boycotts, blockades and demonstrations that have grown into nationwide unrest.

“I have asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement,” Macron said during a visit to the southern port city of Marseille, where protesters briefly stormed City Hall on 17 October.

“The prime minister and government ministers will announce several major, concrete measures this afternoon,” Macron said.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and other government officials were scheduled to meet with high school and university students later Monday.

Macron and his centrist government have faced criticism for failing to address students’ grievances since high school blockades began in mid-September. The protests have led to mass arrests and scrutiny of police riot-control weapons blamed for life-changing injuries suffered by some teenagers.

The 17 October demonstrations against rising living costs and poor school conditions descended into violence, with groups setting fires, storming public buildings, looting shops and clashing with police in France’s worst unrest in years.

Another round of nationwide demonstrations on Saturday saw less violence. Authorities estimated turnout at more than 400,000, while organizers put it at nearly 800,000.

The government is expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France’s national online university admissions platform, French media reported. The platform has been a focus of the protests, with students criticizing unclear selection criteria, unequal opportunities and barriers to pursuing their preferred courses of study.

Students are also demanding more teachers to cover staff absences, school renovations, changes to teaching hours and smaller classes. On 8 October, the government said it would deploy 3,000 additional substitute teachers to struggling high schools.

The demands for better-resourced schools, particularly in poorer communities, come as France grapples with record poverty and record public debt.

item.title: Israel army advances beyond Gaza's Yellow Line as 15 killed
item.description: Gaza residents fear repeated incursions could pave the way for a permanent expansion of Israeli control, amid continued deadly attacks
item.content:encoded:
Several Israeli tanks and military vehicles advanced further west of the so-called 'Yellow Line' in central Gaza on Monday morning, sources told The New Arab, amid fears that Israel is seeking to expand its occupation of the besieged Palestinian territory.

This came as Israeli attacks continued to kill people across the Gaza Strip.

On Monday afternoon, two Palestinians were killed and another injured in an Israeli strike on a vehicle in Deir al-Balah.

Earlier on Monday, civil defence spokesperson Mahmoud Bassal reported that at least 13 people had been killed and 60 injured by Israeli fire and airstrikes across Gaza over the previous 24 hours.

Eyewitnesses reported hearing heavy gunfire in eastern Deir al-Balah at dawn on Monday, followed by the westward movement of Israeli military vehicles and bulldozers into an area home to hundreds of displaced families.

Osama al-Kahlout, a resident of Deir al-Balah, said the Israeli army had advanced west of the demarcation line several times over the past week.

"These movements have forced residents to flee their homes and shelters, only to return when the forces pull back, leaving families in a constant state of uncertainty and fear," al-Kahlout toldThe New Arab.

Residents, he added, were growing "increasingly concerned that these advances could be part of a gradual effort to reposition troops and expand the Yellow Line westward, rather than temporary military operations."

The so-called 'Yellow Line', marked by large yellow concrete blocks, delineates areas under Israeli military control.

Although the initial arrangement under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan was intended to be temporary and followed by a gradual Israeli withdrawal, the Israeli military has instead expanded its area of control. Estimates now suggest Israel controls nearly two-thirds of the besieged Palestinian territory.

Al-Kahlout said residents’ main fear was that Israeli forces would eventually reach Salah al-Din Street, a major road connecting northern and southern Gaza that lies well west of the current demarcation line.

Mustafa Ibrahim, a Gaza-based political analyst, told The New Arab that any westward expansion towards the road "could further fragment the Strip and increase the territory under Israeli control".

Monday’s advance comes just weeks after dozens of Palestinian families in Gaza City’s Shuja’iyya neighbourhood were forced to flee when Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks marking the line towards their tents without warning.

Military expansion ahead of elections

Ibrahim said the "repeated advances and withdrawals could indicate an attempt to gradually expand the area under Israeli control and establish new military positions."

"Maintaining Israeli military control over parts of Gaza and expanding the area under its control could serve the objectives of [Benjamin Netanyahu’s] far-right coalition, which opposes a full Israeli withdrawal and seeks to impose new realities on the ground," Ibrahim told The New Arab.

With Israel heading to the polls on Tuesday, Ibrahim argued that Netanyahu’s continued military operations in Gaza were closely tied to his political survival.

Netanyahu "seeks to project an image of strength and security to Israeli voters, particularly among right-wing constituencies that support maintaining military pressure on Hamas," he said.

The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Gaza, also faces fierce criticism from opponents over the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

Gaza has seen an escalation in Israeli attacks in the week preceding the general election. The total death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal campaign has reached 74,555.

"Ultimately, the continuation of these operations risks deepening Palestinian suffering while leaving the political future of Gaza increasingly uncertain," Ibrahim said.

item.title: Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
item.description: Syria has arrested Assad's cousin, senior intelligence officers and former pilots accused of bombing cities, as authorities pursue alleged regime atrocities.
item.content:encoded:
Syrian authorities have arrested several senior officers from Bashar al-Assad's former regime, including his cousin, as part of an ongoing crackdown on suspects accused of atrocities during the country's 14-year-long civil war.

Syrian Interior Ministry spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba announced the arrests on Monday, saying those detained included senior military and intelligence officials, former air force pilots and individuals suspected of involvement in massacres and attacks on civilians.

Among those arrested was Yahya al-Assad, a cousin of ousted president Bashar al-Assad who held the rank of colonel in Branch 105, a unit of the former regime's security apparatus.

Al-Baba said the detainees also included a major general who had commanded the 24th Division and the Air Defence Directorate, as well as senior officials from the Air Force Intelligence Directorate.

Another suspect was allegedly involved in the Tadamon massacre, one of the most notorious atrocities committed by Assad's forces during the Syrian uprising.

The arrests also included a fighter pilot accused of bombing Syrian cities, a brigadier general from the Political Security Directorate, the head of investigations at Air Force Intelligence and a judge who served in the former regime's Counterterrorism Court.

Other detainees included two brigadier generals from the Republican Guard, a senior officer at Tishreen Military Hospital, a military doctor, a helicopter pilot and another fighter pilot accused of taking part in attacks on civilian areas.

The arrests are part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to pursue former military and security officials suspected of committing abuses during the uprising against Assad, including aerial bombardments, arbitrary detention, torture and massacres.

Former regime pilots targeted

Syrian authorities have stepped up arrests of former air force personnel in recent weeks, targeting officers suspected of involvement in bombing campaigns against opposition-held areas.

In September, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of nine former regime pilots in Latakia province.

According to the ministry, preliminary investigations indicated that the pilots had participated in combat missions and airstrikes targeting several areas, including Eastern Ghouta, Aleppo and its countryside, Deir ez-Zor and rural Hama.

On 18 September, authorities detained five former air force officers and commanders in Tartous province, including pilots and officials who had held operational and field responsibilities.

Two days later, security forces arrested Brigadier General Zakaria Mohammed Sannoun, who served as head of operations in the 22nd Division between 2012 and 2020.

Authorities accused Sannoun of overseeing operations at the Hama, Tiyas (T4) and Shayrat military airbases during the conflict.

On 28 September, internal security forces arrested Colonel Khaldoun Hussein Mubarak in the Jableh countryside of Latakia province.

He was accused of participating in combat sorties against Syrian areas during the uprising.

The Interior Ministry has described the arrests as part of continuing investigations into former officers and military personnel suspected of war crimes and other violations, with judicial proceedings expected to follow.

Suspect in 2013 massacres arrested

The latest arrests come less than two weeks after Syrian authorities announced the detention of Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural and nicknamed the "Butcher of Baniyas".

Kayali was arrested on 15 October over his alleged role in the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al-Bayda, in the Tartous countryside.

Syrian authorities accuse him of responsibility for the killings, which took place during the early years of the uprising against Assad.

The successive arrests mark a widening effort to track down former regime figures accused of involvement in atrocities committed during the conflict.

Authorities have said investigations will continue and that suspects will face further judicial proceedings over their alleged roles in abuses against Syrians.

item.title: Russian oil tycoons' bitter feud spills into Dubai courts
item.description: A bitter feud among Russian oil traders has reached Dubai courts, with $500m claims, frozen assets and alleged death threats exposing rivalries.
item.content:encoded:
A bitter feud between Russian oil traders has spilled into courts in Dubai and Brazil, with lawsuits worth hundreds of millions of dollars and allegations of stolen trade secrets and death threats.

The dispute involves Igor Soglayev, a former Deutsche Bank executive, and traders linked to the sanctioned Coral oil network, according to an investigation published by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday.

The fallout began when a tanker carrying Russian diesel worth tens of millions of dollars failed to deliver its cargo in Brazil.

The dispute has since led to claims exceeding $500 million, a $42 million arbitration award and a Dubai court order freezing assets worth up to $704 million.

Soglayev, who previously advised Igor Sechin, the head of Russian oil giant Rosneft, partnered with traders associated with Coral in early 2024.

He established Dubai-based DIA33 to trade Russian diesel and export it to Brazil, but the partnership collapsed following the failed shipment.

Coral-linked traders accused Soglayev of failing to pay for the fuel and secured a Dubai arbitration ruling ordering him to pay approximately $42 million.

Soglayev then filed lawsuits in Dubai and Brazil, accusing his former partners of undermining his business and misusing confidential commercial information.

He is seeking more than $500 million in damages and claims to have received death threats.

In June, a Dubai judge ordered the freezing of up to $704 million in assets belonging to the defendants and associated companies.

The order remains in place while appeals continue, although questions over the court's jurisdiction have complicated proceedings. No final ruling has settled the competing allegations.

The WSJ reported that the UAE court handling the main case has not made the proceedings public.

Accusations of stolen clients

The dispute has also reached Brazil, where DIA33 accused Coral of recruiting senior employees and using its customer base, offices and infrastructure to establish a rival business.

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that a commercial court in Sao Paulo had identified indications of unfair competition.

Representatives of the defendants denied wrongdoing, arguing that the dispute stemmed from a business partnership that had never been fully formalised.

Coral has separately accused DIA33 of misappropriating a diesel shipment.

A sanctioned oil network

Coral Energy, renamed 2Rivers in 2024, has been a major player in Russian oil trading, with commercial roots in Azerbaijan and offices in Dubai and Singapore.

Western officials accuse traders associated with the network of helping Moscow maintain oil exports and finance its war in Ukraine despite sanctions.

Britain sanctioned the group in December 2024 and added five executives to its sanctions list in May 2025.

The European Union has also sanctioned associated entities, accusing them of facilitating Russian oil exports, disguising the origin of shipments and using vessels linked to Moscow's so-called shadow fleet.

The network has denied breaching sanctions and announced plans to wind down operations in August 2025, citing Western pressure.

Dubai has become an important hub for Russian oil trading since Moscow redirected exports away from Europe following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

item.title: Egypt parliament authorises defensive support to Saudi Arabia
item.description: The parliament, stacked with supporters of Sisi, had held three rare secret meetings on the matter and postponed the vote twice.
item.content:encoded:
Egypt's parliament authorised on Monday sending military support to Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Houthis, following a request from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.

The House of Representatives "approved authorising President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia", state newspaper Al-Ahram reported.

The parliament, stacked with supporters of Sisi, had held three rare secret meetings on the matter and postponed the vote twice.

Sisi last week had asked parliament to authorise military support to Saudi Arabia, "if requested".

It was not immediately clear what defensive support could be provided by Egypt, the Arab world's largest military, which boasts hundreds of thousands of active personnel, fighter jets and complex air defences sourced from countries including the US, China, France and Russia.

Sisi said on Wednesday that his country's support would be to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen".

"We are talking about defending the land and borders of the kingdom," he said in a speech, adding that the top priority was for a diplomatic solution.

Egypt has undertaken a flurry of diplomatic manoeuvres since, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty consulting with the so-called R4, which includes members of the Meccah defence pact, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, which Cairo has not agreed to join.

On Monday, he said he was "talking daily with the Iranians" to push for regional de-escalation.

item.title: Writers pledge royalties to Sally Rooney after books pulled
item.description: Ireland's and Wales's children's laureates pledge to donate their royalties to Sally Rooney, whose books have been pulled over her support for Palestine Action.
item.content:encoded:
Popular children's writers Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies have pledged to donate their royalties to fellow author Sally Rooney, after her books were pulled from circulation over her vow to use proceeds from her work to support Palestine Action.

Rooney had said that proceeds from her books would be used to support the group, which has been proscribed as a "terrorist" organisation in the United Kingdom since July 2025.

The proscription has put the direct action group on the same legal footing as groups like al-Qaeda and the Islamic State group, and has led to the arrests of thousands of protesters for allegedly expressing support for Palestine Action --  a charge which carries a prison sentence of up to 14 years.

By pledging financial support to the group, the Irish author risks similar prosecution under UK law.

Haughton, who is Ireland's children's laureate, described the situation as a "farce".

“I really want to express my full support for Sally Rooney. As someone who is in the UK a lot of the time, I can’t do what she has done, but I can support her instead of supporting Palestine Action," he told The Guardian.

“The entire situation is just a farce. Sending Sally Rooney the money adds another level of absurdity to this absurd situation, it’s making a mockery of the law.”

Davies, who is Wales's children's laureate, said that her advocacy for children was the reason she had to speak up for Rooney.

“I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment," she said.

"Gaza is smaller than the Welsh county of Flintshire, and it’s as if all Wales’s children were concentrated there and being bombed."

She added that she will donate her half-year royalties from the book "The Day War Came", which she said had been boosted in sales "by the conflicts in Ukraine and Palestine".

Since the UK's ban on Palestine Action, thousands of protesters have been arrested for allegedly expressing support for the group.

Last week, prominent arts figures signed an open letter published in The New Statesman expressing solidarity with Rooney. Among them were Zadie Smith, Ahdaf Soueif, Arundhati Roy and Nobel Prize-winning writer Annie Ernaux, alongside actors Paul Mescal, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Tilda Swinton and Susan Sarandon.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has so far resisted calls for the ban on Palestine Action to be repealed, however the UK's Supreme Court will hear an appeal on 4-5 November.

item.title: Palestine, Iran, world leaders welcome Lula Brazil election win
item.description: Lula's historic fourth-term victory in Brazil signals continuity in support for Palestine, as world leaders react and Bolsonaro challenges the result.
item.content:encoded:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian have joined world leaders in congratulating Brazil's Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his historic re-election, with Abbas praising the Brazilian leader's support for Palestinian rights and Tehran calling for closer bilateral ties.

The messages came on Monday after Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential run-off, securing a fourth, non-consecutive term with 51.76% of the vote against his rival's 48.24%.

In a congratulatory telegram, Abbas praised Brazil's longstanding support for the Palestinian people and their national rights, as well as its condemnation of crimes committed against Palestinians.

He expressed appreciation for Brazil's solidarity with Palestine and confidence that Lula would maintain these positions during his new term.

Abbas also described the election result as a reflection of the Brazilian people's confidence in Lula's domestic and international policies, praising what he called the president's courageous and responsible positions.

Brazil has emerged under Lula as an important international voice in support of Palestinian rights, with his re-election expected to ensure continuity in the country's foreign policy towards the Middle East.

Iran calls for stronger ties and multilateral cooperation

Iranian President Pezeshkian also congratulated Lula, expressing hope that relations between Tehran and Brasilia would expand during the Brazilian leader's new term.

According to Iran's IRNA news agency, Pezeshkian called for greater cooperation in areas of mutual interest and efforts to strengthen multilateralism and international peace.

Iran and Brazil maintain friendly diplomatic relations and are both members of BRICS, the grouping of emerging economies that has sought to strengthen cooperation among countries outside traditional Western-led institutions.

The congratulations follow diplomatic contacts between the two countries, including a telephone conversation between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Brazilian counterpart Mauro Vieira on 19 October, ahead of the presidential run-off.

Lula's victory is also expected to reinforce Brazil's role in the Global South and its engagement with international organisations such as BRICS, at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions and strained relations with Washington.

China and Russia hail Lula's re-election

China and Russia were among the major international powers to welcome Lula's victory, highlighting Brazil's growing importance in international diplomacy.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun congratulated the Brazilian president and said Beijing was ready to continue developing its relationship with Brasilia.

China hoped to advance the two countries' shared strategic vision and strengthen cooperation during Lula's new term, he said.

The Kremlin also welcomed the result, with spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praising Lula's contribution to relations between Russia and Brazil and his role in developing BRICS.

Peskov expressed hope that Lula would continue pursuing closer cooperation with Moscow and other members of the grouping.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Lula, describing the result as a victory for democracy and multilateralism.

She pledged to continue working with Brazil on trade, climate action and the international rules-based order.

French President Emmanuel Macron called for stronger strategic cooperation between Paris and Brasilia, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed Lula's victory as part of what he described as a broader progressive resurgence.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also celebrated the result, declaring that democracy and the Brazilian people had prevailed.

Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel praised Lula's victory as a continuation of policies centred on sovereignty, peace and social justice.

Leaders from Canada, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay and Ecuador were also among those to congratulate the Brazilian president.

Divided reactions in the United States

The election prompted contrasting reactions from political figures in the United States, where relations with Brazil have been strained.

Donald Trump Jr, the son of US President Donald Trump, criticised the decision to extend voting hours by two hours during Sunday's run-off, accusing the American mainstream media of applying double standards in its coverage of the controversy.

The extension had been ordered by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin following procedural irregularities that disrupted the transportation of voters to polling stations in several Brazilian states.

Both candidates had requested additional voting time, but Bolsonaro subsequently called for the election to be annulled, describing the extension as unacceptable.

Progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders, meanwhile, congratulated Lula on his re-election, praising his record on workers' rights and democracy.

Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna welcomed the result as a rejection of extremism and urged Trump to respect Brazil's election outcome.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also celebrated Lula's victory, while California Governor Gavin Newsom's office welcomed continued cooperation with Brazil on democratic institutions, environmental protection and workers' rights.

item.title: Israel's 942 barriers are reshaping life in the West Bank
item.description: Israel's West Bank closures restrict Palestinian movement and worsen economic hardship, advancing Israel's ever more explicit goals of annexation and expulsion.
item.content:encoded:
Before leaving home for work or travelling to a university in another town, Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are now used to checking their phones for road updates.

Telegram groups dedicated to traffic throughout the occupied West Bank have become part of daily life, with Palestinian residents sharing information about open and closed checkpoints, where traffic congestion and what alternative routes exist.

The status of a single checkpoint can change several times within minutes, as Israeli closures increasingly sever roads between West Bank cities and villages—a trend which has escalated since Israel launched its war on Gaza on 7 October 2023.

The Israeli military's announcement that it would seal off all land crossings into the occupied West Bank on Tuesday 27 October, the day of Israel's elections, has once again drawn attention to Israel's restrictions over Palestinian movement.

Israel has long imposed such measures during religious holidays, special occasions and elections. While these used to focus more on closing crossings between the occupied West Bank and Israel within its 1967 borders, closures within the occupied West Bank itself have expanded significantly since October 2023.

Linking West Bank settlements

Statistics released by the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission on 25 September reveal the scale of the shutdown. There are now 942 checkpoints, closure points, and physical barriers across the occupied West Bank—comprising 824 permanent checkpoints and closure points, alongside 118 linear obstacles (such as earth mounds, trenches, and road blocks) that span approximately 107.7 km.

Hebron governorate tops the list with 221 permanent checkpoints and roadblocks, followed by Ramallah and al-Bireh with 160, Nablus with 120, Bethlehem with 78 and occupied Jerusalem with 62.

The commission also documented the installation of 13 additional gates and fixed checkpoints in the two months preceding its report, including 10 iron gates in Jenin governorate.

These installations enable the Israeli army to control movement between Palestinian communities, as closing a single gate can block access to a town or village, forcing residents to take alternative routes that considerably lengthen their journeys.

The commission also documented settlers installing iron gates on Palestinian roads, including two near Kafr Ni'ma and Umm Safa in Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.

Dr. Ibrahim Rabaia, a political science professor at Birzeit University, told The New Arab that Israel has spent decades developing a complex, multilayered system to control Palestinian movement. This extended from closing the crossings linking the West Bank to the territories occupied in 1948, affecting people and goods, to restricting travel between cities and towns within the occupied territories.

Israel tightens these measures during elections, holidays and other occasions, or on security grounds, Rabaia said, adding that the restrictions also served settlement projects which themselves required limiting Palestinian movement.

He described the measures accompanying the current Israeli elections as neither new nor exceptional. However, they coincide with an Israeli military campaign in Hebron and other parts of the West Bank, alongside escalating settler attacks.

Israel has made significant progress in fragmenting the occupied West Bank into separate Palestinian enclaves through complex geographical, security and administrative arrangements, while consolidating the territorial continuity and communication networks between Israeli settlements, Rabaia said.

He argued that Israel was exploiting international, regional and domestic circumstances to advance this project.

The priority given to settler movement has been reflected in statements by Israeli officials. In August 2023, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said his right, and that of his wife and children, to travel on West Bank roads was more important than Palestinians' freedom of movement, citing security concerns.

Following the outbreak of the Gaza war, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for buffer zones around settlements and roads used by settlers, barring Palestinians from entering them even to harvest olives.

The closures also carry mounting economic costs. A March 2025 study by the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute (MAS), examining the northern and central West Bank, estimated that delays at checkpoints cost Palestinians approximately 191,000 working hours daily.

The resulting losses amounted to around $764,600 a day, or $16.8 million a month, in addition to approximately $6 million annually in extra fuel costs.

These losses coincide with rising unemployment. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics recorded a West Bank unemployment rate of 27.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 284,000 people unemployed amid shrinking employment opportunities, declining economic activity and the repercussions of the war.

From restricted movement to displacement

Some Israeli closures are linked to colonial policies intended to tighten control over Palestinian movement, often justified as measures to prevent attacks on Israelis. However, these security arguments alone do not explain the nature of the restrictions, according to Adel Shadid, a specialist in Israeli affairs.

He told The New Arab that the measures are also part of a policy of collective punishment and revenge pursued by far-right settler forces within the Israeli government, including Smotrich, Ben-Gvir, and lawmakers Orit Strock and Avi Maoz.

Shadid pointed to Smotrich's public celebration of the demolition of Palestinian buildings and confiscation of land, as well as Ben-Gvir's statements about punitive measures against Palestinian prisoners.

He argued that the political dimension was paramount, adding that the Israeli government sought to subdue Palestinians into accepting a long-term reality of restrictions and control in line with the ideological project of religious Zionism and Smotrich's "Decisive Plan" for annexing the West Bank, proposed in 2017.

The closures also aim to intensify economic and social pressures, pushing Palestinians to reconsider their political choices and fuelling internal disputes over responsibility for deteriorating living conditions, Shadid added.

Israeli affairs specialist Muawiya Musa, meanwhile, told The New Arab that in his eyes there was no direct link between the closures and the elections. Instead their origins could be traced to a policy that began taking shape during the second intifada in 2000.

Musa distinguished between what he called "Israel 1", representing the traditional Israeli political current, and "Israel 2", represented by the settler right and religious Zionism.

He argued that the former sought to turn closures into de facto borders confining Palestinians to Areas A and B under the Oslo Accords, while the latter openly advocated complete separation and the expulsion of Palestinians from the West Bank altogether.

The two interpretations share the view that Israeli closures extend beyond immediate security concerns, even if analysts differ over their precise objectives. Geographical fragmentation and economic and social pressure, they argue, operate together to consolidate control over Palestinians and restrict their ability to move, work and maintain stable lives.

The policy takes on added significance amid increasingly explicit Israeli calls for displacement. In February, Smotrich announced plans to "encourage migration" from the West Bank and Gaza, linking this to the cancellation of the Oslo Accords and the imposition of Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank.

The strangulation of the occupied West Bank, therefore, is not the result of a temporary security situation or an election season. Rather, it reflects an accumulation of restrictions and settlement policies that have accelerated since the war on Gaza, gradually turning the territory into an increasingly unliveable spaces for Palestinians.

By narrowing the geographical space available to Palestinians and undermining the foundations of their economic and social lives, the expanding network of checkpoints, gates and road restrictions is intensifying pressures on residents' ability to remain in their communities, as the displacement of Palestinians becomes an increasingly explicit component of the Israeli right's political agenda.

item.title: Jordan says three family members behind Karak church attack
item.description: Jordanian authorities announced early on Monday that they had arrested all three suspects following an armed confrontation at an abandoned house.
item.content:encoded:
Jordanian authorities on Monday identified three suspects arrested at dawn over last week's deadly church attack as members of the same family.

"The perpetrators of the attack on the church were two brothers and the third was their relative by marriage," Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said at a press conference. He named the three as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.

The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, in Karak governorate, killed nine people and wounded 34 others during a funeral service.

Speaking at a joint press conference with Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya and Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani, the security chief described the suspects as extremists who had adopted an extremist ideology.

He said the three men lived near Hamoud village and had acted without prior planning.

According to the security chief, the suspects were following the funeral procession when they decided to carry out the attack, a decision he attributed to their extremist beliefs.

He said the three men had developed the idea together while following the procession, rather than preparing the assault in advance.

Following the shooting, the suspects fled the scene in a single vehicle, which was later recovered by investigators.

Security forces also seized firearms and a large quantity of ammunition following their arrest.

Suspects arrested after shootout

Jordanian authorities announced early on Monday that they had arrested all three suspects following an armed confrontation at an abandoned house in the village of Al-Jadida, approximately five kilometres from Hamoud.

The Public Security Director said security teams had spent three days searching designated areas before narrowing their operation to a number of abandoned buildings.

Shortly after midnight on Sunday night, officers divided part of Al-Jadida into sectors and identified several abandoned houses for inspection.

The operation led security forces to the building where the suspects were hiding.

According to the Public Security Directorate, the men refused to surrender and opened fire on officers, prompting an exchange of gunfire.

All three suspects were wounded before being taken into custody and transferred to hospital. No members of the security forces were injured during the operation.

The security chief said investigators had pursued two lines of inquiry immediately after the attack.

The first focused on criminal investigations, intelligence gathering and collecting evidence from the scene.

The second involved emergency response measures, surveillance operations and tracking the suspects' movements and escape routes.

No evidence of links to wider groups

Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said investigators had found no indications that the suspects were connected to other extremist cells or organisations.

He stressed, however, that the investigation remained ongoing and that authorities would pursue anyone found to have helped plan, encourage or facilitate the attack.

Al-Faraya described the killings as the product of an extremist ideology that was alien to Jordanian values and traditions.

He said tackling terrorism required more than arresting those responsible, calling for efforts to address the roots of extremism, hate speech and incitement.

The minister also referred to King Abdullah II's visit to survivors in hospital, during which the monarch pledged a firm response against those responsible for the killings.

Al-Faraya said the successful arrest operation demonstrated the authorities' commitment to protecting citizens and ensuring accountability.

Jordan warns against sectarian divisions

Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani urged Jordanians not to allow the attack to fuel religious hatred or divisions within society.

He described the killings as a turning point in the country's efforts to confront extremist and takfiri ideology, announcing that the government would continue working to combat radicalisation across different sectors.

Al-Momani said royal directives had called for a review of policies aimed at countering extremist thought and addressing its underlying causes through a systematic national strategy.

He stressed that confronting extremism was a shared responsibility involving government institutions, religious authorities, schools, the media and wider society.

Protecting the public, he argued, required challenging not only acts of violence but also the ideas and rhetoric used to justify them.

The minister also warned against misinformation and rumours, saying misleading information could spread fear, undermine public confidence and encourage incitement during times of crisis.

He urged the public to avoid discussions that could deepen religious or social divisions, stressing that the actions of extremists should not be used to blame entire communities.

"We must not allow terrorism to achieve through words what it failed to achieve through crime," Al-Momani said.

He added that Jordanian citizenship was not determined by religious or social identity and that no citizen should have to prove their belonging to the country.

The government would not allow extremist ideology to redefine relations between Jordanians or undermine the shared national identity that united them under the rule of law, he said.

Al-Momani also praised the solidarity shown by Jordanians towards the families of those killed, describing it as a demonstration of the country's rejection of hatred and division.

"This solidarity embodies our belief that the suffering of any Jordanian is the suffering of us all, and that our national unity is firmly rooted and cannot be undermined by terrorism," he said.

The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud took place during a funeral service, leaving nine people dead and 34 others injured.

Authorities have pledged to continue investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings and bring anyone involved to justice.

item.title: Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
item.description: They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the occupied West Bank.
item.content:encoded:
An alleged ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report Monday.  They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the occupied West Bank.

The report has multiple graphic accounts of sexual assaults by Israeli prison guards and soldiers on Palestinian detainees since October 2023. 

The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.

The report released on Monday said Israel was "continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza."

Much of the harm has come, the report says, from Israel’s expansion deeper into Gaza during that period. Since October 2025, when the US-brokered ceasefire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53% of Gaza to at least 60%, the commission said.

The report also accused Israel and members of its security forces of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.

The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison. 

The commission says it drew its conclusions after investigating seven cases between November 2023 and June 2026, where Israeli forces caused bodily harm on Palestinians, often children, who did not appear to be posing a threat.

Since October 2023, Israel has killed over 75,000 Palestinians in Gaza—mostly women and children.

item.title: Could Syria help Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis without troops?
item.description: Analysis: Syrian deployment to fight the Houthis is unlikely given the country's domestic challenges, but support for Saudi Arabia could take other forms
item.content:encoded:
Reports have continued to circulate about a possible deployment of Syrian fighters to Yemen despite Damascus' denials.

But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said such a move was unlikely given Syria’s own domestic security challenges, and suggested that any military support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis could take other forms, without involving troops on Yemeni territory.

Citing unnamed Yemeni intelligence sources, Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Riyadh and Damascus had held talks on transferring up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to Yemen.

It said a Syrian military delegation had recently visited the Saudi capital and the kingdom’s southern regions to assess the proposed deployment.

According to the newspaper, Brigadier General Khaled Khattab, formerly leader of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and now commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army, spent four days in the southern Saudi regions of Asir and Najran, accompanied by Saudi officers. The delegation reportedly visited sites being prepared to receive Syrian fighters.

Meanwhile, Brigadier General Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army’s Third Corps and a former Hayat Tahrir al-Sham commander, was said to have met Saudi officers at the defence ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, benefits and their expected military role. Al-Akhbar said the delegation had finalised logistical preparations for the transfer.

The New Arab could not independently verify Al-Akhbar’s claims.

Could Syria support Riyadh without entering Yemen?

Muaz al-Abdallah, a Syria analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), told The New Arab that any Syrian military support to Saudi Arabia would not necessarily involve deploying troops inside Yemen.

He said one possibility was that Syrian forces could be sent to help protect Saudi Arabia’s southern border, rather than take part directly in the fighting against the Houthis on Yemeni territory. Al-Abdallah said this statement left open the possibility of military cooperation with Riyadh, even if Damascus maintained that it had not deployed forces inside Yemen.

"Damascus has said it has not sent forces to Yemen, while also expressing support for Saudi security and saying military cooperation would take place through official channels and bilateral agreements," Al-Abdallah said.

He added that deploying Syrian personnel to the Saudi side of the border would not necessarily contradict the government’s denial that it had sent forces to Yemen, but could instead represent another way of supporting Riyadh.

Al-Abdallah suggested that Saudi Arabia could increase its financial assistance and investments in Syria’s reconstruction in return for military support.

Syrian drone expertise could help Saudi Arabia

Al-Abdallah also pointed to the potential for Syria to offer expertise in drone operations, particularly given its forces' experience operating drones during the war against Bashar Al-Assad’s regime. He said drones had played an important role in the lightning rebel offensive that toppled Assad, giving Syrian forces considerable experience in their use.

That expertise could prove useful to Saudi Arabia amid its confrontation with the Houthis, particularly if cooperation were to involve training or the use of smaller attack drones.

Al-Akhbar also reported that Syrian drone specialists were already involved in training forces in Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and that Syrian operators had helped establish drone units within Saudi emergency forces. However, these claims have not been independently verified.

Despite the reports, Al-Abdallah said ACLED had not documented evidence of Syrian fighters currently operating in Yemen. The organisation had found no reports of Syrian casualties, captured fighters or funerals linked to a deployment there, he said, noting that such evidence had helped establish the presence of Syrian fighters in other conflict zones, including Libya.

Al-Abdallah also questioned reports, including those published by Axios, that Syria could send its 84th Division to Yemen. He said the division was deployed around Suweida, in southern Syria, which remains largely outside the central government’s control after last year's sectarian clashes.

"Given the situation there, and reports of heavy Israeli arming of the National Guard and a possible escalation with the Syrian government, I don’t see how this division would leave Suweida," he said.

Syria's unresolved issues make deployment unlikely

The prospect of Syria deploying fighters to Yemen remains unlikely given the transitional government’s security challenges at home, according to Benjamin Schmida, a Middle East researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).

Schmida told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia likely requested that Syria send forces to Yemen, but Damascus appears to have declined.

"It does not seem like these discussions proceeded very far beyond consulting CENTCOM," he said, adding that the Syrian government’s public rejection of the request suggested the talks had not continued.

Schmida said it remained unclear what forces Syria could realistically deploy, given the security challenges facing the country, including Kurdish areas in the northeast, Druze militia control over Suweida, sporadic Islamic State group attacks, and repeated Israeli incursions in the southwest.

He also cautioned against assuming that foreign fighters integrated into Syria’s military would be available for deployment abroad.

"Foreign fighters, such as Uyghur Turkistan Islamic Party fighters that are integrated into the Syrian Defence Ministry, represent some of Syria’s most elite units," he said.

"The Syrian government likely views integrated foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, as vital assets for Syria's defence and internal security that must remain in Syria in the event of a future crisis."

Would Syrian fighters change the balance in Yemen?

The possibility of transferring foreign fighters to Yemen was also raised in Al-Akhbar's report, which suggested that Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks, Afghans, and Chechens who joined Syrian opposition factions before Assad’s fall could be among those considered for deployment.

However, Schmida said the potential impact of any Syrian deployment would depend on the number of fighters sent and where they were integrated into the conflict.

Axios recently reported that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 fighters. Schmida said this would represent a sizeable proportion of Syria’s total army manpower and could meaningfully bolster forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose forces he estimated at around 100,000.

But he noted that the Houthis are a much larger force, while government-aligned fighters remain spread across several frontlines, including Taiz, Marib, and Jawf.

More importantly, he said, sending additional fighters would not necessarily address the divisions undermining the Yemeni government’s war effort.

"Merely sending more fighters - though they may be experienced - is unlikely to solve one of the primary challenges for the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis: its own internal disunity," Schmida said.

He pointed to the political fragmentation and poor military coordination among government-aligned forces, warning that they could struggle to integrate Syrian fighters effectively, limiting their ability to change conditions on the battlefield.

Ultimately, Schmida said a meaningful Syrian deployment was unlikely "at this time or in the foreseeable future," as the government’s focus on domestic stability took precedence over Saudi requests.

While Riyadh could potentially use aid and investment to encourage Damascus to provide military support, he warned that doing so "could risk souring the Syrian-Saudi relationship and pushing Syria closer to Turkey or Saudi rivals like the UAE".

Louay Faour is a journalist at The New Arab focusing largely on the Levant, with a particular interest in Lebanese affairs

item.title: Israel puts Palestinian prisoners in solitary for making a cake
item.description: Authorities have thrown eight Palestinians into solitary confinement for making a cake to celebrate the possible departure of Itamar Ben-Gvir at the election
item.content:encoded:
Israeli authorities have thrown eight Palestinian prisoners into solitary confinement for making a cake to celebrate the possible departure of extremist national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir following Tuesday's election.

The prisoners at Lavi prison had saved up food over several days to make the cake in order to express hope that the vote will lead to the minister's exit from the government.

Prison guards found the cake in a cell, prompting officials to take disciplinary measures against the eight and send them to solitary confinement.

Ben-Gvir praised prison officials for the decision and mocked prisoners' lack of access to food.

"The terrorists in Lavi Prison sat and hoarded what little food they had, a spoonful of jam here, a slide of bread there, day after day," he wrote in a social media post.

"They did this for several days, all so they could make an improvised cake and celebrate if I am not elected," he continued.

המחבלים בכלא לביא ישבו ואגרו מהמעט מזון שיש להם. כף ריבה ועוד כף ריבה, פרוסת לחם ועוד פרוסת לחם, כך במשך כמה ימים, הכל כדי להכין עוגה מאולתרת ולחגוג ביום שלישי, במידה ולא אבחר. אלא שנציב שב״ס המצוין ואנשיו איתרו את העוגה, והאסירים הועמדו לדין משמעתי, והועברו לצינוק. הם כבר תכננו את החגיגות, אבל אצלנו נגמרה החגיגה. ביום שלישי אסור לתת להם לחגוג, מצביעים ב׳ בקלפי!

— איתמר בן גביר (@itamarbengvir) October 25, 2026

Ben-Gvir, who leads the Kahanist Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power party, has attempted to make conditions for Palestinian inmates as unbearable as possible since taking control of Israeli prisons in 2022.

He has also personally taken part in the abuse and humiliation of Palestinian prisoners, as well as captured activists from the Gaza Freedom Flotilla.

Israeli rights group B'Tselem has described Ben-Gvir's prison system as a "network of torture camps" that subjects Palestinians to physical and psychological abuse, starvation and inhuman conditions.

Ben-Gvir also led efforts to introduce the death penalty for Palestinian prisoners.

Otzma Yehudit is expected to gain seats in the Knesset following Tuesday's vote, profiting from the growing radicalisation of young Israelis.

Polls tracked by The New Arab project the party to pick up eight seats and become joint fifth-largest party in the assembly.

In 2022, the party was only able to make it into the Knesset by forming a joint list with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and another small far-right group.

item.title: As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
item.description: Green MPs attacking the passing of the Zionism is racism motion undermine both the party's democratic process and Palestinian voices, writes Amro Tabari.
item.content:encoded:
It has become almost customary for Palestinians, whenever we speak about Palestine, to begin by telling the story of our suffering. We are expected to explain how we became refugees, how our parents and grandparents were displaced, and which members of our families were killed, imprisoned or disappeared under Israeli occupation.

We are expected to expose our deepest wounds, relive generations of trauma, and to offer our grief as evidence that our demands for justice deserve to be heard.

This is nothing but emotional labour.

And today, I refuse to audition for anyone’s sympathy.

I refuse to bare my wounds for the world to see, simply to validate the decisions and actions we take on the path towards our liberation.

Palestinian rights are not conditional upon our ability to move an audience to tears.

This is why when Green Party members voted to adopt the historic motion declaring Zionism to be racism and calling for a free Palestine from the river to the sea, it felt like a historic movement in UK solidarity efforts.

As a Palestinian and a Green Party member who co-authored and helped develop and advance this motion, I saw this as more than a political victory. It was also an affirmation that Palestinian voices could shape the policies of a major British political party without having to surrender their own understanding of their oppression or dilute their demands to be palatable.

Yet what should have been a moment of collective reflection and celebration quickly became overshadowed by opposition from several Green Party MPs and figures within the party leadership.

A democratic victory that some refuse to accept

The motion did not emerge overnight. Outsiders did not impose it, nor was it the product of some mysterious group of extremists, as some have suggested. 

It was drafted and championed by ordinary Green Party members, including Palestinians and anti-Zionist Jews, who spent months organising workshops, seminars, discussions and fringe events to engage fellow members.

Even after the motion was denied a hearing following procedural delays and filibustering during the party’s spring conference, we continued organising, discussing and engaging.

We believed in the Green Party’s commitment to grassroots democracy, even when its procedures appeared to work against us.

Nevertheless, once the motion finally passed, some elected representatives responded not by acknowledging the democratic outcome, but by questioning the motivations of those who brought the motion forward, portraying our organisation and determination as something threatening.

MP Ellie Chowns called for protecting the party from extremists and entryists.

Ironically, only months earlier, party leadership was enthusiastically celebrating a remarkable surge in membership.

Apparently, welcoming new members is something to celebrate until those members organise, exercise their democratic rights and successfully influence party policy.

Even my own MP, Sian Berry, whom I personally contacted to engage with the motion and its arguments, did not respond. Yet, once the media attacks started, Berry weighed in by publicly distancing herself from the motion, describing it as seriously flawed and accusing its Palestinian proposers of being unwilling to compromise.

She has even called on the party to revisit a decision reached through its own democratic processes.

MP Adrian Ramsay, the party's former co-leader, has publicly encouraged Green council groups to distance themselves from the democratically adopted policy. In a recent public statement

Ramsay praised council groups that rejected the motion, described the conference decision as a distraction from their work, and said it did not reflect the views of most party members.

It is deeply disappointing to see a former party leader effectively encouraging a division between elected council groups and the democratic decisions of the party’s own membership.

Selective silencing

Whilst disagreement is a legitimate part of political life, actively encouraging local representatives to distance themselves from a policy adopted through the party’s highest democratic forum raises serious questions about whose voices are ultimately respected.

What message does this send to party members who invest their time, energy and conviction in the democratic process, only to see its outcome publicly undermined by those elected to represent them?

What makes this particularly painful is that these Green MPs are now among the most vocal opponents of a motion written by Palestinians, for Palestinians, and supported through the party’s democratic process.

Not long ago, Palestinians within the Green Party extended a gesture of solidarity and goodwill to those very MPs. After Israeli authorities imposed entry bans on them, we sent a letter replacing that exclusion with an invitation to visit a Free Palestine, to stand alongside us and to hear directly from Palestinians about our aspirations for freedom, dignity and self-determination.

It was an invitation to listen, to engage and to recognise that Palestinians are not merely subjects of political debate, but people with voices, histories and a right to determine their own future. Judging by some of the responses to the motion, it feels like the invitation was buried under a pile of political calculations and selective solidarity.

Palestinians are also not the only ones who’ve been silenced by opposing MPs and the subsequent media storm.

A leading accusation against the motion is that it threatens the safety of Jewish members of the Green Party. But Jewish safety is not at risk from a motion that defines and confronts Zionism as a settler colonial ideology, examining its historical and contemporary manifestations, and reaffirming the Palestinian struggle for liberation, including ending occupation and confronting the structures of displacement and dispossession.    

Not only is this argument, which conflates Zionist views with Jewish identity, antisemitic in itself, but it also completely ignores anti-Zionist Jewish members. Many of those members participated in drafting the motion and organising discussions and public meetings in support of it, but opponents have shown they’re not interested in this part of the story.

No one’s safety should ever come at the expense of another people’s freedom, dignity or right to self-determination.

Amro Tabari is a British Palestinian renewable energy engineer, activist and writer. Born a refugee in Syria and raised in Jordan, his family originates from Tiberias, Palestine. He has lived in the UK since 2014 and is actively involved in grassroots campaigns for Palestinian liberation, social justice and environmental sustainability. A member of the Green Party and Greens for Palestine, he was recognised as one of The Big Issue’s 100 Changemakers in 2026 for his work in politics and activism.
