item.title: Jordan unites as victims' families recount Karak church massacre
item.description: Families of victims of the massacre in a Jordanian church last week recall the horror of the attack, vowing it will not divide Muslims and Christians.
item.content:encoded:
Grief, anger and shock have consumed the village of Hammoud in Jordan's southern Karak governorate following the deadly attack on St George's Church on Friday 23 October which saw nine lose their lives.

Relatives recalled the moment gunfire erupted and desperate attempts to rescue the wounded, while stressing the deep-rooted relationship between Muslims and Christians in Karak and insisting the attack will not undermine social cohesion or national unity.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate announced early on Monday that the three gunmen who carried out the massacre had been arrested following an armed confrontation with security personnel.

Sultan al-Khitan, a Hammoud resident who witnessed the horrific scenes on Friday, told The New Arab that the incident began as people gathered in the church courtyard and exchanged greetings. Heavy gunfire suddenly rang out, sending people scrambling for cover.

The attackers continued firing from the street behind the church, while those present attempted to assist the wounded and get them out of the area.

Al-Khitan said he helped transport two people to safety, one wounded in the shoulder and the other in the neck. The gunfire continued for a while before gradually subsiding, and residents used their cars to take the injured to hospitals before returning to help evacuate others, he said.

He described seeing a blue Dyna pickup truck carrying two people, one of whom was armed with what looked like a Kalashnikov rifle.

Al-Khitan said the attack was unprecedented, with life in Hammoud characterised by close ties, regular visits and shared celebrations and condolences. To his knowledge, there had been no previous disputes or feuds that could explain the violence.

Waad al-Halsa, a relative of some of the victims, told The New Arab that those inside the church had been attending the funeral of their uncle's wife when the firing erupted without warning, leaving those present confused and initially unsure how to act.

He insisted that the massacre will not affect relations between Karak's Muslims and Christians, describing their bonds as strong and deeply rooted in everyday life.

Al-Halsa said one example was his friend Louay al-Halalmeh, who contacted him immediately after the attack to offer help transporting the injured—such gestures reflected the genuine solidarity between residents, which was demonstrated through practical action, particularly during times of hardship.

Khaled Barqan, a cousin of one of the victims, told The New Arab that Jordan had lost young people and skilled professionals in an immense tragedy without precedent in the country's history.

The victims were peaceful residents of Hammoud who had gone to a funeral, never expecting that a social obligation would turn into a scene of violence and bloodshed, he said.

Barqan described the attack as an act of terrorism that was difficult to comprehend, and condemned its violation of all laws, customs and human values.

Ehab Haddadin, another relative of a victim, said the tragedy extended far beyond the bereaved families to encompass the whole country.

"No matter how much a person tries to speak, there are no words that can express the scale of this tragedy," he told The New Arab.

He said relations between Muslims and Christians in Jordan were based on fraternity and solidarity, with no history of religious division, adding that he was shocked that such an attack had taken place.

Lina al-Halsa, whose cousins were among the dead and wounded, called for the harshest possible penalties against those responsible, so they would serve as a warning to anyone contemplating attacks on places of worship or peaceful civilians.

Sarah Haddadin said residents were still struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy. She saw the targeting of the church as an attempt to sow discord between Muslims and Christians, but believes it will fail to change the nature of relations between Jordanians.

The scenes of mourning and solidarity at the funerals in the village had demonstrated national unity and rejection of discrimination and division, she said, expressing confidence that security forces would pursue those responsible and bring them to justice.

Tribal figures in Karak also stressed that the attack had struck the entire country.

Firas Madallah Ali al-Assasfeh told The New Arab that Jordanians shared a commitment to national unity and social cohesion. He pointed to members of the Habashneh tribe, including Saed Mahmoud Ahmed Faleh al-Habashneh and Raji al-Aroud al-Habashneh, who were wounded alongside Christian victims outside the church church.

The scene embodied the shared fate of Jordanian communities and underscored the importance of safeguarding the country's security and stability.

Tribal figure Ismat al-Majali likewise called the attack a "painful tragedy" for Karak and Jordan as a whole, insisting that it would not damage the longstanding bonds between Muslims and Christians in the governorate.

Karak had historically been a unified community in which religious affiliation did not divide its residents, he said, pointing to the family and social ties reflected in shared celebrations, condolences and regular visits.

Some of the victims had worked in humanitarian professions, particularly medicine, and were accustomed to treating patients and helping those unable to afford healthcare, al-Majali added.

item.title: Erdogan sacks senior adviser amid Turkey-Azerbaijan hijab row
item.description: Erdogan dismisses senior adviser Oktay Saral amid a growing row with Azerbaijan over hijab restrictions, following reports that Baku demanded his removal.
item.content:encoded:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has dismissed his senior adviser Oktay Saral following his criticism of Azerbaijan over restrictions on hijabs in schools, as tensions between the two close allies continue to grow.

Turkish media reported on Sunday that Saral was removed from his position amid a diplomatic dispute between Ankara and Baku, with reports suggesting Azerbaijan had demanded his dismissal as a condition for restoring relations.

Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet first reported the dismissal, which was later confirmed by journalist Talat Atilla after he spoke directly to Saral.

In a post on X, Atilla quoted the former presidential adviser as acknowledging that his departure appeared to be linked to his criticism of Azerbaijan.

"Yes, we do not remain in positions of power forever. The president appointed me to this position, and I left on his instructions. I hold no grudge against anyone," Saral reportedly told the journalist.

Asked whether his dismissal was connected to his remarks about Azerbaijan, Saral replied: "Yes, it seems so."

He added that the interests of Turkey and the success of Erdogan remained his priorities.

Saral was among several prominent Turkish figures who criticised Azerbaijan over what amounted to an effective ban on hijabs in schools, which affected both female students and teachers.

The controversy sparked widespread criticism in Turkey and fuelled a growing dispute between the two countries, reflected in negative media coverage, although neither government has formally addressed the diplomatic tensions.

Azerbaijan subsequently banned 31 Turkish nationals from entering the country, including politicians and public figures who had criticised the restrictions.

Among those barred was Fatih Erbakan, leader of Turkey's Islamist New Welfare Party.

The dispute has presented an unusual challenge to relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan, which have traditionally maintained close political, military and cultural ties.

The two countries frequently describe their relationship through the slogan "one nation, two states", reflecting their shared linguistic, historical and ethnic connections.

Recently, despite the tensions, Erdogan held a telephone conversation with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, inviting him to attend an upcoming summit of Turkic states in Ankara later this month.

Turkish journalists and social media users have circulated claims that Azerbaijan set several conditions for normalising relations and securing Aliyev's participation in the summit, including Saral's dismissal.

However, these alleged demands have not been officially confirmed by either government.

Saral's removal has been seen as an indication that Erdogan is seeking to contain the dispute and prevent further damage to Ankara's strategic partnership with Baku.

item.title: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
item.description: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey agree to continue security talks after a Tehran meeting aimed at reducing tensions and preventing another regional war.
item.content:encoded:
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey agreed on Monday to continue security consultations and strengthen regional cooperation following high-level talks in Tehran, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

A joint statement issued after the first meeting between Iran and senior representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement confirmed that the four countries had agreed to maintain dialogue and consultations, particularly on regional peace, security and stability.

The meeting was hosted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.

The statement said the participants had agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation between their countries, but did not announce any specific security agreement or new joint mechanism.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also received the three visiting officials earlier on Monday, calling on regional countries to overcome their differences and work together to address common security threats.

Pezeshkian said historical and religious ties between Muslim countries should provide the foundation for closer cooperation, expressing hope that the meeting would help establish mechanisms for regional security based on shared interests.

He accused Israel, with US support, of committing widespread crimes in Gaza, Lebanon and other countries before extending its attacks to Iranian territory, including strikes that killed military commanders, scientists and civilians.

The Iranian president argued that military and economic pressure had failed to weaken Iran or force it to surrender, instead strengthening domestic solidarity and determination to defend the country's sovereignty.

He also urged regional governments to turn political understandings into practical measures rather than limiting cooperation to statements and agreements that remain unimplemented.

Pezeshkian called for stronger economic, scientific and cultural ties, as well as easier movement and exchanges between neighbouring countries.

He warned against attempts to inflame sectarian and political divisions, accusing Washington and Israel of seeking to weaken Muslim countries and deal with them individually.

Iran calls for regional security without foreign interference

Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the talks formed part of efforts to establish a regional security framework led by Middle Eastern countries rather than external powers.

Speaking to Iranian state television earlier on Monday, Bagheri Kani said the initiative had emerged during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when Iranian officials were informed of the three countries' intention to hold joint consultations.

He expressed hope that the discussions would contribute to regional stability and enable the participating countries to draw on one another's experience in addressing security threats.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the meeting would address developments in the occupied Palestinian territories and Lebanon, Israeli policies in the region and the consequences of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Baghaei described the talks as an opportunity to explore regional security arrangements based on the shared interests of neighbouring countries.

He said the initial consultations were intended to identify priorities and establish an agenda for further discussions.

Pezeshkian reiterates Iran's nuclear position

During his meeting with the visiting delegation, Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran was not seeking nuclear weapons and that its nuclear programme was intended for peaceful purposes.

He stressed Tehran's right to peaceful nuclear activities under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

The Iranian president also criticised Washington's contradictory approach of expressing willingness to negotiate while threatening military strikes against Iranian facilities.

He argued that such threats undermined confidence in diplomacy and made it more difficult to reach lasting agreements.

Pezeshkian said Iran would continue defending its rights and interests under international law and urged regional countries to coordinate their positions to prevent further military attacks.

Saudi Arabia backs efforts to reduce tensions

Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said the visit by Prince Khalid bin Salman and representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was part of continuing efforts to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.

The ministry said the discussions supported mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan aimed at preventing another confrontation between Iran and the United States.

Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Raed Krimly also said the talks reflected the role the agreement's member states hoped to play in promoting regional stability through dialogue.

The diplomatic efforts come amid intensifying tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement, which has continued launching attacks against the kingdom.

The possibility of renewed US-Israeli military action against Iran has also raised concerns that another confrontation could spread across the region.

Qatar steps up mediation amid fears of renewed war

Monday's meeting followed the arrival of a Qatari delegation in Tehran on Sunday evening as part of Doha's efforts to prevent further escalation between Washington and Tehran.

A source familiar with regional mediation efforts told The New Arab that the visit was intended to build on continuing diplomatic contacts aimed at preventing the conflict from worsening.

The source said Iran had already communicated its positions and demands clearly to mediators.

Baghaei confirmed that the Qatari delegation's visit formed part of ongoing regional consultations, covering both bilateral cooperation and Doha's mediation efforts.

He said the exchange of messages and diplomatic initiatives between regional countries was important amid the current tensions.

Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States throughout the conflict.

Iran warns against another military confrontation

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday against renewed US military action, saying Tehran would maintain its regional policies regardless of whether another war broke out.

Araghchi said that although there was growing discussion of another conflict, he was already considering what would happen after it ended.

He argued that previous military confrontations had demonstrated the consequences of attempting to resolve disputes with Iran through force.

The foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's position that lasting regional security could only be achieved through cooperation between neighbouring countries without foreign interference.

He stressed that Iran remained prepared to work with Gulf states and other regional countries to establish a more stable security environment.

item.title: Trump ramps up Islamophobic attacks on Abdul El-Sayed
item.description: Trump escalates Islamophobic attacks on Muslim Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, falsely linking him to extremism ahead of the US midterms.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has intensified his Islamophobic rhetoric against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, baselessly accusing him of extremism and suggesting his election would threaten American traditions, including Christmas.

Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, Trump repeatedly targeted El-Sayed's Muslim faith as he sought to rally support for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

The US president described El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and former public health official, as a "jihadist" and falsely linked him to the Muslim Brotherhood, while suggesting that the candidate posed a security threat simply because of his religious identity.

"He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate," Trump told supporters. "I want him to have a metal detector."

Trump also accused El-Sayed of seeking to introduce Islamic law in the United States, despite the candidate having made no such proposal.

"So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness," Trump said.

The attacks escalated when Trump warned supporters that an El-Sayed victory would lead to an influx of extremists and the erosion of American traditions.

"If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas," he said.

The remarks formed part of a broader campaign message portraying the Muslim candidate as a threat to national security, despite there being no evidence linking El-Sayed to extremist organisations.

El-Sayed, who was born in the United States, has pledged to uphold the US Constitution and has centred his campaign on economic issues, including healthcare affordability and the rising cost of living.

He has previously dismissed Trump's attacks on his religion as political distractions intended to divert attention from issues affecting American voters.

Islamophobia takes centre stage in Senate race

Trump's rhetoric was echoed by Rogers, who appeared alongside the president at Sunday's rally and repeated allegations linking his Democratic opponent to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Rogers also accused El-Sayed of receiving financial support from organisations associated with Hamas, Hezbollah and the Muslim Brotherhood, without presenting evidence to substantiate the claims.

"This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah," Rogers said.

El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

The accusations come as Republicans fight to retain control of the Senate, with Michigan emerging as a closely contested battleground.

El-Sayed and Rogers are competing for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

Republicans currently hold 53 of the Senate's 100 seats, making the outcome in Michigan important to both parties' efforts to control the chamber.

During the rally, some Trump supporters shouted "traitor" when El-Sayed's name was mentioned, underscoring the hostility surrounding the contest.

A pattern of anti-Muslim rhetoric

Trump's attacks on El-Sayed recall his earlier use of anti-Muslim rhetoric during his first presidential campaign.

In December 2015, Trump called for a sweeping ban on Muslims entering the United States, a proposal that became one of the defining controversies of his campaign.

After taking office in 2017, he introduced travel restrictions targeting several Muslim-majority countries, triggering widespread protests and legal challenges.

The latest remarks also follow weeks of attacks on El-Sayed's religious identity, including Trump's repeated misrepresentation of the candidate's name as "Mohammed".

The rally also came amid mounting economic pressure on Trump's administration over the continuing US-Israeli war against Iran.

Nearly eight months after the war began on 28 February, rising energy prices have added to concerns over the cost of living, particularly in Michigan.

Petrol prices in the state reached an average of $4.83 per gallon on Sunday, compared with $2.91 before the war.

Obama condemns attacks on El-Sayed's Muslim identity

Former US President Barack Obama has pushed back against the attacks on El-Sayed, drawing parallels between the Islamophobic rhetoric targeting the Democratic candidate and the racist conspiracy theories he faced during his own presidential campaigns.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday, a day before Trump's remarks, Obama accused Republicans of exploiting fear and religious prejudice to discredit their political opponents.

He warned that political attacks could use a candidate's name or faith to portray them as dangerous, untrustworthy or less American than their opponents.

"We have seen this movie before. I starred in it. I've got a long-form birth certificate to prove it," Obama said, referring to the racist "birther" conspiracy that falsely claimed he was not born in the United States.

"This stuff didn't work on me—not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."

Obama defended El-Sayed's American identity, pointing to his upbringing in Michigan, his family's ties to the automotive industry and his career as a doctor.

He also challenged Republican attempts to portray El-Sayed as a political extremist, arguing that his campaign priorities, including affordable healthcare and housing, reflected concerns shared by ordinary Americans.

In a pointed rejection of the religious divisions surrounding the Senate race, Obama highlighted the possibility of El-Sayed serving alongside Michigan's incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is Jewish.

"You've got a Muslim man. You've got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That's something, Michigan, you can be proud of," he said.

Obama also criticised the Trump administration's handling of the war against Iran, accusing Republicans of supporting a conflict that has driven up fuel prices for American households.

item.title: Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide
item.description: Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children’s agency said in September.
item.content:encoded:
Seven years after Lebanon's devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.

A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the "Chic Taouk," pricing it at around $13—nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut.

The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities.

Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing".

The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle.

Debate pulls focus away from urgent crises

Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality.

"So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month," Nader told Reuters.

Lebanon's Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it.

Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s occupation of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises.

Lebanon's 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook.

GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the global headline inflation rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July.

Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children's agency said in September.

'People can't keep up' 

The country’s middle class has "disappeared," Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years.

Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon's energy ministry.

For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400.

"Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up," said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. "We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by."

The years of economic instability, he said, have produced "a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in."

item.title: Jordan arrests three suspects over deadly Karak church attack
item.description: The attack on the Greek Orthodox Church in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.
item.content:encoded:
Jordanian security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox Church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.

The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects were arrested following a dawn shootout and that all three were wounded. No members of the security forces were injured in the dawn operation in Karak, south of Jordan's capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

The attack on the Greek Orthodox Church in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.

There was still no claim of responsibility, and no armed group has been accused of the attack.

Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya identified the three men as those responsible for the attack.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," he said in a phone interview with state TV Al-Mamlaka. "They put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there "are three individuals involved; they were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."

King Abdullah II directed authorities to respond with "an iron fist" against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

item.title: Saudi-led talks in Tehran seek to avert renewed Iran, US war
item.description: Iran is set to meet members of the Mecca Pact, as US and Israel focus domestically on their upcoming elections.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome,

Here are the updates:

  • Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei is expected to hold security talks with defence officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey in Tehran
     
  • US President Donald Trump said there will not be an imminent military attack on Iran, telling reporters yesterday, "There will not be a strike today."
     
  • War in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised Yemeni government against the Iran-backed Houthis continues with no end in sight
     
  • Israeli forces continue to attack Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria despite any so called ceasefires


And so we continue our live coverage of the day...

item.title: Brazil's Lula wins, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede
item.description: Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed.
item.content:encoded:
Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father's lead by refusing to concede defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential election.

Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for corruption charges and a coup attempt, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled.

"It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.

Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.

Still, Bolsonaro's refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say.

Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.

Lula defies expectations

Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. The result will disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.

Financial markets also expressed initial concerns at the shock result. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory, while analysts expected the Brazilian real to fall against the US dollar.

Lula had trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.

Speaking at a hotel in São Paulo late on Sunday, he took a conciliatory tone.

"I won’t speak of national unity, because that doesn’t always fit the reality of this country. No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," Lula said.

During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.

He will have to work alongside a Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast Brazil's legislature in favor of the president's enemies.

"The challenges are countless," said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper in São Paulo.

item.title: CENTCOM chief flies over Hormuz, says key routes clear of mines
item.description: Adm. Brad Cooper's visit coincided with what CENTCOM hailed as a 'milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude'.
item.content:encoded:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm. Brad Cooper flew over the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday aboard a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to conduct a review of operations.

The command said the visit coincided with with a "milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer".

The statement added that US CENTCOM had supported more than 3,000 commercial vessels to transit the Strait of Hormuz in the last six months.

"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said . "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."

The statement added that US forces had successfully cleared international shipping lanes in the strait of naval mines over recent months, alleging that the mines had been laid by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Cooper, it said, “met with service members who supported the mine-clearing mission and thanked them for their commitment and dedication.”

CENTCOM said that the main transit routes through the strait remain free of naval mines and that more than 95% of vessels sailing through it had “passed through safely” in recent months.

Meanwhile, Iran has tied the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to the fulfilment of its seven conditions, which include lifting the US naval blockade of its ports, easing sanctions on its oil exports, and halting hostilities on all fronts.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Washington must implement these conditions before the strait can be reopened, while reports have indicated that negotiations have stalled over disagreements concerning Iran’s demands.

item.title: Netanyahu lobbying Trump for more election support: report
item.description: Netanyahu's Likud Party has denied the Channel 2 report, which said that the Israeli leader is desperate for Trump to step up his endorsement.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked US President Donald Trump to provide additional support for his election campaign ahead of Israel's Knesset vote, Israel's Channel 2 reported on Sunday.

The channel cited a US source familiar with the details and a separate Israeli source who had been briefed on the matter, saying Netanyahu had stepped up his contacts with Trump in recent days in an effort to secure new statements supporting his continued tenure as prime minister.

The US source told the channel that Netanyahu had spoken with Trump twice over the previous three days and asked him to strengthen the endorsement he had expressed the previous week on the Truth Social platform. The source added that Netanyahu had personally proposed wording for additional statements of support that the US president could issue before the election.

The channel also quoted an Israeli source briefed on the communications as saying that Netanyahu had suggested Trump make phone calls to Israeli journalists to express his support for him, in an attempt to amplify the US president’s position during the final days of the election campaign.

According to the US source, White House officials view Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to secure additional support as a “sign of desperation” and an indication that the Israeli prime minister believes he is trailing in the electoral race.

The Likud Party, however, denied the report, insisting that Netanyahu had not asked Trump for any support, either in recent days or before Trump first announced his endorsement. The Israeli prime minister’s office declined to comment, while the White House had not immediately responded to the channel’s request for comment.

Regarding the White House’s calculations, the channel quoted a US official as saying that Trump’s support for Netanyahu could serve the US president’s interests regardless of the election outcome. If Netanyahu wins or remains prime minister in a caretaker government, Trump could claim credit for politically rescuing him and use that leverage to pressure him into making concessions.

If Netanyahu loses and his rivals succeed in forming a new government, its leaders would have an interest in maintaining good relations with Trump, potentially diminishing the significance of his support for their opponent. The channel noted that some of Trump’s advisers see an opportunity to advance his Middle East agenda through an Israeli government led by someone other than Netanyahu, despite the close relationship between the two men, which has also experienced periods of tension.

On October 18, US President Donald Trump announced his full support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Knesset elections, following weeks of hesitation about publicly taking a position. On Truth Social, Trump suggested that electing a different prime minister could affect cooperation between the United States and Israel, particularly on confronting Iran. He described Netanyahu as a key partner for Washington.

item.title: Israeli forces advance in Syria’s Quneitra; Daraa officer killed
item.description: Israeli troops resumed earthworks in Quneitra amid warnings of further escalation, while gunmen killed a Syrian security officer in neighbouring Daraa
item.content:encoded:
Israeli forces entered Syria’s southwestern Quneitra province on Sunday to resume excavation in the occupied territory, while a Syrian highway security officer was killed and two others wounded in a separate attack in neighbouring Daraa.

An Israeli force accompanied by a bulldozer and an excavator entered the al-Akar area, southwest of Hanout farm near Abu al-Ghaythar hill in rural Quneitra, according to the Horan Free League monitoring group.

The group said Israeli troops were continuing construction of a six-metre-high earth embankment, alongside excavation of a road within it measuring four metres deep and up to five metres wide.

The Golan Media Foundation said the work marked the resumption of the "Sufa 53" project after a pause of about six weeks. It warned that the embankment could extend into farmland and grazing areas, restricting residents’ access and threatening their livelihoods.

The foundation’s director, Fadi al-Asmai, told The New Arab that recent developments on the ground pointed towards an escalation ahead of the Israeli elections.

He linked the movements to two possible developments: an offensive by Suweida’s National Guard militia to retake the province’s western countryside, and Israeli efforts to establish a security belt beyond the Sufa 53 line.

Al-Asmai suggested that a National Guard offensive could seek to win support within the Druze community, which he linked to political calculations surrounding the Israeli elections. He said a wider Israeli security belt would leave local communities more vulnerable to pressure.

The developments come amid tensions in neighbouring Suweida, where Syrian government forces and Druze armed groups have faced off and Damascus has reinforced its positions along the province’s western front.

Israeli forces committed at least 88 violations across Quneitra, Daraa, Damascus and rural Damascus between 8 and 14 October, according to documentation by the Sijil Center.

Security officer killed in Daraa

Separately, a Syrian highway security officer was killed and two others wounded in an attack on a checkpoint in southern Daraa province early on Sunday.

Four gunmen riding two motorcycles attacked the checkpoint at Kharba village, on the road linking Bosra al-Sham and Daraa.

The officer killed was identified as Mohammed al-Miqdad, from Bosra al-Sham, and the wounded men as Omar al-Diyyat and Abdel Mawla al-Diyyat. Both were taken to Daraa National Hospital for treatment.

Checkpoint personnel captured two of the attackers, one of whom was wounded in the exchange of fire, while the other two fled, the network reported.

State news agency SANA said security forces had arrested attackers following a clash, without identifying their affiliations. Al-Miqdad’s funeral took place on Sunday with officials in attendance.

item.title: Dakar Rally 2027 will not be held in Saudi Arabia
item.description: The Dakar Rally is the latest sports event in Saudi Arabia to be disrupted amid attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis
item.content:encoded:
The 2027 edition of the Dakar Rally has been moved out of Saudi Arabia due to security concerns, organisers Amaury Sport Organisation said on Sunday.

The event, due to take place in January and which has been held in Saudi Arabia since 2020, would move to a different territory, with the location to be announced in the coming days, the ASO said in a statement.

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the Dakar Rally would take place in Africa, citing sources involved in the World Rally-Raid Championship.

"Amaury Sport Organisation and Saudi Motorsport Company have jointly decided that Dakar Saudi Arabia 2027, scheduled from 1 to 15 January, 2027, will not be held in the Kingdom, following recent developments in the region," the ASO said.

"This decision is exceptional and one-off."

The Dakar Rally is the latest sports event in Saudi Arabia to be disrupted amid attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

Golf's Asian Tour postponed the Saudi International indefinitely and cycling's Urban World Championships was cancelled earlier this month, while the tennis tournament Six Kings Slam was postponed to December.

The World Rally Championship also dropped Saudi Arabia from its calendar.

The ASO said that the Dakar Rally would return to Saudi Arabia for its landmark 50th edition in 2028.

item.title: Iran's Ghalibaf calls for cut in gas consumption as winter nears
item.description: During the most intense phase of the fighting, the US and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure, including natural gas refineries
item.content:encoded:
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10 percent, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.

While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by war with the United States and Israel that began in February.

During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the two countries struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.

Winter in Iran often sees temperatures drop below freezing, especially in the country's north.

"To get through the approaching winter, a nationwide effort is essential ... to reduce gas consumption by at least 10 percent," said Ghalibaf in a video carried by Iranian media.

"Anyone who saves gas, regardless of the amount, will immediately receive the corresponding proceeds in their bank account, allowing everyone to see the tangible impact of those savings on their household budget."

Earlier in October, First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref said the government anticipated a daily "gas shortfall of 100 million to 250 million cubic metres during the cold season because of the damage caused by the war," according to the official IRNA news agency.

He added that he hoped to restore the supply of around 100 million cubic metres by the start of winter.

An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.

Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossings without its authorisation.

In response, Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign on Iran aimed at strangling its already battered economy.

item.title: Israeli-founded app Waze 'mapped sensitive areas of Malaysia'
item.description: The head of Malaysia's cyber security agency has reiterated concerns over Waze's terms of service, which say it is governed by Israeli law and jurisdiction.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli-founded navigation app Waze has mapped out sensitive locations not registered on public maps in Malaysia, the head of the country's National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA) has said.

The app, which is now owned by Google's parent company, has come under scrutiny from the Malaysian government in recent weeks over concerns about data being accessible to the state of Israel. 

"We do not deny that the data is with them, including locations that may not have been placed on the map, sensitive areas," said NACSA head Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin in a Malay-language statement carried by local media.

"If you remember, in the early stages of Waze's development, if we wanted to go back to our hometown, the directions given were not correct. However, after years of use, we Malaysians have provided the information the application needs."

He also said Malaysia had around 6.9 million Waze users in 2019, making it the app’s fifth-largest national user base at the time.

"Because of the input provided by us, Waze has a huge amount of information on locations and mapping in Malaysia," Megat said.

Earlier this week, Malaysia's government barred civil servants from using the app while on official duties, citing the need to "protect government information and users' personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime".

Several Malaysian officials have raised concerns over Waze’s terms of service, which state that the agreement is governed by Israeli law and disputes fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of courts in Israel’s Tel Aviv district.

Waze has rejected Malaysia’s claims, saying allegations that the platform collected sensitive information or allowed any entity to exploit users’ personal data were entirely false. 

Earlier this month, Iraq banned the navigation app citing similar concerns.

Israel, which has no diplomatic ties with Malaysia, has previously been accused of conducting operations within Malaysia targeting Palestinians. This includes the 2018 assassination of engineer Fadi al-Batsh in Kuala Lumpur, and a failed attempt to kidnap a Palestinian computer engineer in 2022.

item.title: Algeria senate approves sending troops to Niger
item.description: Algeria's highly unusual measure to deploy troops outside its territory requires the approval of two-thirds of its parliament
item.content:encoded:
Algeria's upper house of parliament on Sunday approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger to "protect energy facilities", a senator speaking on condition of anonymity told AFP.

Any overseas deployment would mark a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.

The legislator said 148 senators in the 174-seat body voted in favour of the move. The parliament's lower house is set to vote on the proposal later in the day, likely to approve it as well.

The rare measure from Algeria comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.

Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.

The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.

"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher.

"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.

The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.

'Strong signal'

Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" - two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.

Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".

Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means - dialogue, international law, multilateral forums," Porter told AFP.

"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved toward more tangible means - actual physical presence."

"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."

Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.

"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on 3 October. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."

"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."

Algeria's highly unusual measure to deploy troops outside its territory requires the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.

Gifted warplanes

The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.

A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.

The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.

The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.

Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.

Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.

The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.

Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.

Niger has been run by General Tiani since a coup in July 2023 that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.

item.title: UK peers seek to bar Macklemore ahead of pro-Palestine concert
item.description: Fifty House of Lords members have moved to block the rapper’s entry before his Wembley show, targeting his fundraising for the Palestinian Youth Movement
item.content:encoded:
Fifty British peers have called on Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to bar US rapper Macklemore from entering the UK ahead of a pro-Palestine concert in London, citing his plans to raise money for the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM).

The letter, organised by Lord Walney, a former chairman of Labour Friends of Israel, urges Mahmood to revoke the artist’s electronic travel authorisation before his scheduled performance at the OVO Arena Wembley on 30 October. The peers argue that his presence would not be "conducive to the public good".

Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, has pledged proceeds from his "Free Palestine Tour" to PYM. Shows in London, Dublin and Paris reportedly sold out shortly after tickets went on sale.

The intervention by the unelected lords seeks to use immigration powers to prevent a fundraising performance by one of the most prominent musicians supporting the Palestinian cause. The peers’ objections centre on PYM’s political campaigning and statements about the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

"A foreign national proposes to come to Britain to raise money, from a British audience, for an organisation whose record of glorifying terrorism and of intimidating elected representatives should concern any government," the letter alleges, according to The Telegraph. PYM denies allegations that it celebrates terrorism or has links to terrorist organisations.

Several named signatories have established links to pro-Israel advocacy organisations. Alongside Walney, they include Lord Eric Pickles, whose parliamentary biography records his leadership of Conservative Friends of Israel in the Lords, and Lord David Pannick, a patron of UK Lawyers for Israel. The latter organisation campaigns against the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement and describes its mission as countering Israel’s "delegitimisation".

Other named signatories include former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster, former Conservative 1922 Committee chairman Graham Brady, former minister Zac Goldsmith, and historian Andrew Roberts.

Walney, a former government adviser on political violence, also criticised PYM’s "siege on Labour" campaign, which sets out tactics for protests targeting party offices and elected representatives. He characterised such demonstrations as an attempt to coerce MPs "through fear".

The dispute follows Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after he led pro-Palestinian chants at two New Jersey concerts in September. Several other supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity.

item.title: Netanyahu rebuked for crypto plan to bypass economic sanctions
item.description: The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.

In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.

Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.

"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."

Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.

The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.

"The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said.

Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers.

Plan draws criticism

On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.

"As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read.

"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest."

Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran."

Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

item.title: Iran's Araghchi commits to national positions amid war threats
item.description: Despite the April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States putting an end to the most intense fighting, plans have been drawn up for renewed US strikes
item.content:encoded:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on 28 February.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.

"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.

Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation - moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.

In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.

Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," said Araghchi.

"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

item.title: US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
item.description: Washington cites potential Houthi attacks and alleged Iranian plots against US officials, while reducing staffing at four embassies
item.content:encoded:
The United States has updated travel advisories for 13 countries across the Middle East, citing the risk of further attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and alleged Iranian efforts to target American officials in the region. The revisions come alongside reductions in staffing at several US embassies amid concerns over a wider escalation.

The advisories, dated 23 October, cover Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The updates revise the security warnings rather than raise the countries’ existing advisory levels.

"The possibility of regional effects, including the potential for flight disruptions, makes a region-wide advisory update important and prudent," a State Department official said in comments shared by PBS correspondent Nick Schifrin.

The department said the revisions reflected increased potential for armed attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials. Those claims come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition, including missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.

Advisories by country, and what they mean:

Eight countries are listed at Level 3, meaning Americans should reconsider travel, while five remain at Level 4 — "do not travel", the State Department’s highest warning. The country-specific warnings are:

  • Bahrain: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
  • Iran: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism, wrongful detention and other risks.
  • Iraq: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
  • Israel: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and unrest.
  • Jordan: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
  • Kuwait: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. Washington cites crime and other risks.
  • Lebanon: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
  • Oman: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
  • Qatar: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists “other” risks, rather than a separate terrorism, crime or unrest indicator.
  • Saudi Arabia: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks. The update follows Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, including the 10 October strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
  • Syria: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
  • United Arab Emirates: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
  • Yemen: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.

 

US authorities have urged Americans to monitor embassy alerts and airline operations, prepare for possible flight cancellations or airspace closures, and maintain emergency departure plans that do not depend on US government assistance. They also recommend enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program to receive security updates.

The warnings follow Friday’s reports that Washington was reducing staffing at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE. Axios first reported an intelligence memo alleging that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages"; the Associated Press subsequently obtained the memo and confirmed the staffing reductions with US officials.

Those four embassies remain open under restricted operations, and personnel are not subject to the same compulsory departure order issued on Wednesday for non-essential US staff and their families in Saudi Arabia.

US officials have denied that the staffing changes are linked to prospective new US or Israeli strikes on Iran. The advisory updates themselves do not establish that another military operation is imminent, although the move comes amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, with US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warning that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran before the upcoming US midterm elections.

item.title: Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
item.description: Saudi Arabia has faced a barrage of strikes from the group, involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, in recent weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Yemen's Houthis launched wide-ranging strikes across swathes of southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the kingdom announced the partial reopening of Riyadh's international airport despite repeated attacks by the group.

Alerts warning of possible attacks were activated across the kingdom's south throughout the day, with the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis saying at least 10 ballistic missiles were intercepted.

Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.

The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.

"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning - may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity.

Further north, Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.

However it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.

The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".

"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines - as well as staff and travellers - against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.

"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."

Attack warning

As the airport prepared to open, AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.

The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the capital area.

"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.

Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.

Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.

The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that - in the space of 24 hours - they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.

The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.

The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie".

The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.

The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.

The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

item.title: Israeli forces demolish Hebron homes, displace thousands
item.description: Homes and businesses razed in the occupied West Bank city as Israeli leaders threaten a wider offensive and announce election-day crossing closures
item.content:encoded:
Israeli forces have demolished Palestinian homes and businesses in Hebron and forcibly displaced around 2,500 people, according to Palestinian rights monitors, as a sweeping military crackdown entered its third day on Sunday with further raids and arrests across the southern occupied West Bank.

Bulldozers have torn through residential and commercial areas, with footage showing homes reduced to rubble across several blocks. The demolitions follow Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s threat to destroy the neighbourhood from which two Palestinian gunmen allegedly came after an attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday.

The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR), citing preliminary estimates from Hebron municipality, said approximately 500 families comprising around 2,500 people had been forced from their homes in an area spanning 350 dunums, or 35 hectares. Israeli forces have sealed the area and continued house searches, leaving displaced residents uncertain when they will be allowed to return.

The operation has targeted Ein Deir Baha and surrounding neighbourhoods, alongside homes, businesses and industrial facilities in Farsh al-Hawa.

PCHR documented the demolition of a three-storey house, a commercial facility selling car parts and the walls surrounding a tile and ceramics business’s yard. The organisation said the house was demolished despite its owner having obtained an interim court order following an earlier demolition notice.

Families were ordered out over military loudspeakers late on Friday, according to PCHR. Soldiers searched residents and vehicles at checkpoints as they fled, while some families sought shelter with relatives. One displaced resident told the organisation that soldiers had not said when his family could return.

The destruction has accompanied a broader closure of Hebron, with Israeli forces blocking entrances and restricting movement between the city and surrounding towns and villages. Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Ja’bari said that the city and several neighbouring villages were under a complete blockade.

Raids and arrests spread across Hebron

Israeli forces arrested 20 Palestinians in the latest wave of raids across Hebron, as the military expanded its incursions into the city and surrounding towns.

Overnight on Saturday, soldiers raided homes in most of Hebron’s neighbourhoods and "abused" their occupants, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa. Further raids were reported in the nearby towns of Dura, Yatta, as-Samu and Tarqumiya, where residents were forcibly taken from their homes.

On Sunday morning, Israeli forces fired tear gas during raids on al-Fawwar refugee camp and the town of Taffuh, both near Hebron.

Visiting Hebron on Friday with Defence Minister Israel Katz, Netanyahu pledged to destroy and transform the neighbourhood from which the attackers allegedly came.

"First of all, we will act to destroy this place, to change it completely," he said. "We are going to implement the successful and aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are essentially terrorist strongholds."

His remarks referred to military operations in northern West Bank refugee camps, including Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams, where tens of thousands of Palestinians were forcibly displaced in 2025. Katz explicitly linked the Hebron operation to those campaigns, saying: "The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron."

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a defence ministry role overseeing civilian affairs in the occupied West Bank, called for a military campaign "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon". He said he had personally ordered the immediate demolition of a row of structures near the site of Friday’s shooting, describing them as illegally built.

The escalation comes days before Israel’s general election on Tuesday, 27 October, when the military says it will close all land crossings with the occupied West Bank.

Restrictions announced on Saturday also bar Palestinian workers from entering Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Jordan Valley, with limited exceptions before a broader closure takes effect on election day. Tuesday’s restrictions will include industrial zones.

item.title: Trump campaigns in Michigan a day after Obama rallies Democrats
item.description: Despite repeatedly attacking El-Sayed from the Oval Office and at rallies across the country, the Republican president had not yet campaigned in Michigan.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections.

Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests, an open-seat race between former Republican Representative Mike Rogers and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that will help decide control of the chamber.

Despite repeatedly attacking El-Sayed from the Oval Office and at rallies across the country, the Republican president had not yet campaigned in Michigan this year.

If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist and repeatedly mocked his middle name, Mohamed, a common Muslim name.

El-Sayed has dismissed the accusation and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there's just too little of in Washington."

Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

"If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers said at a debate last week.

El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group and says it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States.

At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks on El-Sayed as an attempt by opponents to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are."

The former president compared it to his experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya.

"We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."

Trump's rally in Port Huron, part of an area of Michigan that he won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote, will also highlight the US-Canada tariff standoff.

The trade fight has affected the Detroit-based US auto industry, prompting Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US Senate and US House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

item.title: Lula, Bolsonaro Jr neck and neck as Brazil heads to runoff polls
item.description: Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days
item.content:encoded:
Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.

The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.

A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.

Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro's trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.

Lula has cast the Trump administration's proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labelling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.

On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters' minds.

Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offences.

Candidates are neck and neck

Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.

Historical precedent favours Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.

Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.

The senator's first-round win sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.

His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him or complicate governance for Lula.

item.title: Saudi downs 10 Houthi missiles as Riyadh airport reopens
item.description: Saudi Arabia continues to intercept Houthi ballistic missiles and drones fired at it as it seeks to reopen Riyadh's international airport.
item.content:encoded:
The New Arab's live blog is now closed. Here were the top stories:

  • Saudi Arabia has downed 10 Houthi ballistic missiles and a drone fired against the capital, Riyadh, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised Yemeni government. Explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to AFP.
  • King Khalid International Airport has reopened terminals one and two following Houthi missile strikes in early October that killed 17 people and wounded over 330. Terminals three and four, which were struck by the Houthis, are yet to reopen.
  • Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi is warning that any Israeli and US attack will not change the country's position, saying at an event in Tehran: "Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same."
